questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding random errors in epidemiological studies?
options: Sampling errors are examples of random errors
Random errors can cause bias in a study
Random errors cannot be completely eliminated
Systematic errors are different from random errors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Random errors can cause bias in a study

Random error refers to chance variation in measurements or sampling. It affects precision, not validity.

• Bias = systematic error, not random error
• Random error causes imprecision (results fluctuate around the true value)
• It does not consistently push results in one direction, so it does not cause bias

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old lady with submucosal fibroid was undergoing myomectomy. The surgeon was using 1.5% glycine as irrigating fluid for the cavity. During the surgery, the nurse informs that there is a 500ml deficit of the irrigating fluid. What is the next step to be done?
options: Change the fluid to normal saline
Continue the surgery with careful monitoring of fluid status
Give furosemide to the patient and continue surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continue the surgery with careful monitoring of fluid status

This is a young patient with no comorbidities, subjected to an electrolyte poor fluid for irrigation. Since the deficit is 500 mL, it is recommended to continue the surgery with careful monitoring of fluid status.

The criteria for terminating the procedure for

• Electrolyte deficient fluid is—- a deficit of 1 L
• Electrolyte rich fluid is—-- a deficit of 2.5 L

Glycine irrigation causes hyponatremia. The earliest symptom of hyponatremia is nausea which typically requires fluid absorption (deficit) of at least 1000 mL in women undergoing surgical procedures.

There are two types of distension medias

Electrolyte deficient fluid
Electrolyte rich media

• 1.5% glycine
• 3% sorbitol
• 5% mannitol

• Ringer lactate
• Normal saline

Instruments that can be used-

monopolar / bipolar instruments

Only bipolar instruments

Complications:

• Water intoxication
• Hyponatremia (except mannitol)

• Causes Shock & burns when used with monopolar instruments

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for esophageal varices ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoscopic variceal ligation

The first-line treatment for active variceal bleeding is endoscopic therapy, with endoscopic variceal ligation (banding) preferred.

Esophageal variceal bleeding is a complication of portal hypertension, most commonly due to cirrhosis. . After initial resuscitation and stabilization, endoscopic intervention is the mainstay of treatment for bleeding esophageal varices. The two most commonly used techniques are endoscopic band ligation (EVL), where rubber bands are applied to the base of the varix, and endoscopic sclerotherapy, which involves injecting a sclerosant into or around the varix.

Endoscopy is usually performed in a head-down position with good suction and visualization using a double-channel endoscope and power washers. Once the bleeding site is identified, treatment is focused only on the active varices. Both EVL and sclerotherapy effectively control bleeding, but EVL is preferred as it significantly reduces the risk of rebleeding, and a single session is often sufficient.

Initial management of variceal bleeding involves the following:

* Admission to the intensive care unit

* Placement of two large-bore peripheral cannulae

* Blood transfusion

* Correction of coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma, vitamin K, and tranexamic acid

* Terlipressin, a splanchnic vasoconstrictor

* Prophylactic antibiotic

* Endotracheal intubation for airway protection if bleeding is uncontrolled

* Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy

TIPSS or Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Stent Shunt placement involves the placement of a shunt to redirect blood flow and reduce portal pressure. It is very effective but requires analgesia, sedation, and fluoroscopic guidance. It is done if medical and endoscopic measures fail to control bleeding.
questions.learning: Endoscopic variceal ligation — The first-line treatment for active variceal bleeding is endoscopic therapy, with endoscopic variceal ligation (banding) preferred.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The single most important treatment and prognostic factor in alcohol-related liver disease is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cessation of alcohol consumption

Complete abstinence from alcohol is the single most important treatment and the strongest predictor of long-term survival in patients with alcohol-related liver disease (ALD), irrespective of the stage of liver disease. Abstinence halts ongoing hepatocyte injury, improves liver function, reduces portal hypertension, and decreases the risk of progression to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Why not the other options?

• A. N-acetylcysteine (NAC): Primarily used for acetaminophen toxicity; may be used as an adjunct in severe alcoholic hepatitis with corticosteroids but is not the cornerstone of treatment.
• C. Liver transplantation: Reserved for end-stage liver disease or selected patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis who fail medical therapy; it is not the first-line treatment.
• D. High-dose vitamin E: Has a role in selected patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), not alcohol-related liver disease.
questions.learning: Cessation of alcohol consumption Complete abstinence from alcohol is the single most important treatment and the strongest predictor of long-term survival in patients with alcohol-related liver disease (ALD), irrespective of the stage of liver disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with a history of obstructed labor and cesarean section presents with continuous dribbling of urine through vagina on day 7. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vesicovaginal fistula

The clinical scenario is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula.

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of genital fistula, which is an abnormal communication between the genital tract and the urinary tract.

Vesicovaginal fistulae occur mostly due to obstetric injuries such as prolonged labor, and instrumental or manipulative deliveries. Patients present with true incontinence characterized by constant dribbling of urine. The presence of urine in the undergarments is uncomfortable and leads to pruritus and excoriation of the genital area

In obstructed labour, ischemia necrosis occurs as a result of prolonged compression effect on the bladder base between the head and symphysis pubis leading to infection → sloughing → fistula. Thus, it takes around 3–5 days following delivery to produce a fistula.

Clinical assessment by the introduction of a speculum helps to determine the size, number, and location of the fistulae. A methylene blue test helps confirm the diagnosis and determine the type of repair operation.

Small fistulas due to difficult childbirth can heal spontaneously. Most established fistulas need to be repaired vaginally usually after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside.

The repair operation includes the Latzko procedure. The procedure involves denuding the vaginal epithelium around fistulous edges and approximating the raw surfaces. Another is the Chassar-Moir technique of widely separating the bladder and vagina and suturing them separately in two layers.

Post-operatively, continuous bladder drainage for 14 days along with antibiotics is recommended. Vaginal or speculum examination and intercourse are not advised for 3 months. Avoiding pregnancy for a year is also recommended. A cesarean section is usually done for future pregnancies.

Other options:

Option A: Vesicouterine fistula occurs during cesarean section or uterine rupture or placenta accreta. Patients complain of cyclical hematuria due to the trickling of menstrual blood into the bladder through this anomalous condition. But the urinary continence of the patient remains normal. This is also known as Youssef syndrome.

Option B: In urethrovaginal fistulae, the patient is continent and dry, but may dribble urine during micturition. This usually follows surgery for a paravaginal cyst or urethral diverticulum, or after a penetrating injury from a fall or criminal abortion. The fistulous opening is visible on speculum examination.

Option C: Ureterovaginal fistulae result from direct injury to the ureter during gynecologic surgery (Eg: Wertheim's procedure for Ca cervix). Urine dribbles from both vagina and urethra post-surgery. The three-swab test will not stain with methylene blue, but with urine.

Pearl PF1921: Methylene blue - 3 swab test

Procedure:

A catheter is introduced into the bladder through the urethra. The vaginal cavity is packed with three (or four) sterile cotton swabs.

50–100 mL of dilute methylene blue dye is injected into the bladder using a catheter.

Results:

* Upper swabs get wet and not stained - the leak is from the ureter: Ureterovaginal fistula

* Upper swabs get stained - the leak is from the bladder: Vesicovaginal fistula

* Lower swabs get stained - the leak is from the urethra: Urethrovaginal fistula.

Pearl PF2104: Difference between bladder fistula & ureteric fistula

Bladder fistula
Ureteric fistula

Etiology

Obstetric causes:

• Prolonged obstructed labor
• Instrumental deliveries
• Iatrogenic injury during caesarean section or sling operations

Surgical injury during:

• Abdominal hysterectomy
• Vaginal hysterectomy
• Wertheim's hysterectomy
• Laparoscopic surgeries
• Caesarean section

Clinical features

Dribbling of urine present from the vagina

The patient is unable to micturate

Dribbling of urine present from the vagina

The patient is able to micturate

Methylene blue 3-swab test
Middle swab stains with methylene blue
Uppermost swab stains with urine, but not with methylene blue

Intravenous pyelography
Normal
Hydronephrosis and hydroureter present on the affected side
questions.learning: Vesicovaginal fistula — The clinical scenario is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula. Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of genital fistula, which is an abnormal communication between the genital tract and the urinary tract.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding mechanisms of depolarisation, repolarisation, and hyperpolarisation in a skeletal muscle action potential?

1. Depolarisation due to influx of Na+ through voltage-gated channels
2. Depolarisation due to influx of Na+ through ligand-gated channels
3. Repolarisation due to efflux of K+ through a voltage-gated channel
4. Repolarisation due to efflux of K+ through a ligand-gated channel
5. Hyperpolarisation due to efflux of K+
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, and 5 are correct

Statements 1, 3, and 5 are correct.

Action potential in skeletal muscle:

• Motor-neuron discharge causes end-plate potential, which when reaches to a threshold value, causes action potential in the muscle fibre.
• The depolarization of the muscle fibre is caused by the activation of the voltage-gated sodium channels, which causes the influx of sodium.
• During repolarization, the sodium channels are closed, and voltage-gated potassium channels open, which causes efflux of potassium.
• The voltage-gated potassium channels close slowly. As a result, the potassium efflux continues, leading to hyperpolarization of the membrane.

The steps in an action potential in muscle fibre and the neuron, are similar except for the quantitative differences, such as:

• RMP is -80 to -90 mV in skeletal muscle fibres, while it is about -70mV in neurons.
• The duration of the action potential in skeletal muscle is 1 to 5 msec, which is about 5 times longer than in the largest myelinated nerve fibre.
• The velocity of conduction is about 3-5m/s, which is about 1/13th of the velocity of the nerve fibre.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presented with a lower abdominal mass and lower abdominal discomfort. On examination, the uterus appears uniformly enlarged and adnexa is free. MRI shows the presence of a myometrial cyst. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenomyosis

Multiparous women >40yrs, presenting with abdominal mass (free from adnexa) and myometrial cysts on MRI, point towards a diagnosis of adenomyosis.

Adenomyosis refers to the growth of the endometrium (both stromal and glandular components) directly into the myometrium. It is predominantly seen in multiparous women above the age of 40 years. Patients generally present with menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea, and sometimes dyspareunia. On examination, there is a gross symmetrical enlargement of the uterus corresponding to 12-14 weeks size. The uterus is soft and tender on bimanual examination.

Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS) reveals a salt-and-pepper appearance of the myometrium and the presence of sub-endometrial striations producing the Venetian blind appearance. MRI can also be done for diagnosis. However, the only definitive mode of diagnosis is histopathological examination.

Since most women affected by the condition are past the childbearing age, total hysterectomy is the treatment of choice. Localized excision/Levonorgestrel containing IUCD can be tried in younger women.

Other options:

Option A: Endometriosis refers to the presence of endometrial tissue outside the endometrial lining (uterus). They usually present as dysmenorrhea and lower dull abdominal pain. Vaginal examination reveals a tender fixed retroverted uterus. They can be managed medically (oral contraceptives, aromatase inhibitors, etc)  and surgically (if failed medical management). Abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is performed in advanced cases.

Option C: Leiomyoma (fibroid) is the commonest benign tumor arising from the uterus. They present as abnormal uterine bleeding, infertility, and abdominal pain. On bimanual examination, the uterus is enlarged and the mass moves with the cervix. It can be managed medically (mifepristone or newer progesterone) and surgically. A myomectomy is performed for large fibroids with significant symptoms.

Option D: Endometrial hyperplasia can be simple, glandular, or atypical. They are seen in women with estrogen excess states like obesity, PCOD, or on tamoxifen therapy. They usually present as abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB).
questions.learning: Adenomyosis Multiparous women >40yrs, presenting with abdominal mass (free from adnexa) and myometrial cysts on MRI, point towards a diagnosis of adenomyosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. An abdominal X-ray reveals marked dilatation of a particular segment of the intestine. Based on the radiographic image provided, which part of the bowel is predominantly involved?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays dilated loops of "small bowel" characterized by the "valvulae conniventes" (plicae circulares), which are mucosal folds that "extend across the entire diameter" of the lumen. This creates the classic "step-ladder pattern" seen in mechanical bowel obstruction. Valvulae conniventes are most prominent and numerous in the "jejunum" (Option A). The ileum (Option B) has fewer folds and appears smoother on imaging. The duodenum (Option C) is largely retroperitoneal and obstruction there usually presents with a "double bubble" sign. The transverse colon (Option D) is characterized by "haustra," which are thicker folds that "do not cross the entire width" of the lumen, giving the large bowel a distinct peripheral and sacculated appearance. Small bowel obstruction is a surgical emergency often caused by adhesions or hernias. Identifying the jejunal pattern on X-ray is vital for distinguishing high small bowel obstruction from large bowel pathology
questions.learning: The X-ray displays dilated loops of "small bowel" characterized by the "valvulae conniventes" (plicae circulares), which are mucosal folds that "extend across the entire diameter" of the lumen.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A young adolescent male is brought to the emergency department after suspected drug abuse at a party. He presents with excessive sweating, headache, anxiety, and marked restlessness. Examination shows tachycardia, hypertension, and dilated, fixed pupils. Based on these clinical features, which substance is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient is exhibiting a "sympathomimetic toxidrome," which is pathognomonic for Cocaine intoxication. Cocaine prevents the reuptake of catecholamines, leading to an overstimulation of the sympathetic nervous system. Key clinical markers provided include tachycardia, hypertension, and dilated (mydriatic) pupils. Symptoms of restlessness, sweating, and agitation further support this stimulant-induced state. Alcohol (Option A) is a CNS depressant and would typically cause sedation and slurred speech. Opioids (Option C) cause the opposite effect: "pinpoint" (miotic) pupils, bradycardia, and respiratory depression. Cannabis (Option D) usually causes conjunctival injection (red eyes), increased appetite, and a dream-like state, but not fixed dilated pupils and severe hypertension. Therefore, the combination of sympathetic arousal and dilated pupils definitively identifies Cocaine as the responsible substance
questions.learning: The patient is exhibiting a "sympathomimetic toxidrome," which is pathognomonic for Cocaine intoxication. Cocaine prevents the reuptake of catecholamines, leading to an overstimulation of the sympathetic nervous system.

• Gloves – protect hands.
• Gowns/ aprons – protect skin and clothing.
• Masks protect the mouth/nose and respirators protect the respiratory tract from airborne infectious agents.
• Goggles – protect eyes.
• Face shields – protect face, mouth, nose, and eyes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 30-year-old patient came with chest pain shortness of breath, and pedal edema. JVP showed rapid y descent. On auscultation, he had high-pitched diastolic sound. What is the diagnosis?

RHD-Rheumatic heart disease
options: Bicuspid aortic valve with Aortic regurgitation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic constrictive pericarditis

The combination of the given clinical history and JVP showing rapid y descent is highly suggestive of chronic constrictive pericarditis.

Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic type of pericarditis that results when there is healing of acute fibrinous pericarditis or absorption of chronic pericardial effusion. The most common cause in developing countries is tuberculosis, following viral pericarditis, cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, or as a manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis and SLE. The main abnormality that occurs in constrictive pericarditis is the inability of the ventricles to fill because of the rigid and thickened pericardium. The restriction is not uniform through the diastole as seen in tamponade. Ventricular filling is normal early in the diastole but stops suddenly when the elastic limit of the pericardium is reached.

Y-descent on the JVP curve is prominent in constrictive pericarditis because it represents the rapid early filling of the ventricles. A sudden stop in ventricular filling and subsequent rising pressure is seen as a square root sign in the JVP curve.

The patient presents with exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. There may be a paradoxical rise in venous pressure during inspiration (Kussmaul's sign) reflecting impaired right ventricular compliance. The ECG often shows low-voltage QRS complexes and diffuse flattening of T-waves. A chest radiograph may show pericardial calcification, especially in tuberculous pericarditis.

The waveforms seen in a normal JVP are:

• a wave corresponds to atrial contraction and occurs just after the P wave (on ECG) and just before the first heart sound.
• c wave represents the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during ventricular systole.
• x descent corresponds to the atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.
• v wave represents atrial filling during ventricular systole and peaks at the second heart sound.
• y descent represents passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after tricuspid valve opening.

A normal tracing of the jugular venous pulse is given below:

Other options:

Option B: Cardiac tamponade:  On JVP tracing, cardiac tamponade characteristically shows a prominent x-descent and absent y-descent.

The image of JVP in cardiac tamponade is given below:

Option C: Mid-diastolic murmur is seen in mitral stenosis (MS). It occurs most commonly in rheumatic fever. A loud S1 (first heart sound) with an opening snap following S2 (second heart sound) is heard. S2 is followed by a low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur, which is best heard at the apex with the patient in a lateral recumbent position.

Option D: Aortic regurgitation can occur due to bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic fever, degeneration of the valve, etc. Auscultation will have a high-pitched, blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur, heard best in the third intercostal space along the left sternal border. Mid systolic ejection murmur can also be heard.
questions.learning: Chronic constrictive pericarditis — The combination of the given clinical history and JVP showing rapid y descent is highly suggestive of chronic constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old nulligravida presents with third- degree uterine prolapse but has no cystocele or rectocele. What is the most appropriate management for her condition?
questions.explanation: For a young, nulligravida woman with significant uterine prolapse, the primary goal of management is to preserve the uterus and future fertility. Abdominal sling surgery (such as Shirodkar’s or Purandare’s abdominal cervicopexy) is the most appropriate choice. This procedure uses a synthetic or fascial sling to anchor the cervix to the anterior abdominal wall or sacrum, providing durable support without compromising the vaginal canal or uterine function. LeFort colpocleisis (Option A) involves closing the vagina and is reserved for elderly, sexually inactive women. The Fothergill operation (Option B) involves cervical amputation, which can cause infertility and cervical incompetence, making it less ideal for a nulligravida. While Shirodkar described a vaginal approach for cervical incompetence, the "abdominal sling" specifically refers to the corrective procedure for nulligravida prolapse. This approach addresses the underlying ligamentous laxity while maintaining the potential for childbearing
questions.learning: For a young, nulligravida woman with significant uterine prolapse, the primary goal of management is to preserve the uterus and future fertility. Abdominal sling surgery (such as Shirodkar’s or Purandare’s abdominal cervicopexy) is the most appropriate choice.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a Delhi-based study, 100 individuals who regularly exercised were followed for one year, after which researchers assessed how many developed coronary heart disease. What type of study design does this represent?
questions.explanation: This is a cohort study because it identifies a group of people based on an exposure (exercise) and follows them over time to observe the development of an outcome (coronary heart disease). Cohort studies are observational, longitudinal designs ideal for establishing temporal relationships and calculating incidence. Case-Control studies (Option A) start with the outcome (disease) and look back at past exposures. While this is a "Prospective study" (Option B), "cohort study" is the more specific and accurate epidemiological classification. Cross-Sectional studies (Option C) measure exposure and outcome simultaneously at a single point in time, unlike the one-year follow-up described here. By tracking the participants prospectively, researchers can directly measure the risk associated with the exercise habits of the Delhi cohort
questions.learning: This is a cohort study because it identifies a group of people based on an exposure (exercise) and follows them over time to observe the development of an outcome (coronary heart disease).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby presented with abdominal pain. On examination, a mass is palpated in the right lumbar region. A barium enema is done, and the image is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intussusception

Intussusception is a condition where a portion of the bowel is telescoped into an adjacent segment, with the apex of the intussusceptum being more prone to ischemia which leads to gangrene. The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic. It is commonly seen in infants during the weaning period following the introduction of new food, vaccination, or upper respiratory tract infection. The currently approved rotavirus vaccines are associated with very minimal risk of intussusception. An area of enlarged submucosal Peyer's patch acts as a lead point for intussusception.
questions.learning: Intussusception Intussusception is a condition where a portion of the bowel is telescoped into an adjacent segment, with the apex of the intussusceptum being more prone to ischemia which leads to gangrene.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Out of the four given statements, which is true about coughing?

1. Forceful Expiration against closed glottis
2. Slow Expiration against open glottis
3. Begins with a shallow inspiration
4. Remove harmful substances
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. i, iv

Coughing is a type of forceful expiration. During forceful expiration, when pressure builds up, the glottis opens and then the air comes out. The cough reflex is a protective mechanism of the larynx to expel irritants and keep the airway clear.

Coughing begins with a deep inspiration followed by a forced expiration against a closed glottis. This increases the intrapleural pressure to 100 mm Hg or more. The glottis is then suddenly opened, producing an explosive outflow of air at velocities up to 965 km (600 ml) per hour.

Both chemical and mechanical stimuli can initiate the cough reflex. Chemical or mechanical irritation of the respiratory mucosa stimulates the afferent internal laryngeal nerve, which is the branch of the superior laryngeal nerve of the vagus nerve. These sensory fibres synapse in the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla oblongata. Complex neural networks here generate the conscious 'urge to cough' while also sending efferent signals to the various muscles involved in generating an effective cough which include the adductors of the vocal cord, the diaphragm, the external intercostals and the muscles of the anterior abdominal wall.

Other Options

Statement ii and iii: It is the forceful expiration, not just a normal expiration or deep inspiration which opens the glottis.
questions.learning: i, iv Coughing is a type of forceful expiration. During forceful expiration, when pressure builds up, the glottis opens and then the air comes out.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In the image shown, identify the function of the marked structure on the endotracheal tube.
options: Prevention of air leakage and aspiration
Suctioning of lower respiratory tract secretions
questions.explanation: The marked structure on the endotracheal tube (ET) is the inflatable cuff. Its primary function is to create a physical seal between the tube and the tracheal wall once it is inflated with air. This seal serves two critical purposes: it ensures that positive pressure ventilation is efficient by preventing air leakage around the tube, and it protects the airway from aspiration by blocking secretions or vomit from entering the lower respiratory tract. Monitoring airway pressure (Option B) is done through the ventilator circuit, and suctioning secretions (Option D) requires a separate suction catheter. Visualization of the vocal cords (Option A) is achieved using a laryngoscope during the initial intubation. Proper cuff pressure management (typically 20–30 cm H₂O) is essential to prevent tracheal mucosal ischemia
questions.learning: The marked structure on the endotracheal tube (ET) is the inflatable cuff. Its primary function is to create a physical seal between the tube and the tracheal wall once it is inflated with air.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the followings are seen in GDM except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malformations

Malformations are not associated with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Malformations occur due to the disruption of organogenesis, usually occurring in the first trimester. The abnormal glycemic status in GDM manifests only in the second trimester.

Overt diabetes (pregestational diabetes) is associated with higher rates of malformations compared to the general population. Neural tube defects (encephalocele, meningomyelocele, anencephaly), transposition of great vessels (TGA), ventricular septal defect (VSD), atrial septal defect (ASD), hypoplastic left heart, aortic stenosis and coarctation of the aorta are commonly seen.

Caudal regression syndrome is rare, but a specific anomaly seen in infants of diabetic mothers. Small left colon syndrome is a rare anomaly that develops in the second and third trimesters.

Other options:

Option B:  In GDM, increased blood glucose in the mother leads to fetal hyperglycemia. This can cause polyhydramnios due to increased fetal urine production.

Option C: Fetal hyperinsulinemia causes increased hepatic glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, accelerated lipogenesis, and augmented protein synthesis resulting in macrosomia

Option D: Fetal hyperglycemia in GDM triggers fetal hyperinsulinemia, resulting in neonatal hypoglycemia
questions.learning: Malformations Malformations are not associated with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Malformations occur due to the disruption of organogenesis, usually occurring in the first trimester.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman who has had 2 children through normal delivery presents with a dull aching pain over the abdomen, with irregular menses. Per vaginal examination revealed a mass felt through the posterior fornix. A USG showed a clear ovarian cyst of size 5 x 5 cm. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Follow up after 6 weeks

A clear ovarian cyst with size less than 7 cm in a woman of reproductive age group is most likely to be a functional ovarian cyst. The next best step in the management of this case is to follow up after 6–12 weeks and perform a repeat USG.

A simple unilocular cyst under 7 cm is often a functional cyst and should be observed. Most functional cysts resolve spontaneously within 4-6 months. A follow-up ultrasound will detect any persistent cyst, which may necessitate laparoscopic evaluation. To expedite resolution or to treat symptoms like pain and irregular menses, oral combined pills may be prescribed for 3-4 months in women of reproductive age.

Features of a functional cyst:

• Related to temporary hormonal variation
• Benign and rarely become complicated
• Usually 6–8 cm in diameter
• Usually asymptomatic
• Unilocular
• Contains clear fluid, unless hemorrhage occurs
• Lining epithelium corresponds to the functional epithelium of the unit from which they arise

Management of functional cysts in women of child-bearing age group is summarized in the flowchart attached below.

Other options:

Option A: Tumour markers such as CA-125 and CEA are particulary useful in postmenopausal women suspected of having a malignant epithelial cell tumor.

Option C: If the cyst does not resolve spontaneoulsy it can be removed laparoscopically or by laparotomy.

Option D: Imaging modalities such as CT scan and MRI help to detect ovarian neoplasms and assist in staging of ovarian cancers.
questions.learning: Follow up after 6 weeks — A clear ovarian cyst with size less than 7 cm in a woman of reproductive age group is most likely to be a functional ovarian cyst.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What type of collagen is predominantly found in cartilage?
questions.explanation: Cartilage is a specialized connective tissue, and its extracellular matrix composition varies by type. However, hyaline cartilage, which is the most abundant type in the body, predominantly contains Type 2 collagen fibers. This specific collagen provides the structural framework necessary to resist compressive forces within joints, the nose, and the respiratory tract. In contrast, Type 1 collagen is the primary component of bone, skin, and tendons, offering high tensile strength. Type 10 collagen is associated specifically with hypertrophic chondrocytes during endochondral ossification, marking the transition from cartilage to bone during growth. Type 7 collagen forms anchoring fibrils that secure the epidermis to the dermis at the basement membrane zone. Understanding these distribution patterns is fundamental for histology and pathology, as genetic defects in Type 2 collagen synthesis lead to skeletal dysplasias and early-onset osteoarthritis. Therefore, while various minor collagens exist in the matrix, Type 2 remains the defining structural protein of the cartilaginous framework
questions.learning: Cartilage is a specialized connective tissue, and its extracellular matrix composition varies by type. However, hyaline cartilage, which is the most abundant type in the body, predominantly contains Type 2 collagen fibers.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following conditions can cause euvolaemic hyponatraemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypothyroidism

Euvolemic hyponatremia is characterized by low serum sodium with normal extracellular fluid volume, without clinical evidence of edema or dehydration. It is most commonly caused by syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), but hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency are important endocrine causes that must always be excluded.

• Hypothyroidism can cause euvolemic hyponatremia by:

• Decreasing cardiac output and GFR
• Increasing ADH secretion
• Reducing free water clearance

• The resulting water retention dilutes serum sodium without causing significant edema.

Why not the other options?

• A. Adrenocortical failure: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) usually causes hypovolemic hyponatremia due to aldosterone deficiency causing sodium loss. (Secondary adrenal insufficiency may present with euvolemic hyponatremia.)
• C. Nephrotic syndrome: Causes hypervolemic hyponatremia due to edema and water retention.
• D. Burns: Cause hypovolemic hyponatremia because of fluid and sodium losses.
questions.learning: Hypothyroidism Euvolemic hyponatremia is characterized by low serum sodium with normal extracellular fluid volume, without clinical evidence of edema or dehydration.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient is evaluated for primary infertility. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. A testicular biopsy is done and the image is shown below. The shown finding is consistent with
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sertoli cell only syndrome

The given clinical scenario and the biopsy findings are consistent with the diagnosis of Sertoli cell-only syndrome.

Patients with Sertoli cell-only syndrome typically present between the age of 20 to 40 years with complaints of primary infertility. Diagnosis can be made on testicular biopsy findings. The histopathology of the biopsy specimen typically shows the tubules which are populated by only Sertoli cells, with a thickening of the tubular basement membrane and absence of germ cells which is characteristic of Sertoli cell-only syndrome.

The below image shows normal histology of testis:

The Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules and have receptors for follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and testosterone. There are four sperms per Sertoli cell. It produces a testosterone-binding protein that maintains a high level of testosterone within the testis which is necessary for continuous spermatogenesis.

In Sertoli cell-only syndrome, only Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules of the testis, and the patients have very low or absent spermatogenesis. There is no feedback inhibition due to absent spermatozoa, which results in increased FSH levels, but testosterone levels and LH levels remain unaffected since Leydig cells are not affected.

Physical examination is normal as this condition presents with infertility without sexual abnormality. Most cases are usually multifactorial and idiopathic. Patients can still reproduce with assisted reproductive technology.

Other options:
Option B: Testicular atrophy may be characterized by marked hyalinization and thickening of the basement membrane of the spermatic tubules with the absence of spermatids or germ cells. It may occur due to cryptorchidism, atherosclerotic changes of the supplying vessels, cachexia, and end stage of inflammatory orchitis.

Option C: Sex cord-stromal cells are benign and include Sertoli cell tumors and Leydig cell tumors. Leydig cells are characterized by the presence of crystalloids of Reinke.

Option D: Orchitis is characterized by the inflammatory infiltration of neutrophils and may progress to the formation of a frank abscess. The end-stage may lead to atrophic changes.
questions.learning: Sertoli cell only syndrome — The given clinical scenario and the biopsy findings are consistent with the diagnosis of Sertoli cell-only syndrome. Patients with Sertoli cell-only syndrome typically present between the age of 20 to 40 years with complaints…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following eggs to the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A

The correct match is 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A.

The Hymenolepis nana egg is roughly spherical or ovoid. It has a thin colorless outer membrane and inner embryophore that encloses the hexacanth oncosphere. They are non bile-stained. The eggs float in saturated salt solution.

The image below shows an egg of H. nana.

Ascaris lumbricoides (Roundworm) are round or oval in shape. They are always bile-stained which gives them golden-brown color. They have a thick smooth translucent shell with:

• an outer coarsely mammillated albuminous coat
• a thick transparent middle layer, and
• an inner lipoidal vitelline membrane.

The eggs float in a saturated salt solution. The image below shows the egg of A. lumbricoides.

The unfertilized eggs of Ascaris are elliptical, narrower, and contain a small atrophied ovum. It has a mass of disorganized refractile granules. The shell is thinner and the egg does not float in a saturated salt solution.

The egg of Ancylostoma duodenale or hookworm is oval or elliptical. They are colorless, not bile-stained. The eggs are surrounded by a thin transparent hyaline shell membrane. It contains a segmented ovum, usually with 4-8 blastomeres. There is a clear space between the ovum and the shell. It floats in saturated salt solution. The image below shows the egg of A. duodenale.

The eggs of Taenia solium and Taenia saginata are indistinguishable. The egg is spherical. The inner embryophore is radially striated and is yellow-brown due to bile staining. A fully-developed embryo (oncosphere) with three pairs of hooklets (hexacanth embryo) is present in the center.

The eggs of T. saginata are infective only to cattle and not to humans, whereas the eggs of T. solium are infective to pigs and humans. The eggs do not float in a saturated salt solution. The image below shows the egg of Taenia.
questions.learning: 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A The correct match is 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A. The Hymenolepis nana egg is roughly spherical or ovoid.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with diabetes presents with severe ear pain and persistent ear discharge that does not improve with antibiotics. Otoscopic examination shows granulation tissue in the external auditory canal, along with facial nerve palsy. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Malignant otitis externa (MOE), also known as necrotizing otitis externa, is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external auditory canal and skull base. It typically occurs in elderly diabetic patients or immunocompromised individuals. The causative organism is almost always Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Key clinical features—intense ear pain out of proportion to clinical signs, persistent foul-smelling otorrhea, and the presence of granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction—are classic. Facial nerve paralysis indicates that the infection has spread to the skull base, causing osteomyelitis. Option A (Otomycosis) involves fungal growth and itching rather than deep pain. Option B (Serous otitis media) presents with hearing loss and fluid behind the drum, not external canal findings. Option D is an allergic/inflammatory condition with itching and redness. MOE requires urgent intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics and meticulous diabetic control to prevent further cranial nerve involvement or intracranial complications
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa (MOE), also known as necrotizing otitis externa, is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external auditory canal and skull base.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome, results from mutations in which category of genes?
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2. A failure in these proteins prevents the correction of base-pairing errors during replication, leading to microsatellite instability (MSI) and a high risk of colorectal and extracolonic cancers. The APC gene (Option A) is a tumor suppressor mutated in Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP). The MYC proto-oncogene (Option C) is involved in Burkitt lymphoma. TERT1 mutations (Option D) affect telomerase activity and are linked to other familial cancers but not HNPCC. Therefore, the hallmark of Lynch syndrome is a defect in the MMR system, resulting in the characteristic MSI observed in these tumors

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Three female children graphs were plotted on an IAP growth chart, which of them signals growth failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only 3

Out of the growth curves (weight-for-age), only growth curve 3 shows growth failure. This pattern shows fluctuation in growth percentiles, which might indicate a history of growth issues or inconsistent growth. The drop to below -2SD is significant and suggests growth failure as it indicates the child is significantly below the normal range.

The nutritional status of a child is assessed in terms of anthropometry:

The World Health Organization (WHO) has established international standards for normal child growth from birth to 5 years of age. The normalization of the anthropometric measures is done in terms of z-scores (standard deviation scores). The anthropometric indicators are marked in a growth chart which is compared with a reference curve.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

• Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition. It is also mentioned as wasting.
• High weight-for-height indicates overweight.
• Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.
• Low weight-for-age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

The below image shows the WHO growth chart for girls (6 months-2years). Boys have similar charting in blue color.
questions.learning: Only 3 Out of the growth curves (weight-for-age), only growth curve 3 shows growth failure. This pattern shows fluctuation in growth percentiles, which might indicate a history of growth issues or inconsistent growth.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with the complaint of blurring of vision. On examination, you note that there are aqueous flares with numerous keratic precipitates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iridocyclitis

The features of aqueous flares and keratic precipitates indicate a diagnosis of Fuch's heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHI).

Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a chronic, non-granulomatous anterior uveitis, that is usually unilateral. It is normally seen in middle-aged people who may complain of symptoms such as blurring of vision and persistent floaters.

Heterochromia iridis (the affected eye is hypochromic/hyperchromic) is noted in FHI. Rubeosis iridis and posterior subcapsular cataract are also fairly common findings.

On examination, stellate keratic precipitates known as endothelial dusting are seen. Tiny crystals (Russell bodies) and iris nodules (Koeppe nodules)  may also be found on the iris surface. Iris atrophy which appears as a smooth-looking iris can also be seen.

Long-term monitoring is indicated to detect glaucoma and other complications.

The below image shows an example of heterochromia iridis (the left eye is hypochromic when compared to the right eye).

Other options:

(a) Intermediate uveitis: Intermediate uveitis primarily involves inflammation in the vitreous humor, which is the jelly-like substance in the middle of the eye. It is less likely to present with aqueous flares and keratic precipitates, making it an incorrect option.

(c) Posterior uveitis: Posterior uveitis involves inflammation in the posterior segment of the eye, including the choroid and retina. Aqueous flares and keratic precipitates are less likely to be observed in posterior uveitis, making it an incorrect option.

(d) Toxoplasma uveitis: Toxoplasma uveitis is a specific type of uveitis caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. While it may involve the anterior or posterior segment of the eye, the presence of aqueous flares and keratic precipitates is not specific to Toxoplasma uveitis alone.

questions.learning: Iridocyclitis — The features of aqueous flares and keratic precipitates indicate a diagnosis of Fuch's heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHI). Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a chronic, non-granulomatous anterior uveitis, that is usually unilateral.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the outpatient department with a deformity visible in the accompanying image. Based on this clinical presentation, what would be the appropriate line of management for this child?
questions.explanation: The image displays Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV), also known as clubfoot. The gold standard for initial management of CTEV, especially in an infant as young as 6 months old, is the Ponseti method. This involves gentle serial manipulation and casting (Option A) started ideally within the first few weeks of life to progressively correct the four components of the deformity: cavus, adductus, varus, and equinus. If the child is already 6 months old and has not been treated, Ponseti casting remains the primary first-line therapy. Surgical options like posteromedial soft tissue release (Option B) are now reserved for cases that fail conservative casting. Evan’s procedure (Option D) is used for children between 4 and 8 years of age. Triple arthrodesis (Option C) is a radical corrective surgery for skeletal maturity, typically performed after 10–12 years of age. Therefore, conservative manipulation and casting is the definitive starting point
questions.learning: The image displays Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV), also known as clubfoot. The gold standard for initial management of CTEV, especially in an infant as young as 6 months old, is the Ponseti method.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which condition is characterized by hypocalcemia, thymic hypoplasia, cardiac abnormalities, and a deletion on chromosome 22q11.2?
questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome is a microdeletion syndrome caused by the absence of a portion of chromosome 22q11.2. It is characterized by the classic mnemonic CATCH-22: Cardiac abnormalities (often conotruncal defects like Tetralogy of Fallot), Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia (leading to T-cell deficiency), Cleft palate, and Hypocalcemia (due to parathyroid underdevelopment). Option A (Williams syndrome) involves a deletion on chromosome 7 and is associated with "elfin" facies and hypercalcemia. Option B (Pitt syndrome) and Option D (Cri-du-chat syndrome, caused by a 5p deletion) present with different constellations of intellectual disability and structural anomalies. Because the question explicitly links the 22q11.2 deletion with hypocalcemia and thymic underdevelopment, DiGeorge syndrome is the definitive diagnosis. Clinically, these patients require careful monitoring of calcium levels and immune function, alongside surgical management of cardiac defects. The phenotypic spectrum can vary significantly between affected individuals

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with a stab wound over the right chest. The supine X-ray image of the patient is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right hemothorax

The history of stab injury to the right chest and the X-ray showing opacity of the right hemithorax, with a slight tracheal deviation towards the opposite side, indicates a diagnosis of right hemothorax.

In a plain chest radiograph, it's difficult to differentiate an acute hemothorax from other collections of pleural fluid as they are indistinguishable. As blood clots, it often leads to localisation, occasionally forming a fibrin body. Pleural thickening and calcification are acknowledged as potential consequences.

The following are the findings commonly seen in a case of hemothorax:

• Blunting of Costophrenic Angle: Hemothorax results in the accumulation of blood in the pleural cavity, causing the lung to collapse partially. This can lead to the blunting or obliteration of the costophrenic angle on the affected side.
• Increased Opacity: The presence of blood in the pleural space leads to increased opacity or density in the affected hemithorax. This can manifest as a homogenous shadowing that obscures the lung markings.
• Mediastinal Shift: Depending on the volume of blood in the pleural cavity, there may be a mediastinal shift towards the opposite side. However, in mild to moderate hemothorax, this may not be readily apparent on supine X-rays.
• Air-Fluid Level: In cases where there is concurrent pneumothorax (air in the pleural cavity), an air-fluid level may be visible, with the blood layering dependently and the air layer superiorly.
• Unilateral Findings: The abnormalities will typically be limited to one side of the chest, corresponding to the side of the hemothorax.

In cases of suspected hemothorax, a lateral decubitus or chest X-ray in erect position may be more sensitive for detection. Additionally, other imaging modalities such as ultrasound or computed tomography (CT) scans can provide more detailed information about the presence and extent of a hemothorax.

Other options:

The following image is characteristic of a pneumothorax (left-sided) with radiolucency over the left lung, lung collapse, and mediastinal shift on x-ray.

The given radiograph is a case of diaphragmatic hernia that shows elevation of the left hemidiaphragmatic line along with the bowel loops and stomach seen in the pleural cavity.

The following is an image of a right-sided pulmonary contusion post-blunt chest trauma. Note the increased opacity just below the horizontal fissure.
questions.learning: Right hemothorax — The history of stab injury to the right chest and the X-ray showing opacity of the right hemithorax, with a slight tracheal deviation towards the opposite side, indicates a diagnosis of right hemothorax.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The image shows a histological section of the thyroid gland. Which substance is secreted by the cell labeled X in the image?
questions.explanation: The provided histological image shows thyroid follicles lined by follicular cells, with a distinct cluster of parafollicular cells (also known as C-cells) labeled as 'X'. These C-cells are responsible for the synthesis and secretion of calcitonin, a peptide hormone that plays a role in calcium homeostasis by inhibiting osteoclast activity and lowering blood calcium levels. Thyroxine (T4) (Option A) is produced by the follicular cells that surround the colloid. Parathormone (Option C) is produced by the parathyroid glands, which are distinct organs usually located posterior to the thyroid. Serotonin (Option D) is primarily produced by enterochromaffin cells in the gut or neurons in the brain. Because the cell labeled 'X' is clearly situated between the follicles (parafollicularly), its hormone product is definitively calcitonin. Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from these specific C-cells
questions.learning: The provided histological image shows thyroid follicles lined by follicular cells, with a distinct cluster of parafollicular cells (also known as C-cells) labeled as 'X'.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following hormones have an inhibitory effect on hormone-sensitive lipase?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leptin

Leptin and insulin inhibit hormone-sensitive lipase, whereas the other hormones given in the options stimulate it.

Leptin is a hormone produced by adipose tissue in proportion to the amount of body fat. It acts as a long-term regulator of energy balance. It functions by signalling the brain, specifically the hypothalamus, to regulate appetite and energy expenditure. It suppresses appetite and increases energy expenditure to maintain body weight within a certain range.

In addition to its central effects, leptin also has peripheral effects on adipose tissue. Leptin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) activity, which reduces the breakdown of triglycerides into fatty acids in adipocytes. This inhibition of HSL leads to reduced release of free fatty acids into the bloodstream, contributing to the overall regulation of energy storage and utilization.

Other options:

Option A: Glucagon is produced by the pancreas, glucagon stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) to break down triglycerides into free fatty acids, which can be released into the bloodstream for energy production.

Option B: Epinephrine is produced by the adrenal glands, and epinephrine is released during the body's stress response. It activates HSL, promoting the breakdown of stored fat to provide energy in fight-or-flight situations.

Option C: ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone) is produced by the pituitary gland, ACTH indirectly stimulates HSL activity. ACTH signals the adrenal glands to release cortisol, which can lead to the mobilization of fatty acids from adipose tissue.
questions.learning: Leptin Leptin and insulin inhibit hormone-sensitive lipase, whereas the other hormones given in the options stimulate it. Leptin is a hormone produced by adipose tissue in proportion to the amount of body fat.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following hormones use receptor tyrosine kinase signalling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Insulin

Insulin uses the receptor tyrosine kinase signalling to exert its functions.

Other hormones acting in a similar fashion includes

• Growth hormone
• Growth factors like VEGF, PDGF, FGF, NGF
• Prolactin
• Leptin
questions.learning: Insulin Insulin uses the receptor tyrosine kinase signalling to exert its functions. Other hormones acting in a similar fashion includes • Growth hormone • Growth factors like VEGF, PDGF, FGF, NGF • Prolactin • Leptin

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following tests cannot be used to assess nasal mucociliary clearance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Electron microscopy

Among the given options, electron microscopy will be the least useful in assessing nasal mucociliary clearance. Other tests mentioned can be used in humans to detect mucociliary transit time and total nasal clearance in humans.

Electron microscopy can be used to best assess the normalcy of cilia structure and its function, but it might not be able to detect any other abnormality that might interfere with nasal mucociliary clearance like any obstruction in the nasal cavity.

Test for mucociliary clearance include:

• Saccharine with or without color test in vivo (Option A)
• Radioisotope transport testing in vivo
• Measuring ciliary activity in vitro
• Nasal nitric oxide
• Scintigraphy (Option D) is the nuclear medicine equivalent of the dye disappearance test to assess functional and anatomic obstruction

The charcoal method (Option C) is a less commonly used method to detect nasal mucociliary clearance. In this method, a very small amount of charcoal is placed behind the head of the inferior turbinate. The pharynx is then observed to detect the presence of charcoal.

Mucociliary clearance tests are used to diagnose inborn disorders of mucociliary transport such as primary ciliary dysfunction and cystic fibrosis.
questions.learning: Electron microscopy Among the given options, electron microscopy will be the least useful in assessing nasal mucociliary clearance. Other tests mentioned can be used in humans to detect mucociliary transit time and total nasal clearance in humans.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with hematemesis and is found to have splenomegaly on examination. His history reveals that he underwent exchange transfusion for neonatal jaundice. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of hematemesis (from esophageal varices) and splenomegaly in a young child, particularly with a history of neonatal umbilical vein manipulation (such as exchange transfusion or catheterization), is strongly suggestive of portal vein thrombosis. This is a common cause of pre-hepatic portal hypertension in children. Splenic vein thrombosis (Option A) can cause localized portal hypertension but is less common and doesn't explain the generalized portosystemic shunt as well as the history does. Budd-Chiari syndrome (Option C) involves hepatic vein obstruction and typically presents with hepatomegaly and ascites, which are not the primary features here. Liver cirrhosis (Option D) can cause portal hypertension but is rare in a 5-year-old without a known history of chronic liver disease or metabolic disorders. Thus, the neonatal history is the key to identifying portal vein thrombosis
questions.learning: The combination of hematemesis (from esophageal varices) and splenomegaly in a young child, particularly with a history of neonatal umbilical vein manipulation (such as exchange transfusion or catheterization), is strongly suggestive of portal vein thrombosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with chronic pain along the medial side of the elbow that is aggravated by weightlifting. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial epicondyle and a positive reverse Cozen’s test. Which nerve is most likely involved in this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms of medial epicondylitis, commonly known as "golfer's elbow," which involves inflammation of the common flexor origin. The "reverse Cozen's test" is a diagnostic maneuver used to confirm this condition by having the patient resist wrist flexion, which elicits pain at the medial epicondyle. The ulnar nerve is anatomically the most vulnerable nerve in this region, as it passes immediately posterior to the medial epicondyle within the cubital tunnel. Chronic inflammation or repetitive stress at the medial elbow can lead to ulnar nerve irritation or entrapment (cubital tunnel syndrome). The median nerve (Option A) passes anteriorly and is less likely to be directly involved at this bony prominence. The radial and axillary nerves (Options C and D) are located in the lateral and superior aspects of the limb, respectively. Thus, ulnar neuropathy is the most logical complication
questions.learning: The patient presents with symptoms of medial epicondylitis, commonly known as "golfer's elbow," which involves inflammation of the common flexor origin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: While studying metabolic pathways and their intracellular locations, which metabolic pathway is known to occur exclusively in the cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is the metabolic pathway that converts glucose into pyruvate, and it occurs exclusively within the cytoplasm of all human cells. Every enzyme required for this ten-step process is located in the cytosol. Beta oxidation of fatty acids (Option A) and the TCA (Krebs) cycle (Option B) occur exclusively within the mitochondrial matrix. The urea cycle (Option D) is unique because it is split between the mitochondria (the first two steps) and the cytoplasm (the remaining steps). Other purely cytoplasmic pathways include the HMP shunt and fatty acid synthesis. Understanding the sub-cellular compartmentalization of these pathways is essential for grasping how the cell regulates metabolic flux; for example, the separation of fatty acid synthesis (cytoplasm) from beta-oxidation (mitochondria) prevents a futile cycle. Therefore, glycolysis stands out as the fundamental energy-generating pathway that does not require mitochondrial involvement for its initial steps
questions.learning: Glycolysis is the metabolic pathway that converts glucose into pyruvate, and it occurs exclusively within the cytoplasm of all human cells. Every enzyme required for this ten-step process is located in the cytosol.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
A 28-year-old woman with a severe headache is scheduled to undergo a CT scan. During history taking, which of the following will you definitely ask for before the commencement of the scan?

LMP - Last menstrual period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LMP

The most important information that should be ascertained during history taking in a 28-year-old woman of reproductive age group posted for a CT scan is the last menstrual period (LMP). CT scan is avoided during pregnancy due to the potential adverse effects of radiation on the fetus; hence, LMP is ascertained to rule out pregnancy.

CT is a high-resolution technique using x-rays to generate cross-sectional images of any area of the body. It is associated with high radiation doses.

Other options:

Option A: Use of cochlear implant is a contraindication for MRI and not CT. CT scan can be performed on a patient with a cochlear implant.

Option B: History of fall in a patient with a headache is asked for suspected head trauma. A CT scan in this patient can help in the diagnosis and assess extent of damage.

Option C: History of hypertension points to a possible intracranial bleed. A CT scan can be useful in ruling out the bleed.

Since it is imperative to rule out pregnancy before taking a CT scan, last menstrual period is the most appropriate answer to this question.
questions.learning: LMP — The most important information that should be ascertained during history taking in a 28-year-old woman of reproductive age group posted for a CT scan is the last menstrual period (LMP).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not a branch of the external carotid artery in Kiesselbach’s plexus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior and posterior ethmoidal

Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries are branches of the ophthalmic artery which in turn is a branch of the internal carotid artery.

Kiesselbach’s plexus is an arterial anastomosis at the anterior inferior part of the nasal septum (Little's area). It includes the anterior ethmoidal artery, septal branch of the superior labial artery, septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery, and septal branch of the greater palatine artery. It is the usual site of epistaxis in children and young adults.

The blood supply of the nasal septum can be divided into two main systems, the internal carotid system, and the external carotid system.

• Internal carotid system: Branches of the ophthalmic artery, anterior ethmoidal artery, and posterior ethmoidal artery.
• External carotid system: Sphenopalatine artery (branch of the maxillary artery) gives nasopalatine and posterior medial nasal branches, septal branch of the greater palatine artery (branch of the maxillary artery), and septal branch of the superior labial artery (branch of the facial artery).
questions.learning: Anterior and posterior ethmoidal Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries are branches of the ophthalmic artery which in turn is a branch of the internal carotid artery.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with recurrent blisters on areas of minor trauma since infancy. The blisters heal with atrophic scarring and milia formation. Examination reveals nail dystrophy and mucosal involvement. Immunofluorescence mapping shows the level of cleavage at the sublamina densa of the basement membrane zone. Which protein defect explains this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Collagen VII

This child has dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). Key clues are blistering since infancy after minor trauma, healing with atrophic scarring and milia, nail dystrophy, mucosal involvement, and cleavage below the basement membrane (sublamina densa) on immunofluorescence mapping. DEB is caused by defects in collagen VII, which forms anchoring fibrils that attach the basement membrane to the underlying dermis. Loss of these fibrils leads to deep blistering and scarring.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Collagen IV – Component of the basement membrane, not anchoring fibrils.

C. Laminin-332 – Defective in junctional epidermolysis bullosa (cleavage within lamina lucida).

D. Keratin 14 – Defect causes epidermolysis bullosa simplex (intraepidermal, no scarring).
questions.learning: Collagen VII — This child has dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). Key clues are blistering since infancy after minor trauma, healing with atrophic scarring and milia, nail dystrophy, mucosal involvement, and cleavage below the basement membrane…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman came with complaints of fever, night sweats, generalized itching, and unintentional weight loss of 10% in the last 3 months. On examination, she has enlarged cervical and axillary lymph nodes. The lymph node examination and biopsy showed the following picture. What would the likely diagnosis and treatment option be?
options: NHL - advanced stage - treated with radiotherapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hodgkin's Lymphoma - ABVD regimen

Correct answer is A because the biopsy shows Reed–Sternberg cells (large binucleate “owl eye” nuclei), characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma, and the clinical features include B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss, pruritus).

Lymphadenopathy

↓

B symptoms present

↓

Pruritus

↓

Biopsy: Reed-Sternberg cells

↓

Hodgkin lymphoma

Standard first-line treatment is ABVD regimen (Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine).

| Feature | Hodgkin | NHL

| ------- | ------- | ---

| Spread | Contiguous | Non-contiguous

| RS cells |  Present | Absent

| B symptoms | Common | Variable

| Treatment | ABVD | R-CHOP etc.

NHL usually lacks Reed–Sternberg cells. Radiotherapy alone is not used for advanced disease. Sarcoidosis shows non-caseating granulomas, not RS cells. Most common subtype:

• Nodular sclerosis HL
• Mediastinal involvement common

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to a 5-day history of left lower abdominal pain, nausea, and poor appetite. Although she has a history of chronic constipation, she has been having 2–3 loose, nonbloody bowel movements daily. History is notable for hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 15 years ago. Rectal and pelvic examinations elicit exquisite left-sided tenderness. Stool testing for occult blood is negative. Laboratory results include a white blood cell count of 16,500/mm³. Which of the following is the best next step in diagnosis?
options: Stool PCR testing for Clostridioides difficile
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT scan of the abdomen

Older patients presenting with acute left lower quadrant (LLQ) abdominal pain, leukocytosis, nausea/anorexia, and localized tenderness are most suspicious for acute diverticulitis, even if they report loose stools (diarrhea can occur due to colonic irritation around an inflamed diverticulum). A history of chronic constipation is a common predisposing factor. The presence of exquisite LLQ tenderness and elevated WBC count supports an intra-abdominal inflammatory process rather than infectious diarrhea.

The best next diagnostic step in suspected acute diverticulitis is a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast, because it:

• Confirms the diagnosis (colonic wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding)
• Detects complications: abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction
• Helps guide management (antibiotics vs drainage vs surgery)

Endoscopy (flexible sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy) is avoided in the acute setting due to risk of perforation and is performed later (after resolution) if needed to rule out malignancy. Stool cultures and C. difficile testing are appropriate when infectious diarrhea predominates, but here the clinical picture is primarily localized LLQ abdominal pain with systemic inflammation, favoring diverticulitis. Therefore, the next best diagnostic step is CT abdomen (Option A).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the mechanism responsible for the release of secretions from the gland seen in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Holocrine

The gland depicted in the image is a sebaceous gland, which releases its secretions through the holocrine mechanism.

Identification features of sebaceous gland:

• Lobular structure with clusters of cells.
• Foamy cytoplasm due to lipid content.
• Holocrine secretion with disintegrated cells.
• Found near hair follicles in the dermis.

Sebaceous gland cells synthesize and accumulate lipid-rich sebum within their cytoplasm.

Holocrine secretions are produced in the cytoplasm of the cell and released by the rupture of the plasma membrane, which destroys the cell and results in the secretion of the product into the lumen.

Examples of holocrine glands are

• Sebaceous glands of the skin and
• Meibomian glands of the eyelid

Other options:

Option A: Apocrine: involves partial loss of the apical portion of the cell (e.g., mammary glands).

Option B: Merocrine: involves secretion via exocytosis (e.g. sweat glands).

Option C: Eccrine glands are a type of sweat gland responsible for thermoregulation through the secretion of sweat. They use the merocrine mechanism for secretion.
