questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acid plays a key role in the buffering capacity of blood at physiological pH?
questions.explanation: Histidine is the primary amino acid responsible for the buffering capacity of proteins at physiological pH (around 7.4). This unique property is due to its imidazole side chain, which has a pKa of approximately 6.0. Since this pKa is relatively close to physiological pH, the side chain can easily accept or donate protons, allowing histidine-rich proteins like hemoglobin to stabilize blood pH effectively. Methionine (Option A) is a sulfur-containing amino acid primarily involved in methylation. Alanine (Option B) is a key participant in glucose-alanine cycling between muscle and liver. Arginine (Option C) is highly basic (pKa ~12) and is involved in the urea cycle and nitric oxide production. The buffering action of histidine in hemoglobin is particularly important for the Bohr effect, where the protein picks up protons released during production in the tissues, helping to regulate oxygen release and maintain acid-base balance. This makes histidine a critical component for maintaining systemic pH homeostasis
questions.learning: Histidine is the primary amino acid responsible for the buffering capacity of proteins at physiological pH (around 7.4). This unique property is due to its imidazole side chain, which has a pKa of approximately 6.0.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding hypernatremia in children? I. Diabetes insipidus due to a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) may cause hypernatremia II. Addison disease may be associated with hypernatremia III. Use of boiled skimmed milk can lead to hypernatremia IV. Use of lactulose can lead to hypernatremia Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, III and IV

Hypernatremia is defined as a serum sodium concentration >145 mEq/L and usually results from water deficit exceeding sodium loss or, less commonly, excessive sodium intake. In children, the common causes include gastrointestinal water loss, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diarrhea, and improper infant feeding practices.

Why is A correct?

• I. Diabetes insipidus due to a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) may cause hypernatremia. ✔

• Correct.
• Central diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency) causes excessive free water loss, resulting in polyuria, dehydration, and hypernatremia.

• II. Addison disease may be associated with hypernatremia. ✘

• Incorrect.
• Addison disease causes hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension due to aldosterone deficiency.

• III. Use of boiled skimmed milk can lead to hypernatremia. ✔

• Correct.
• Feeding infants with boiled skimmed milk or improperly prepared concentrated feeds increases the renal solute load and predisposes to hypernatremic dehydration.

• IV. Use of lactulose can lead to hypernatremia. ✔

• Correct.
• Lactulose can cause osmotic diarrhea, leading to excessive free water loss and hypernatremia if fluids are not adequately replaced.
questions.learning: I, III and IV Hypernatremia is defined as a serum sodium concentration >145 mEq/L and usually results from water deficit exceeding sodium loss or, less commonly, excessive sodium intake.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Identify the correctly matched pair of substances with their renal clearance from the graph given below.

PAH - Para-aminohippurate
options: A - Glucose, B - PAH, C - Bicarbonate and D - Inulin
A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH
A - PAH, B - Inulin, C - Glucose and D - Bicarbonate
A - Inulin, B - Glucose, C - Bicarbonate and D - PAH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH

The correctly matched pair of substances and their renal clearance is A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH.

The concentration of the substance changes as it passes through the tubules. The tubular cells may remove the substance from the filtrate (tubular reabsorption) or add more of the substance to the filtrate (tubular secretion) or both. The amount of the substance finally excreted equals the amount filtered plus the net amount transferred out by the tubules.

PAH is filtered by the glomeruli and secreted by the tubular cells. Its concentration increases on moving through the length of the nephron due to secretion into tubules. It is represented by curve D.

Inulin is freely filtered by glomeruli and does not undergo any reabsorption or secretion. Hence, its concentration does not change throughout the length of the nephron and its excretion is constant and equal to the glomerular filtration rate. It is represented by curve C.

The majority of bicarbonate reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule and a small amount of it flows into the distal tubules and collecting ducts. Its reabsorption occurs in all parts of the tubules, except the descending and ascending thin limbs of the loop of Henle. It is represented by curve B.

Substances like amino acids or glucose are reabsorbed along with sodium in the early portion of the proximal tubule. They have a graph that is sloping down as shown in curve A.
questions.learning: A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH The correctly matched pair of substances and their renal clearance is A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child fell down the stairs. An X-ray was done. Identify the structure injured as marked in the X-ray.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tibial tuberosity

The given X-ray points towards the tibial tuberosity. This image shows an avulsion fracture of the tibial tuberosity.

The tibial tuberosity is a bony prominence located on the anterior part of the tibia, just below the knee. It is the attachment point for the patellar tendon. Injury to the tibial tuberosity is common in adolescents, especially those involved in sports or after trauma like a fall.

Other options:

Option A: The medial tubercle refers to part of the medial condyle of the tibia.

Option C: Gerdy's tubercle is located on the lateral aspect of the tibia, where the iliotibial band (IT band) inserts. It is less commonly injured in falls but can be affected in conditions related to the IT band, like IT band syndrome.

Option D: Anterior intercondylar area is an area is located between the medial and lateral condyles of the tibia and serves as an attachment point for the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). Injuries in this region are more commonly associated with ACL tears.
questions.learning: Tibial tuberosity — The given X-ray points towards the tibial tuberosity. This image shows an avulsion fracture of the tibial tuberosity.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a 20-year history of chronic alcohol use (about 500 ml daily) presents with sensation of insects crawling on his skin, agitation, and irritability. He reports that his last drink was 3 days ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms are classic for Delirium Tremens (DT), the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal. DT typically develops 48 to 72 hours (3 days) after the last drink. The sensation of insects crawling on the skin is known as formication (Magnan’s sign), a specific type of tactile hallucination associated with severe withdrawal or cocaine use. Alcohol intoxication (Option A) would present with slurred speech and ataxia while drinking. Tolerance (Option C) refers to the need for increasing amounts of alcohol to achieve the same effect. "Reaction due to alcohol" (Option D) is too vague a term for this specific clinical syndrome. DT is a medical emergency characterized by confusion, hallucinations, and autonomic hyperactivity (fever, tachycardia, hypertension). Management requires high doses of benzodiazepines (like diazepam) and intensive supportive care, as it carries a significant mortality rate if left untreated
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms are classic for Delirium Tremens (DT), the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal. DT typically develops 48 to 72 hours (3 days) after the last drink.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is Gelle's test negative?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Otosclerosis

Gelle’s test is negative when the ossicular chain is fixed as in cases of otosclerosis.

Gelle’s test is a test of bone conduction and examines the effect of increased air pressure in the ear canal on hearing. In normal individuals, due to the increased intralabrynthine pressure applied by the Seigel's speculum, there is immobility of the basilar membrane, as the tympanic membrane and the ossicles are pushed inwards (medially). This results in decreased hearing. But, in diseased individuals, where the ossicular chain and the tympanic membrane are fixed or disconnected, no change in hearing is observed.

Gelle’s test is positive in normal persons and in those with sensorineural hearing loss.

Note: This test was commonly used for the diagnosis of otosclerosis, but has since been replaced by tympanometry.
questions.learning: Otosclerosis Gelle’s test is negative when the ossicular chain is fixed as in cases of otosclerosis. Gelle’s test is a test of bone conduction and examines the effect of increased air pressure in the ear canal on hearing.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about tedizolid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Active against gram positive organisms

Tedizolid is active against gram-positive organisms.

Tedizolid belongs to the class of oxazolidinones. It has poor activity against most gram-negative bacteria and anaerobes. It inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the P site of the 50S ribosomal subunit.

It is used for the treatment of skin and soft tissue infections, respiratory tract infections caused by streptococci, and S. aureus including MRSA.

Common adverse effects include myelosuppression leading to anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and pancytopenia.
questions.learning: Active against gram positive organisms Tedizolid is active against gram-positive organisms. Tedizolid belongs to the class of oxazolidinones.

questions.text: Korsakoff psychosis is true except? 1. Amnesia 2. Confabulation 3. Ophthalmoplegia 4. Ataxia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4

Korsakoff psychosis is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B₁) deficiency, most commonly seen in chronic alcoholism. It is characterized by anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation (fabrication of stories to fill memory gaps).

Ophthalmoplegia and ataxia are features of Wernicke encephalopathy, the acute stage of thiamine deficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following are seen in iron deficiency anemia?

1. Reduced serum iron level
2. Reduced transferrin saturation
3. Increased total iron binding capacity
4. Reduced ferritin level
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3, 4

Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is characterized by reduced serum iron level, reduced transferrin saturation, increased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and reduced ferritin level.

Serum iron level represents the amount of circulating iron bound to transferrin. When the iron stores become depleted in IDA, the serum iron level begins to fall.

TIBC is an indirect measure of the circulating levels of the iron-transporting protein, transferrin. IDA is characterized by more free transferrin (not bound to iron) available in circulation. This increases the TIBC. Transferrin saturation is calculated as: (serum iron ÷ TIBC) x 100. Normal transferrin saturation is 25-50%. Iron deficiency states show low transferrin saturation. A transferrin saturation >50% indicates a large amount of iron being delivered to the tissues, and can cause tissue iron overload. This is seen in hemochromatosis.

Serum ferritin is the most useful laboratory test to assess the levels of iron stores in the body. As iron stores are depleted, serum ferritin levels fall. Levels <15 μg/L are diagnostic of completely absent iron stores.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4 Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is characterized by reduced serum iron level, reduced transferrin saturation, increased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and reduced ferritin level.

His wife says otherwise and says he behaves like this only recently and before that he was working peacefully as a school teacher. He is most likely suffering from?

• Belief that he is the most important person in the world – Delusion of grandeur
• Belief that his neighbours and family members are trying to harm him – Delusion of persecution
• Belief that others feel jealous – Part of delusion of persecution

A scenario of this kind is most likely seen in manic patients with

• Primary delusion of Grandeur (and)
• Secondary delusion of Persecution

Delusion of reference:

• Delusion in which events, objects, or other persons in one’s immediate environment have a particular and unusual significance in reference to the person experiencing the delusion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. Histopathological examination of the mass showed signet ring appearance. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colloidal carcinoma

The given clinical scenario and histopathological findings are suggestive of colloid/mucinous carcinoma of the breast.

Colloidal carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, which shows intra and extracellular mucin deposition. In intracellular type, nuclei are pushed to the peripherally to form signet ring appearance.

Extracellular type shows tumor cells with faint nuclei arranged in clusters floating in pools/lakes of mucin on histopathological examination.

Other options:

Option B: Papillary carcinoma consists of true papillae with a leaf-like arrangement of fibrovascular tissue, lined by the tumor cells.

Option C: Medullary carcinoma of the breast shows sheets of highly pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and pushing border.

Option D: Phyllodes tumor shows the presence of nodules of proliferating stroma covered by epithelium (leaf-like architecture).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the first step after fitting the pessary to check if the pessary is adequately retained?
options: Asking the patient to void and see if the pessary is in place
Seeing if the patient feels any discomfort, which means that the pessary is retained
Asking the patient to perform the Valsalva manouvre and see if the pessary is in place
Being able to admit two fingers between the ring and the pessary.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Asking the patient to perform the Valsalva manouvre and see if the pessary is in place

The first step after fitting the pessary to check if the pessary is adequately retained is to ask the patient to perform Valsalva's maneuver or cough and see if the pessary is in place.

There is some level of descent of the pessary with these maneuvers is to be expected, but the pessary should return to its normal position when these efforts are stopped. If the pessary descends to the introitus with these maneuvers, then a larger size pessary should be tried.

The pessary is well-fitted if you are able to slide the ring of the pessary up and down along the vaginal sidewall. It is well-fitted if you are able to insert one finger between the vaginal sidewall and the edge of the pessary. When the labia are separated, a well-supported pessary is not usually visible.

The patient should be comfortable, and able to void urine with the pessary in place before leaving the clinic.

questions.text: A 23-year-old man presents to the surgery department with abdominal pain and tenderness, having developed acute appendicitis three days earlier. Which type of surgical incision would be most appropriate in this clinical scenario?
questions.explanation: The patient has acute appendicitis, and the most appropriate surgical incision is the McBurney’s incision (gridiron incision). This incision is placed in the right iliac fossa, centered over McBurney’s point (junction of lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the line joining the umbilicus and anterior superior iliac spine). In the given diagram, label 3 corresponds to the McBurney’s (gridiron) incision, which is an oblique muscle-splitting incision. It provides excellent access to the appendix while minimizing muscle damage and promoting faster recovery. This incision follows the direction of external oblique muscle fibers, allowing separation rather than cutting of muscles, thereby reducing postoperative pain and complications. questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the treatment option with the image given below:
questions.explanation: The surgical diagram illustrates Type 3 tympanoplasty, also known as myringostapediopexy. This procedure is performed when the malleus and incus are absent or diseased, but the stapes is intact and mobile. The tympanic membrane graft is placed directly onto the head of the stapes to restore the sound conduction mechanism. Regarding the distractors, Type 1 (Option A) is a simple repair of a perforated ear drum (myringoplasty) where the ossicular chain is intact. Type 2 (Option B) involves placing the graft onto the incus when the malleus is eroded. Type 4 (Option D) is used when only the stapes footplate remains; the graft is placed between the oval and round windows to protect the round window while allowing sound to hit the footplate directly. Therefore, the direct connection to the stapes head as shown in the image is diagnostic of Type 3

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) is used for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn

Inhaled nitric oxide(iNO) is used for persistent pulmonary hypertension in newborns. (Option A)

Inhaled NO selectively dilates the pulmonary vasculature, hence used in diseases associated with increased pulmonary vascular resistance. Inhaled NO is an FDA-approved drug for persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn.

Inhaled NO can also be used during cardiac catheterization to evaluate the pulmonary vasodilating capacity of patients with heart failure and infants with congenital heart disease. Another use of inhaled NO is to determine the diffusion capacity (DL) across the alveolar-capillary membrane. It is more effective than CO2 because of its greater affinity for hemoglobin and its higher water solubility at body temperature.

NO is produced from the nasal passages and the lungs of normal human subjects and can be detected in exhaled gas. The measurement of fractional exhaled NO is a noninvasive marker for airway inflammation in the assessment of respiratory tract diseases, including asthma, respiratory tract infection, and chronic lung disease.

Inhaled NO is administered at low concentrations (0.1–50 ppm) since high concentrations of 50 to 100 ppm can cause significant methemoglobinemia that can cause death.

Other options:

Option B: Unstable angina is treated by anti-platelet drugs such as aspirin and clopidogrel, and anticoagulants such as heparin.

Option C: Obstructive sleep apnoea is mainly treated by using a BiPAP machine during sleep and CNS stimulants such as armodafinil for daytime sleepiness associated with the condition.

Option D: Erectile dysfunction is treated by PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil, tadalafil, etc.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with lethargy, excessive sleepiness, and weight gain. Laboratory evaluation shows low plasma TSH along with reduced T3 and T4 levels, but TSH levels rise after administration of TRH. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
Hypothyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of lethargy and weight gain combined with low T3 and T4 confirm "hypothyroidism". A low or inappropriately normal TSH in the setting of low T4 indicates "central" hypothyroidism (either pituitary or hypothalamic origin). To distinguish between the two, a TRH stimulation test is used. If the TSH level "increases" following TRH administration, it demonstrates that the pituitary gland is healthy and capable of responding, but it was not receiving endogenous TRH from the brain. Therefore, the primary defect lies in the "hypothalamus" (Tertiary Hypothyroidism). If the TSH had failed to increase, the diagnosis would be pituitary disease (Secondary Hypothyroidism, Option B). Options A and D are incorrect because the patient’s labs and clinical picture represent a deficiency (hypo) rather than an excess (hyper) of thyroid hormone. This diagnostic logic is a cornerstone of endocrinology for localizing the exact level of axis failure
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of lethargy and weight gain combined with low T3 and T4 confirm "hypothyroidism". A low or inappropriately normal TSH in the setting of low T4 indicates "central" hypothyroidism (either pituitary or hypothalamic origin).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An unvaccinated 5-year-old child from a migrant worker family is brought to the emergency department with fever and a characteristic skin rash. Ophthalmic examination reveals the presence of Bitot’s spots. What is the most appropriate management in this case?
options: Isolate and give nutritional supply with vitamin A supplement
Give measles vaccine and vitamin A supplement
Institutional Isolation, nutritional management with vitamin A supplement
questions.explanation: The combination of fever, a characteristic skin rash, and Bitot's spot in an unvaccinated child suggests measles complicated by Vitamin A deficiency. Isolation is the first priority to prevent the spread of the highly communicable measles virus. Nutritional support and high-dose Vitamin A supplementation are critical, as measles acutely depletes Vitamin A stores, significantly increasing the risk of blindness (xerophthalmia) and mortality. Giving the measles vaccine (Options B and D) is inappropriate because the child already has the active disease. Institutional isolation (Option C) is generally unnecessary for uncomplicated cases without general danger signs like respiratory distress. Standard management for measles includes antipyretics, fluid intake, and humidification. Vitamin A dosage depends on age, with 200,000 IU typically given on days one and two for children over one year
questions.learning: The combination of fever, a characteristic skin rash, and Bitot's spot in an unvaccinated child suggests measles complicated by Vitamin A deficiency. Isolation is the first priority to prevent the spread of the highly communicable measles virus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of vertigo, a feeling of ear fullness and pressure, hearing loss, and a low-frequency roaring tinnitus. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic clinical tetrad described—episodic dizziness (vertigo), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, aural fullness (pressure), and low-frequency tinnitus (roaring sound)—is pathognomonic for Meniere's disease. This condition is caused by endolymphatic hydrops, which is an over-accumulation of fluid in the inner ear. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) (Option B) involves brief vertigo spells triggered solely by head movement and lacks hearing loss or tinnitus. Labyrinthitis (Option C) presents with sudden, severe vertigo and hearing loss usually following a viral infection, but it is typically a single, intense event rather than intermittent episodes. Syncope (Option D) is a brief loss of consciousness due to reduced cerebral blood flow and is not associated with primary ear symptoms. Therefore, the characteristic constellation of fluctuating auditory and vestibular symptoms confirms Meniere's disease as the potential clinical diagnosis for this patient
questions.learning: The classic clinical tetrad described—episodic dizziness (vertigo), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, aural fullness (pressure), and low-frequency tinnitus (roaring sound)—is pathognomonic for Meniere's disease.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Many children from a particular community coming to a hospital were detected to have acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It was assumed that it is due to the presence of cytotoxic waste in the water of that community. If a case-control study has to be done to find whether the chemical and ALL are associated, what will be taken as the control?
options: Children from the area exposed, but unaffected with the disease
Children from the area not exposed and affected with the disease
Children coming to your OPD, who do not have the disease
All children with ALL irrespective of exposure status
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Children coming to your OPD, who do not have the disease

Children coming to the OPD, who do not have the disease, will be taken as the control for the case-control study.

The prerequisite for selecting a control group is that they must be free from the disease under study. They must be as similar as possible to the cases, except for the fact that they should not have the disease. Usually, the control group consists of persons who have not been exposed to the disease or factor whose influence is under study. Therefore, among the options, the best answer would be the children coming to the OPD, who do not have the disease as controls for the study.

Case-control studies are also called retrospective studies. This study proceeds from effect to cause and is done after the exposure and outcome have occurred.

They focus on diseases or health problems that have already developed. They are less time-consuming and have no risk of attrition because they do not require follow-up.

There are four basic steps in conducting a case-control study:

• Selection of cases and controls.
• Matching- This is done to ensure comparability between cases and controls. Controls are selected such that they are similar to cases with respect to certain factors, like age, that influence the disease outcome.
• Measurement of exposure - This is obtained by interviews, questionnaires, or study of the past records of cases.
• Analysis in the form of exposure rates, risk ratio, and odds ratio.

The Odds Ratio (OR) calculated from a case-control study, is a measure of the strength of the association between risk factor and outcome.
questions.learning: Children coming to your OPD, who do not have the disease Children coming to the OPD, who do not have the disease, will be taken as the control for the case-control study.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old male presents with chronic back pain, easy fatigability, and a history of multiple urinary tract infections over the past 3 months. His ESR is elevated, and a skull X-ray is shown below. Which of the following investigations would be useful for diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum electrophoresis

The clinical scenario is indicative of multiple myeloma, and a useful diagnostic test would be serum electrophoresis.

Multiple myeloma involves a malignant proliferation of plasma cells, resulting in excessive production of abnormal immunoglobulins, causing a spike called the M band in Serum Electrophoresis.

The given image demonstrates a sharp peak ("church spire” or M band) in the gamma globulin region. This is characteristically seen in a patient with multiple myeloma.

Certain common diseases and their electrophoretic pattern:

Condition
Electrophoretic pattern

Chronic infections
Smooth increase in gamma globulins

Multiple myeloma
Gamma globulin part is increased (M BAND)

Liver cirrhosis
Reduced albumin and compensatory increase in globulin

Primary immune deficiency
Gamma globulin reduced

α1 antitrypsin deficiency
α1 band is thin and even lost sometimes

Multiple myelomas:

* Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* Disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

* Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia

* Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions

* Renal failure

* Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20%plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation.)

* Plasma cell tumors are positive for CD138

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Within Freud’s psychosexual stages of development, a patient exhibits stubbornness, rigidity, and frugality, suggesting fixation due to unresolved conflicts during a particular developmental phase. At which stage does this type of behavior typically manifest as a result of fixation?
questions.explanation: Sigmund Freud’s theory of psychosexual development proposes that unresolved conflicts during specific childhood stages lead to adult personality traits or fixations. The anal stage, occurring between ages 1 and 3, focuses on toilet training and the control of bodily functions. Fixation at this stage can result in a character type known as "anal-retentive," which is clinically characterized by a triad of traits: extreme stubbornness, rigidity (obsession with order), and frugality (parsimony). Fixation at the oral stage (Option B) results in dependence or excessive smoking/eating. The phallic stage (Option C) involves the Oedipus complex and concerns about sexual identity. The genital stage (Option D) represents the mature integration of adult sexuality. The specific behavioral pattern of meticulousness and control-oriented stubbornness is classically attributed to the power struggle experienced during the anal phase of development
questions.learning: Sigmund Freud’s theory of psychosexual development proposes that unresolved conflicts during specific childhood stages lead to adult personality traits or fixations.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The image below shows an image of the anus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perianal abscess

The image shows a smooth swelling on the perineum near the anal opening suggestive of perianal abscess.

Anorectal abscess refers to a collection of pus in the anal or rectal region. More commonly seen in men. Anorectal abscess originates from an infection arising in the cryptoglandular epithelium lining the anal canal. Fistula-in-ano, Crohn's disease, diabetes and immunosuppression are some conditions leading to abscess formation.

Anorectal abscess presents as a painful, throbbing swelling in the anal region with constitutional symptoms like fever.

There are four types of anorectal abscesses:

* Peri-anal (most common)

* Ischio-rectal

* Inter-sphincteric

* Supra-levator

Treatment:

* Most of them can be drained under local anaesthesia as an outpatient procedure in the clinic or emergency room.

* Larger, more complicated abscesses may require drainage in the operating room. A skin incision is created, and a disk of skin is excised to prevent premature closure. No packing is necessary, and sitz baths are started the next day.

Pilonidal sinus refers to non-infected, midline openings in the natal cleft overlying the coccyx. Drivers and hairdressers are more commonly affected and is seen more in men, usually after puberty. Patients complain of intermittent pain, swelling and discharge at the base of the spine. Constitutional symptoms such as fever and fatigue are usually absent. The primary sinus may have one or many openings, all of which are strictly in the midline between the level of the sacrococcygeal joint and the tip of the coccyx. The other sites that they can be affected include the interdigital cleft and axilla.

The image given below shows a pilonidal sinus in the natal cleft(midline opening).
questions.learning: Perianal abscess — The image shows a smooth swelling on the perineum near the anal opening suggestive of perianal abscess. Anorectal abscess refers to a collection of pus in the anal or rectal region.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A man with a history of COPD presents with an acute exacerbation. His vitals are given below. According to GOLD criteria, which of the following is/are used in the management of this case? RR - 30/min, Pulse - 112/min, SpO2 - 87% under RA, pCO2 - 60 mmHg 1. Antibiotics 2. Steroids 3. Antivirals 4. Nebulised bronchodilators
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

• RR: 30/min → Tachypnea
• Pulse: 112/min → Distress
• SpO₂: 87% (room air) → Hypoxemia
• pCO₂: 60 mmHg → Hypercapnia

This is acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) with Type II respiratory failure.

Rz: Bronchodilators Steroids Antibiotics (if infection)

Oxygen (target SpO2 88–92%)

If CO2 retention → NIV (BiPAP)

| Treatment | Role | Indication

| --------- | ---- | ----------

| Nebulised bronchodilators | Relieve bronchospasm | ALL patients

| Systemic steroids | Reduce inflammation | Moderate–severe

| Antibiotics | If infection suspected | Purulent sputum / severe

| Oxygen | Correct hypoxemia | Target 88–92%

| NIV (BiPAP) | ↓ CO₂ | Hypercapnia
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 • RR: 30/min → Tachypnea • Pulse: 112/min → Distress • SpO₂: 87% (room air) → Hypoxemia • pCO₂: 60 mmHg → Hypercapnia This is acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) with Type II respiratory failure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What joint is present between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synchondrosis

The joint present between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone is called synchondrosis.

Synchondrosis refers to the primary cartilaginous joints in which the advancing areas of ossification are separated by hyaline cartilage. They are temporary joints and are associated with growth. Hyaline cartilage has the ability to ossify with age, thus making these joints undergo synostosis (fusion) once the growth is complete. An example of this type of joint is the epiphyseal plate between the epiphysis and diaphysis of long bones

Structurally, joints are classified as fibrous joints, cartilaginous joints, and synovial joints (see the table). Sutures, syndesmosis, and gomphosis are fibrous joints. Symphysis and synchondrosis are types of cartilaginous joints.

Type
Subtypes

Fibrous joints
Sutures
Syndesmosis
Gomphosis

Cartilaginous joints
Primary cartilaginous joints (or synchondrosis)
Secondary cartilaginous joints (or symphysis)

Synovial joints
Ball-and-socket or spheroidal joints
Sellar or saddle joints
Condylar or bicondylar joints
Ellipsoid joints
Hinge joints
Pivot or trochoid joints
Plane joints
questions.learning: Synchondrosis — The joint present between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone is called synchondrosis. Synchondrosis refers to the primary cartilaginous joints in which the advancing areas of ossification are separated by hyaline cartilage.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old married woman came for an infertility evaluation. On performing further investigations, intramural fibroids of sizes 7x5cm and 5x3cm were seen at the right and left cornual ends of the uterus. Her husband's semen analysis was found to be normal. What is the appropriate management of this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Myomectomy

The most appropriate management for a woman with infertility due to intramural fibroids at both the cornual ends of the uterus is myomectomy. The infertility, in this case, is due to the fibroids blocking the right and left cornua of the uterus.

Myomectomy refers to the removal of fibroids and preserving the uterus. It is indicated in women presenting with infertility, those who desire pregnancy, or those who wish to retain the uterus.

Intracavitary fibroids can be resected via the hysteroscopic approach, while subserosal or intramural fibroids require laparotomy or laparoscopic myomectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Uterine artery embolization is not done in this case, as it may decrease fertility, as a result of pelvic adhesions. It is a technique in which polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), gel foam particles, or metal coils are injected into the uterine arteries. This embolization reduces vascularity and the size of the fibroid. It is best suited to control menorrhagia in multiparous women.

Option C: Artificial reproductive techniques are not indicated in this case as infertility is seen to be due to the fibroids blocking the cornual ends of the uterus. However, it may be considered at a later stage.

Option D: GnRH analogs when used for 6 months, can reduce the tumor size by targeting the growth effects of estrogen and progesterone. It can be used in women with infertility caused by cornual fibroids. They are often used preoperatively to reduce the size of the fibroid and facilitate a hysteroscopic approach to surgery. However, it is expensive and can cause menopausal symptoms if used for >6 months. Fibroids are known to regrow 3-4 months after stopping the therapy.
questions.learning: Myomectomy — The most appropriate management for a woman with infertility due to intramural fibroids at both the cornual ends of the uterus is myomectomy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient from a Mediterranean country visits Africa, where he develops malaria. He is treated with primaquine and later develops hemolytic anemia. Deficiency of an enzyme involved in which of the following pathways could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway

The deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) enzyme, which is involved in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway, could be the cause behind this presentation.

G6PD is an enzyme that plays a critical role in redox reactions that occur in all aerobic cells. It is the only source of NADPH in erythrocytes, which helps in the formation of reduced glutathione. This reduced form protects erythrocytes against oxidative stress.

G6PD deficiency is an X-linked inheritance disorder. Most patients with this condition are asymptomatic. But when exposed to oxidative agents, they are prone to develop acute hemolytic anemia. The various oxidative triggers include:

• Fava beans
• Infections
• Drugs such as primaquine, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin

A hemolytic attack can present with weakness and abdominal/ lumbar pain. Later, the patient can develop jaundice, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria. Investigations will show elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and low levels of plasma haptoglobin. Anisocytosis and spherocytes can be seen on peripheral smear. Acute renal failure is a complication seen in adults.

Other options:

Option A - Glycolysis, the main pathway of glucose, can occur either aerobically or anaerobically. A deficiency of the enzyme pyruvate kinase can present as hemolytic anemia. Fatigue can be the presentation when there is phosphofructokinase. Both these are enzymes of glycolysis.

Option B - Gluconeogenesis is the process by which non-carbohydrate precursors are used to synthesize glucose. Pyruvate carboxylase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, and glucose-6-phosphatase are the enzymes in the pathway. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency leads to von Gierke disease, which is a glycogen storage disorder. Defective gluconeogenesis results in hypoglycemia.

Option D - Luebering–Rapoport pathway is a shunt mechanism that generates and dephosphorylates 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG). 2,3-BPG mutase is the enzyme involved. A deficiency of this enzyme can cause erythrocytosis.
questions.learning: Hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway — The deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) enzyme, which is involved in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway, could be the cause behind this presentation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman had an IUD inserted at a PHC. After a few months, she conceives. On examination, the IUD is still in place with threads visualised. She wants to continue with her pregnancy. Next best step of management is?
options: Remove IUD gently, then do MTP
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Remove IUD gently

If pregnancy occurs with an IUD in situ and the woman wishes to continue the pregnancy, the IUD should be gently removed, provided the strings are visible.

Early removal reduces the risk of spontaneous abortion, septic abortion, preterm labor, and chorioamnionitis.

Leaving the IUD in situ significantly increases obstetric complications, while MTP is not indicated since the patient desires continuation.
questions.learning: Remove IUD gently If pregnancy occurs with an IUD in situ and the woman wishes to continue the pregnancy, the IUD should be gently removed, provided the strings are visible.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The image illustrates which vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates Casal's necklace, a pathognomonic dermatological sign of Pellagra, which is caused by a deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3) or its precursor tryptophan. Pellagra is classically characterized by the "3 Ds": Dermatitis, Diarrhea, and Dementia. The dermatitis is photosensitive and symmetrically distributed on sun-exposed areas, resulting in a well-demarcated area of hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis around the neck. Vitamin A deficiency (Option A) causes xerophthalmia and follicular hyperkeratosis (phrynoderma). Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) results in scurvy, characterized by petechiae and bleeding gums. Vitamin E deficiency (Option B) is rare and primarily causes neurological issues like ataxia. Pellagra is often seen in populations where corn (maize) is the primary dietary staple, as corn is deficient in both niacin and tryptophan. Treatment involves oral nicotinamide supplementation and a balanced diet
questions.learning: The image demonstrates Casal's necklace, a pathognomonic dermatological sign of Pellagra, which is caused by a deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3) or its precursor tryptophan.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae has 23 serotypes. In which of the following patients is this vaccine most beneficial?
options: A patient with sickle cell disease
A patient with recurrent otitis media
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A patient with sickle cell disease

The polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae (PPSV-23) is most beneficial for patients with sickle cell disease.

S. pneumoniae is an encapsulated organism that is detected by the spleen and is removed. However, in sickle cell disease, the sickled cells block the vessels in the spleen which results in splenic infarction. This hyposplenism results in an increased risk of pneumococcal infection. Hence, pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV-23) is given to these patients as a prophylactic measure to reduce this risk.
questions.learning: A patient with sickle cell disease — The polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae (PPSV-23) is most beneficial for patients with sickle cell disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An 18-year-old previously healthy girl presents with low-grade fever, progressive weight loss, abdominal pain, and amenorrhea for six months. Clinical examination reveals a left-sided pelvic mass along with ascites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In high-prevalence regions, Genital Tuberculosis is a common cause of secondary amenorrhea and infertility in young women. The presentation of systemic symptoms (low-grade fever, weight loss) and local pelvic signs (abdominal pain, pelvic mass, and ascites) is characteristic. The infection often involves the fallopian tubes and peritoneum, leading to the formation of masses and ascitic fluid. Ovarian malignancy (Option B) can present with a mass and ascites but is less common than TB in this age group and doesn't typically explain the systemic fever. A submucous fibroid (Option A) would cause heavy menstrual bleeding, not amenorrhea. Ectopic pregnancy (Option C) would present as an acute crisis or with high hCG levels, not a chronic six-month illness. Therefore, given the constitutional symptoms and pelvic findings, genital tuberculosis is the most probable diagnosis

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The image shows the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve plotted during different conditions. Which among the following conditions would result in curve D?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acidosis

The oxygen hemoglobin curve denoted by the curve D will be observed during Acidosis.

Conditions that cause a right shift (C->D) in the oxygen hemoglobin curve are: (Conditions with the increased requirement of O2 - metabolically active tissues)

* Hypoxia and Hypercarbia - Metabolically active tissues utilize O2 and tissues produce CO2

* ↓ pH (Acidosis)- Secondary to increased CO2 production.

* ↑ in temperature, heat

* ↑ in 2,3-DPG - increased anaerobic glycolysis

Conditions that cause a left shift (B <-C)  in the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve are:

* Decreased carbon dioxide (hypocarbia) (Option B)

* ↑ pH of the blood

* ↓ in the temperature of the body (hypothermia) (Option A)

* ↓ in 2,3-DPG (Option C)

* Fetal hemoglobin

Curve A represents the Myoglobin-O2 binding curve. It is a rectangular hyperbola (unlike a sigmoid curve of Oxy-hemoglobin curve). This is because it only has a single oxygen binding site. It is present in muscle in large amounts and can provide oxygen to muscles even at low blood oxygen levels.

Pearl PF0528: Factors affecting 2,3 -DPG

↑ in 2, 3-DPG
↓ in 2, 3-DPG

• Anemia
• Accilimitization (high altitude)
• Thyroid hormone
• Growth hormone
• Androgens
• Exercise

• Stored blood
• Acidosis
• Chronic hypoxia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ketone bodies are not utilized by the liver because it lacks:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiophorase

Ketone bodies are not utilized in the liver because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase.

Ketone bodies are synthesized in the liver mitochondria (by ketogenesis) and transported in the blood to the peripheral tissues. Here they are utilized by the following steps:

1. β-hydroxybutyrate (the most predominant ketone body) is oxidized to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase producing NADH.
2. Acetoacetate is then activated to acetoacetyl CoA by transferring a CoA molecule from succinyl CoA by succinyl CoA-acetoacetyl CoA transferase (thiophorase).
3. Acetoacetyl CoA is cleaved into two acetyl CoA molecules by thiolase and oxidized into CO2 by the TCA cycle.

Thiokinase or Acyl CoA synthetase catalyzes the only energy-requiring step in fatty acid oxidation. In the presence of ATP and coenzyme A, thiokinase catalyzes the conversion of a fatty acid to acyl-CoA. Acyl-CoA is the active form of fatty acid. This step uses one high-energy phosphate and forms AMP and PPi.

When higher than normal ketone bodies are present in the blood or urine, it is called ketonemia or ketonuria, respectively. The overall condition is called ketosis. The metabolism of free fatty acids to produce ketone bodies is exaggerated in pathologic states such as starvation and diabetes mellitus, thus causing ketosis. The continued buffering and excretion of ketone bodies deplete the alkali reserve, causing ketoacidosis.
questions.learning: Thiophorase Ketone bodies are not utilized in the liver because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase. Ketone bodies are synthesized in the liver mitochondria (by ketogenesis) and transported in the blood to the peripheral tissues.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which antibody is the first to appear and acts fastest during a primary (first) immune response to an infection?
questions.explanation: IgM is the initial antibody produced by naïve B cells upon the first exposure to a foreign antigen. Structurally, it exists as a pentamer, providing 10 distinct antigen-binding sites. This configuration results in very high avidity, allowing it to bind pathogens strongly even before affinity maturation has occurred. IgM is also highly efficient at activating the classical complement pathway to clear systemic infections rapidly. IgG (Option B) dominates the secondary immune response and appears later in the primary response once memory B cells are activated. IgE (Option C) is primarily involved in allergic reactions and the defense against parasitic infections rather than the early general response to bacteria or viruses. IgA (Option D) is the principal antibody in mucosal secretions like tears and breast milk, providing local rather than primary systemic immunity. Thus, IgM is the definitive first responder in primary immunity
questions.learning: IgM is the initial antibody produced by naïve B cells upon the first exposure to a foreign antigen. Structurally, it exists as a pentamer, providing 10 distinct antigen-binding sites.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Positive predictive value is most affected by _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prevalence

If the prevalence of a disease in a population is high, the more accurate will be the positive predictive value of a screening test.

If the prevalence declines, the PPV will be low.

Predictive value is affected the most by prevalence. However, both sensitivity and specificity can change the predictive value.

Pearl PF0045: Validity of a Screening Test

* Validity/ Accuracy of a screening test depends upon the sensitivity, specificity, and predictive accuracy of the test.

* It represents the closeness to a true value/ actual value.

* These are the inherent properties of a screening test.

* PPV and NPV are dependent on the Prevalence of disease.

* Sensitivity & Speciifity are independent of prevalence of disease.

Formulae

Sensitivity
TP
TP + FN

Specificity
TN
FP + TN

Predictive value of a positive test (PPV)
TP
TP + FP

Predictive value of a negative test (NPV)
TN
TN + FN

Percentage of false positives
FP
FP + TN

Percentage of false negatives
FN
TP + FN

* PPV varies directly with prevalence

* NPV varies inversely with prevalence
questions.learning: Prevalence If the prevalence of a disease in a population is high, the more accurate will be the positive predictive value of a screening test. If the prevalence declines, the PPV will be low.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A young man with a paternal family history of bipolar disorder presents to the OPD with three documented manic episodes. Which mood stabilizer would be the most appropriate and effective treatment option for him?
questions.explanation: For a patient with recurrent episodes of classic mania and a strong family history of the disorder, Lithium remains the "gold standard" mood stabilizer (Option D). Lithium is highly effective at both treating acute manic episodes and preventing future recurrences of mania and depression. Valproate (Option A) is an excellent alternative, particularly for "mixed episodes" or rapid cycling, but Lithium is classically favored for pure manic presentations. Lamotrigine (Option B) is primarily effective for the maintenance phase of bipolar depression rather than acute mania. Olanzapine (Option C) is an atypical antipsychotic used for acute stabilization but is not the primary long-term mood stabilizer compared to the established efficacy of lithium. Therefore, given the specific recurrent manic history, Lithium is the most appropriate and historically validated choice for this patient. Monitoring of serum lithium levels and renal/thyroid function is mandatory
questions.learning: For a patient with recurrent episodes of classic mania and a strong family history of the disorder, Lithium remains the "gold standard" mood stabilizer (Option D).

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the reference woman used in the calculation of the recommended daily allowance (RDA)?

On each working day, she must be engaged in 8 hours of occupation/work, which usually involves moderate activity. When not at work she spends 8 hours in bed, 4-6 hours in sitting and moving about, 2 hours in walking, and in active recreation or household duties.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Match the correct answer related to the nerve injuries in various surgeries:

A. Breast surgery
B. Thyroid surgery
C. Submandibular gland excision
D. Thymectomy
1. Long thoracic nerve
2. External laryngeal nerve
3. Hypoglossal nerve
4. Vagus nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4

A-1, B-2, C-3, and D-4 is the correct option.

A: During breast surgery, removal of the axillary lymph nodes is commonly done. This carries a risk of injury to the long thoracic nerve, which originates from the C5-C7 roots of the brachial plexus. It innervates the serratus anterior muscle. Injury to this nerve during surgery results in paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle leading to winging of the scapula.

B: The external laryngeal nerve is a motor nerve that supplies the cricothyroid muscle. The close relationship of the external laryngeal nerve to the superior thyroid artery puts the nerve at potential risk when the artery is clamped during thyroid surgeries.

C: Excision of the submandibular gland results in potential risk to 3 cranial nerves:

• Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
• Lingual nerve
• Hypoglossal nerve

questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following electrolyte abnormality is an independent predictor of adverse outcome in a patient with CHF?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyponatremia

In chronic heart failure, hyponatremia is an independent predictor of adverse outcomes and mortality. It reflects severe neurohormonal activation (↑ ADH, RAAS) and advanced disease rather than a simple electrolyte imbalance.

A) Hypernatremia – Uncommon in CHF and not a standard prognostic marker.

C) Hypokalemia – Increases arrhythmia risk but is usually drug-related, not independent.

D) Hyperkalemia – Seen with renal failure/RAAS blockade; prognostic impact is secondary.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms is not classified as a dimorphic fungus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cryptococcus neoformans

Dimorphic fungi exist in two forms depending on temperature: mold form at 25°C and yeast (or tissue) form at 37°C. “mold in the cold, yeast in the heat”

• Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides, and Talaromyces marneffii are dimorphic fungi
• Cryptococcus neoformans is not dimorphic; it exists only as an encapsulated yeast with polysaccharide capsule seen in India ink preparation.

Key points:

• Histoplasma → intracellular yeast in macrophages
• Coccidioides → spherules with endospores in tissue
• Talaromyces marneffii → yeast with transverse septum

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following hormones, in a lactating mother, is responsible for the growth of breast tissue?
questions.explanation: In a lactating mother, prolactin is the primary hormone responsible for stimulating the growth, development, and maintenance of the milk-producing lobuloalveolar tissue in the breast. It acts on lactotrophs to promote the hyperplasia of mammary glands necessary for milk synthesis. Oxytocin (Option A) is responsible for the milk ejection reflex (let-down) but does not cause tissue growth. Estrogen (Option B) stimulates ductal growth and overall breast enlargement during puberty and pregnancy but is not the specific driver of the alveolar milk-producing tissue growth during established lactation. Progesterone (Option D) supports alveolar development in preparation for milk production during pregnancy but its levels drop significantly after delivery to allow for the full action of prolactin. Therefore, prolactin is the essential hormone for both the development of productive breast tissue and actual milk synthesis in the postnatal period

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Until when can a postpartum intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) be inserted?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 48 hours

Postpartum IUCD should be inserted within 48 hours.

An intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and promotes leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium so that the fertilized egg is unable to implant.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In Breslau's second life test, organ tested is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stomach and Intestine

Breslau's second life test is used in forensic medicine to determine whether a newborn survived long enough after birth to swallow air.

The test examines the stomach and intestines for the presence of swallowed air.

• Positive test: Stomach and intestines float in water due to the presence of swallowed air, indicating the infant lived after birth.
• Negative test: Stomach and intestines sink, suggesting the infant did not survive long enough to swallow air.

Types of Breslau's Tests

1. Breslau's First Life Test (Hydrostatic Lung Test)

• Organ tested: Lungs
• Purpose: Determines whether respiration has occurred.
• Positive test: Lungs float.

2. Breslau's Second Life Test (Gastrointestinal Float Test)

• Organ tested: Stomach and intestines
• Purpose: Determines whether the infant survived long enough to swallow air after birth.
• Positive test: Stomach and intestines float.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Brain – Not used in Breslau's life tests.
• B. Heart – Not examined in Breslau's tests.
• C. Lung – Tested in Breslau's first life test, not the second.

NEET PG Pearl

| Test | Organ Tested | Indicates

| ---- | ------------ | ---------

| Breslau's First Life Test | Lungs | Respiration has occurred

| Breslau's Second Life Test | Stomach & Intestines | Infant survived long enough to swallow air

| Ploucquet's Test | Lungs (lung-body weight ratio) | Evidence of respiration

| Fodere's Test | Middle ear | Presence of air after birth
questions.learning: Stomach and Intestine Breslau's second life test is used in forensic medicine to determine whether a newborn survived long enough after birth to swallow air.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs causes activation of K+-ATP channels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nicorandil

Nicorandil causes activation of K+-ATP channels. This leads to the hyperpolarization of the smooth muscle cells leading to vasodilatation.

It also has nitrate like cGMP dependent action. Nicorandil dilates both arteries and veins leading to a decrease in afterload and preload of the heart.

Molsidomine, isosorbide dinitrate, and nitroglycerin are nitrates. They do not act on K-ATP channels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following marked areas in the histopathological specimen shows calcification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given specimen is that of an epiphyseal cartilage, where zone 3 corresponds to the zone of calcification.

Epiphyseal cartilage is divided into five zones :

• The resting zone consists of hyaline cartilage without morphological changes in the cells (option 1)
• In the proliferative zone, chondrocytes divide rapidly and form columns of stacked cells parallel to the long axis of the bone (option 2)
• The hypertrophic cartilage zone contains large chondrocytes whose cytoplasm has accumulated glycogen. The resorbed matrix is reduced to thin septa between the chondrocytes.
• Simultaneous with the death of chondrocytes in the calcified cartilage zone, the thin septa of cartilage matrix become calcified by the deposit of hydroxyapatite.
• In the ossification zone, endochondral bone tissue appears (option 4). Blood capillaries and osteoprogenitor cells formed by mitosis of cells originating from the periosteum invade the cavities left by the chondrocytes. The osteoprogenitor cells form osteoblasts, which are distributed in a discontinuous layer over the septa of the calcified cartilage matrix. Ultimately, the osteoblasts deposit bone matrix over the three-dimensional calcified cartilage matrix.

The epiphyseal cartilage is responsible for the growth in the length of bone and it disappears in adults, which is why bone growth ceases in adulthood.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with weakness of the right side of the face with the loss of pain and temperature. Pain and temperature sensation of the left leg is also lost. The lesion is most likely located at?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lateral pons

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral pontine syndrome which occurs due to a lesion located at lateral pons.

Lateral pontine syndrome occurs due to the involvement of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery.

• Ipsilateral manifestations include:

• CN VII: Facial paralysis
• CN V: loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face.
• Vestibular nerve or nucleus: Horizontal and vertical nystagmus, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, oscillopsia.
• Auditory nerve or cochlear nucleus: Deafness, tinnitus.
• Middle cerebellar peduncle: Ataxia of limb and gait.

• Contralateral manifestations include:

• Spinothalamic tract: Loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body.

Medial pontine syndrome occurs due to the involvement of the paramedian branch of the basilar artery.

• Ipsilateral manifestation

• CN VI: Diplopia(lateral rectus muscle paralysis - the affected eye looks downwards and inwards)
• Vestibular nucleus: Nystagmus.
• Middle cerebellar peduncle: Ataxia of limb and gait.

• Contralateral manifestation

• Corticobulbar and corticospinal tract: Paralysis of face, arm, and leg.
• Medial lemniscus: loss of touch and proprioception from the body.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who was diagnosed with epilepsy was put on retigabine TDS. Now phenytoin is being added. Which of the following changes should be made to retigabine?
options: Stop retigabine and start on carbamazepine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase the dose

The dose of retigabine should be increased when phenytoin is added because phenytoin can decrease the plasma concentration of retigabine when given together.

Retigabine is also known as ezogabine. Metabolism of the drug occurs by glucuronidation and acetylation. Its half-life is about 7-11 hours and hence requires thrice-daily dosing. When it is administered with phenytoin or carbamazepine there may be a reduction in the plasma concentration of the drug. So the dose of retigabine should be increased when given along with these drugs.

It is a potassium(K+) channel opener that enhancer transmembrane potassium currents mediated by the KNCQ family of ion channels. It was approved as an adjunctive agent for focal onset seizures of patients above 18 years. But because of its adverse effects like retinal abnormalities and blue pigmentation, the production of the drug was discontinued by the manufacturer.

Other drug interactions of phenytoin:

It is an inducer of the enzymes CYP2C8/9, CYP3A4/5, and other CYPs. It is also an inhibitor of CYP2C9/19.

• Phenobarbitone can inhibit the metabolism of phenytoin. But the overall interaction is unpredictable as both the drug enhance each other's degradation by enzyme induction.
• Phenytoin and carbamazepine induce each other's metabolism.
• Valproate increases the level of unbound phenytoin by displacing the protein-bound form and decreasing its metabolism.
• Phenytoin increases the metabolism of steroids, oral contraceptives, doxycycline, theophylline, etc by enzyme induction.
• It produces competitive inhibition of warfarin metabolism. (Increased risk of bleeding when given together)
• Drugs like chloramphenicol, warfarin, isoniazid, and cimetidine can inhibit the metabolism of phenytoin and cause its toxicity.
• Sucralfate decreases the absorption of phenytoin by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.learning: Increase the dose — The dose of retigabine should be increased when phenytoin is added because phenytoin can decrease the plasma concentration of retigabine when given together.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby assessed 5 minutes after birth, is found to be cyanosed with irregular gasping respiration. Heart rate is 60 beats/min, and shows minimal response to stimulation with some flexion of extremities. The Apgar score for this newborn is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

The Apgar score in this baby is 4. It is calculated as:

Appearance: blue - score 0

Pulse: <100 beats/min - score 1

Grimace: with minimal response to stimulation - score 1

Activity: some flexion of the extremities - score 1

Respiratory effort: irregular - score 1

The total score is 4.

Apgar score is not used to guide resuscitation, and resuscitation must be initiated before the 1-minute score. The change of score at sequential time points following birth reflects how well the baby is responding to resuscitative efforts.

Causes for low Apgar score are:

• Fetal distress
• Prematurity
• Drugs like analgesics, narcotics, sedatives, magnesium sulfate
• Acute cerebral trauma
• Precipitous delivery
• Airway obstruction (choanal atresia)
• Congenital pneumonia or sepsis
• Haemorrhage- hypovolemia

False-negative Apgar score is seen in maternal acidosis and high fetal catecholamine levels.

A total score of 10 indicates that the infant is in the best possible condition. An infant with a score of 0-3 requires immediate resuscitation. If the score at 5 minutes remains less than 7, the infant should be assessed again every 5 minutes for the next 20 minutes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The image of a drug is given below. It is used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subglottic stenosis

The given drug is Mitomycin-C. It is used topically in the management of subglottic stenosis.

Mitomycin-C is derived from the Streptomyces caespitosus bacteria. It can modify wound healing at a molecular level by inhibiting DNA synthesis by cross-linking DNA, acting like an alkylating agent (cell cycle non-specific). It has been used to inhibit post-surgical scar formation and as a chemotherapeutic agent for solid tumors.

Mitomycin-C is employed in the treatment of superficial bladder tumors, postoperative glottic and subglottic stenosis, and tracheal scarring after tracheal reconstruction surgery.

Subglottic stenosis is the narrowing of the airway in the subglottis, clinically presenting with biphasic stridor. Diagnosis is made if the subglottic diameter is <4mm in full-term infants and if the subglottic diameter is <3mm, in the case of premature infants.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is not classified as a non- depolarizing muscle relaxant?
questions.explanation: Muscle relaxants (neuromuscular blocking agents) used in anesthesia are divided into two main categories based on their mechanism of action at the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. "Suxamethonium" (Succinylcholine) is the only clinically used "depolarizing" muscle relaxant. It works by mimicking acetylcholine, causing persistent depolarization of the motor endplate, which is often visible as muscle fasciculations. Pancuronium (Option A), Rocuronium (Option B), and Vecuronium (Option D) are all "non-depolarizing" muscle relaxants. These act as competitive antagonists, blocking the receptor without triggering a response. Suxamethonium is favored for rapid sequence induction due to its very fast onset and short duration, but it is associated with side effects like hyperkalemia and malignant hyperthermia. Non-depolarizing agents are used for maintaining relaxation during surgery and their effects can be reversed with agents like neostigmine or sugammadex. Identifying the category is essential for managing the timing of intubation and the reversal of anesthesia
questions.learning: Muscle relaxants (neuromuscular blocking agents) used in anesthesia are divided into two main categories based on their mechanism of action at the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Defective Tyrosine transaminase is associated with _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 2 Tyrosinemia

Defective Tyrosine transaminase is associated with type II tyrosinemia, known as Oculocutaneous tyrosinemia.

There are three types of tyrosinemias:

* Type 1 tyrosinemia: also known as hepatorenal tyrosinemia is an autosomal recessive condition. The defective enzyme is fumaryl acetoacetate hydrolase. Clinical features are liver failure, hypoglycemia, boiled cabbage odor in the urine, and mental retardation.

* Type 2 is known as oculocutaneous tyrosinemia or Richner-Hanhart syndrome. The defective enzyme is tyrosine transaminase. Clinical features are palmoplantar keratosis, painful corneal erosions, photophobia, and mental retardation.

* Type 3 is known as neonatal tyrosinemia. It is due to the deficiency of 4-Hydroxyphenylpyruvate hydroxylase. Clinical features include normal liver function, developmental delay, seizures, and intermittent ataxia.

Alkaptonuria is an inborn error of metabolism due to the deficiency of an enzyme homogentisate oxidase, leading to the accumulation of homogentisic acid in connective tissue resulting in ochronosis. Due to the oxidation and polymerization of homogenetic acid, it shows a characteristic blackening of urine on standing for a long time or black stain in diapers. They often present in the third to the fourth decade of life.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with a history of trauma presents with hearing loss, and a high-resolution CT (HRCT) scan is performed. Which of the following structures is not typically visualized on HRCT?
questions.explanation: High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the gold standard for visualizing the bony architecture of the middle and inner ear. It provides excellent detail of the bony labyrinth, including the 2.5 turns of the cochlea (Option A), the vestibule (Option B), and the semicircular canals (Option C). HRCT is highly effective at identifying temporal bone fractures or ossicular chain disruptions. However, HRCT uses X-rays and is primarily limited to visualizing bone and air spaces; it does not have the soft-tissue resolution to visualize microscopic structures like the Organ of Corti, which is the sensory neuroepithelium within the cochlear duct. To visualize fine soft-tissue details, fluids, or nerves (like the vestibulocochlear nerve), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the required modality. Therefore, while HRCT is essential after trauma, it cannot directly confirm damage to the delicate sensory hair cells of the inner ear
questions.learning: High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the gold standard for visualizing the bony architecture of the middle and inner ear.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to the OPD with complaints of amenorrhoea for the past year. She has a history of postpartum hemorrhage and lactational failure. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sheehan's syndrome

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Sheehan's syndrome.

Sheehan's syndrome (SS) is postpartum hypopituitarism secondary to the necrosis of the pituitary gland. It usually results from severe hypotension or shock caused by massive hemorrhage during or after delivery. Patients with SS have varying degrees of anterior pituitary hormone deficiency. The hyperplastic enlargement of the pituitary, which occurs normally during pregnancy, increases the risk of infarction.

Affected women may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to a deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to a deficiency of gonadotropins). Because deficiencies of some or all pituitary-responsive hormones may develop after the initial insult, Sheehan syndrome can be heterogeneous and may not be identified for years.

It can present acutely as pituitary apoplexy, an endocrine emergency, characterized by a sudden onset of headache, nausea, visual deficits, and in severe cases, severe hypoglycemia, hypotension and shock, CNS hemorrhage, and death.

Also, it can present late with the following features:

• Loss of pubic and axillary hair
• Hypothyroidism due to decreased TSH secretion
• Adrenal insufficiency due to low ACTH

Treatment is by hormone replacement - first glucocorticoids, later - thyroid hormone, sex steroids, vasopressin and growth hormones are given. If there is evidence of progressive visual loss, cranial nerve involvement or loss of consciousness, immediate surgical decompression must be carried out. Fertility can be achieved in these women with hMG and hCG. Clomiphene is ineffective.

Option B: Rotor syndrome is a type of hereditary hyperbilirubinemia with autosomal recessive inheritance. Affected individuals have mild jaundice and hyperbilirubinemia.

Option C: Prolactinoma or pituitary adenoids is the condition of hyperprolactinemia diagnosed by a prolactin level >200 μg/L. It usually presents with infertility, amenorrhea, and galactorrhea.

Option D: Acromegaly is characterized by the signs and symptoms pertaining to excessive growth hormone secretion.
questions.learning: Sheehan's syndrome — The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Sheehan's syndrome. Sheehan's syndrome (SS) is postpartum hypopituitarism secondary to the necrosis of the pituitary gland.

questions.text: cGMP is the second messenger of
questions.explanation:

Vasodilatory actions of NO are mediated by cGMP.

NO is a hormone derived from the amino acid arginine. It activates guanylyl cyclases in vascular smooth muscle cells resulting in the conversion of cGTP to cGMP (2nd messenger). cGMP activates cGMP dependent protein kinase, which causes blood vessels to relax.

cGMP is the second messenger for nitric oxide and atrial natriuretic factor.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which region of the brain regulates and coordinates the vomiting reflex?
questions.explanation: The vomiting reflex is a complex process coordinated by the vomiting center located in the medulla oblongata. A critical component of this system is the Area Postrema (Option C), situated on the floor of the fourth ventricle. The Area Postrema functions as the Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ); it lacks a functional blood-brain barrier, allowing it to detect circulating toxins, drugs, or metabolic waste products in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Once triggered, it sends signals to the vomiting center to initiate the emetic response. The apneustic and pneumotaxic centers (Options A and B) are located in the pons and regulate the rhythm of breathing. The hypothalamus (Option D) regulates temperature, hunger, and thirst but does not directly control the vomiting reflex. The Area Postrema is a primary target for antiemetic medications, making it a vital structure in clinical pharmacology and neurology

questions.text: Which among the following is false regarding Mollaret’s meningitis?
options: Diagnosed by demonstration of HSV abs in CSF
Persistence of HSV DNA in CSF

Correct answer: C. Neurologic sequelae common

Mollaret’s meningitis is a form of benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis; most commonly associated with Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2).

• Recurrent episodes of aseptic meningitis
• Lymphocytic pleocytosis in CSF
• Episodes last 2–5 days and resolve spontaneously
• HSV DNA may be detected in CSF by PCR

Important characteristic:

• The disease is self-limiting and typically does not cause permanent neurological sequelae.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with significant dyspnea and a paradoxical increase in jugular venous distension during inspiration. On examination, no cardiac murmurs are heard. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical finding of neck vein distension during inspiration is known as "Kussmaul's sign." Normally, the jugular venous pressure (JVP) decreases during inspiration due to the negative intrathoracic pressure pulling blood into the heart. Kussmaul's sign occurs when the right ventricle cannot expand to accommodate this increased venous return. This is a classic finding in Constrictive Pericarditis, where the heart is encased in a rigid, calcified pericardium. Patients also present with progressive dyspnea and signs of right-sided heart failure (ascites, edema) but usually have no significant heart murmurs. Aortic regurgitation (Option B) would cause a diastolic murmur. Tricuspid stenosis (Option C) could cause a murmur and an elevated JVP but would show a prominent 'a' wave rather than a positive Kussmaul sign. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (Option D) can cause right heart failure but is less classically associated with a positive Kussmaul's sign than constrictive pericarditis. Therefore, the combination of dyspnea, elevated JVP with inspiration, and no murmurs is highly diagnostic of pericardial constriction
questions.learning: The clinical finding of neck vein distension during inspiration is known as "Kussmaul's sign." Normally, the jugular venous pressure (JVP) decreases during inspiration due to the negative intrathoracic pressure pulling blood into the heart.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Levothyroxine/liothyronine acts by binding to thyroid receptors. Thyroid hormone receptors belong to which of the following class of receptors?
options: Transmembrane receptor linked to tyrosine kinase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nuclear receptor

Thyroid hormone receptors belong to the class of nuclear receptors.

Nuclear receptors are a family of ligand-regulated transcription factors that are activated by various lipid-soluble signals, including retinoic acid, thyroid hormone, and steroid hormones. They primarily function as transcription factors and directly interact with the genomic DNA to regulate gene expression.

Nuclear receptors can either remain anchored in the cytoplasm via chaperone proteins until freed by ligand-binding (e.g., steroid and vitamin D receptors) or can reside in the nucleus bound to specific DNA response elements even in the absence of ligand (e.g., thyroid hormone, PPARγ, and retinoic acid receptors).
