questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with a long history of chronic alcohol use presents with confusion, visual disturbances, gait instability, and impaired short- term memory. These findings are suggestive of a nutritional deficiency. Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely responsible for this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of confusion, vision disturbances (ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus), and unsteady gait (ataxia) in a chronic alcoholic is diagnostic for Wernicke encephalopathy. When accompanied by short-term memory loss and confabulation, it is termed Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. This condition is caused by a severe deficiency of Thiamine (Vitamin B1). Thiamine is a vital cofactor for key enzymes in glucose metabolism, particularly in the brain. Ascorbic acid (Option A, Vitamin C) deficiency causes scurvy. Retinol (Option C, Vitamin A) deficiency leads to night blindness and xerophthalmia. Folate (Option D, Vitamin B9) deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and can contribute to cognitive issues, but it does not produce the specific oculomotor and gait disturbances seen in Wernicke’s. Chronic alcohol use impairs thiamine absorption and storage, making these patients highly susceptible. It is a medical emergency; administering glucose before thiamine can worsen the condition by further depleting the remaining thiamine stores
questions.learning: The clinical triad of confusion, vision disturbances (ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus), and unsteady gait (ataxia) in a chronic alcoholic is diagnostic for Wernicke encephalopathy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A surgeon sees a necrotic bowel when operating on a child for an inguinal hernia. What is true about the resection and anastomosis of the bowel?
options: The surgeon must use chromic catgut
The surgeon must not include the submucosa in the sutures
The surgeon must use the single-layer, extramucosal suture technique
The surgeon must use the single-layer seromuscular suture technique
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The surgeon must use the single-layer, extramucosal suture technique

The standard technique used currently for resection anastomosis of the bowel is a one-layer extra mucosal suture technique since it causes the least tissue necrosis and luminal narrowing. Interrupted and continuous single-layer suture techniques are adequate and safe.

The extra mucosal suture must also include the submucosa because this layer has a high collagen content and it is the most stable suture layer in all sections of the gastrointestinal tract.

Catgut has now been replaced with absorbable synthetic polymers. Stapling devices can be used when speed is required.

The above diagram depicts the rule of halves, which is observed in hypertension, and "number 9" denotes adequately treated subjects.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which statement accurately characterizes radiotherapy?
options: Intensity is inversely proportional to square of the distance
Vomiting is a late adverse reaction
Rapidly proliferating cells are most radioresistant
All the adverse effects are reversible
questions.explanation: Radiotherapy is based on the principles of physics and radiobiology. The statement that "Intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance" (Option A) is an accurate characterization, reflecting the Inverse Square Law. This means as the distance from the radiation source doubles, the intensity of the radiation reaching the patient falls to one-fourth. Vomiting (Option B) is typically an acute (early), not a late, adverse reaction to radiation, often occurring within hours of treatment. According to the law of Bergonié and 'Tribondeau, rapidly proliferating cells (Option C) are actually the most radiosensitive, not radioresistant. While many acute side effects resolve, not all adverse effects are reversible (Option D); late effects like fibrosis, tissue atrophy, and secondary malignancies are often permanent. Accurate knowledge of the inverse square law is vital for medical physicists and oncologists to ensure precise dose delivery to the tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding healthy tissues
questions.learning: Radiotherapy is based on the principles of physics and radiobiology. The statement that "Intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance" (Option A) is an accurate characterization, reflecting the Inverse Square Law.

This patient fulfills all criteria. She has a stable, unruptured ectopic with mass <3.5 cm and β-hCG <5000 IU/L, fulfilling criteria for medical management. Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate is preferred. Surgery (e.g., salpingectomy) is reserved for hemodynamic instability, larger mass or fetal cardiac activity.

≥15% fall in hCG → treatment successful

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 19-year-old female presents with primary amenorrhea. On examination, she has normal breast and pubic hair development, but her vagina ends in a blind pouch, and her uterus is not palpable. What is the next step in the investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pelvic ultrasound

The given clinical scenario of a girl with primary amenorrhea, normal breasts, and pubic hair, with a blind-ending vagina and non-palpable uterus, is suggestive of Mullerian agenesis. The next step would be to do an ultrasound to look for uterine anomalies.

Absent uterus and vagina in a person with female genotype and phenotype are features of Mullerian agenesis, also known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome. In this condition, the ovaries are normal and secondary sexual characters are well-developed with normal external genitalia. This condition is associated with anomalies of the spine/skeleton and the kidneys along with the urinary tract.

Diagnosis is made with the help of pelvic sonography, MRI or laparoscopy. Patients may have rudimentary Mullerian bulbs without an endometrial cavity. These should be surgically excised if they are symptomatic.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with fusion of the carpal bones. Which gene is associated with hand–foot syndrome in this condition?
questions.explanation: Hand-Foot-Genital Syndrome (HFGS) is a rare, autosomal dominant condition characterized by limb malformations and urogenital defects. The syndrome is caused by a mutation in the HOXA13 homeobox gene, which is essential for the development of distal limbs and the genitourinary tract. Clinical features often include shortening of the thumbs and great toes, as well as fused carpal bones. Regarding the distractors, BCL6 (Option B) is a gene primarily associated with B-cell lymphomas and cancer progression. FGFR (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor) mutations (Option C) typically cause skeletal dysplasias like achondroplasia or craniofacial syndromes rather than HFGS. COL11 (Option D) mutations are linked to hearing loss and Stickler syndrome. Thus, the specific combination of hand/foot anomalies and skeletal fusion is a hallmark of HOXA13 pathogenic variants

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: As per the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, until when can an MTP be performed on grounds of contraceptive failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 20 weeks

As per the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act of 2021, the upper limit for termination of pregnancy on grounds of contraceptive failure is 20 weeks.

The MTP Act of 2021 specifies special circumstances for termination of pregnancy beyond 20 weeks till 24 weeks of gestation. These include:

* Survivor of sexual assault, rape or incest.

* Minors

* Mentally ill women including mental retardation

* Change of marital status during the ongoing pregnancy (widowhood and divorce)

* Women with physical disabilities (Major disability criteria - Rights of persons with disabilities act - 2016)

* Women with pregnancy in humanitarian settings or disaster or emergency situations as declared by the government.

* Fetal malformations that have a substantial risk of being incompatible with life or if the child is born, may suffer from serious physical or mental abnormalities to be seriously handicapped. (Option A)

Termination of pregnancy can be done only up to 20 weeks based on grounds of contraception failure.

* Until 20 weeks of gestation - Opinion of one doctor

* 20-24 weeks of gestation - Opinion of two doctors

* The name and particulars of the woman whose pregnancy has been terminated cannot be disclosed. It can only be revealed to a person in force authorised by law. The ground for failure of contraception is extended to women and their partners.

Pearl PF1638: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971

MTP Act with 2021 amendments

Indications:

* Therapeutic - to save the life of the mother

* Eugenic - to prevent the risk of the child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality i.e. first-trimester viral infections, teratogenic drug intake, radiation exposure

* Humanitarian - pregnancy resulted from rape or incest

* Social - pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives

Rules:

* Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in the performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy.

* MTP should be carried out in a government or government-recognized hospital. Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district.

* The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.

Consent:

The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police.

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Confidentiality:

A register for recording the details of MTP must be kept for at least 5 years. The patient's name must not be entered, only the reference number is used. Unlawful disclosure of patient's details is punishable with 1-year imprisonment ± fine.
questions.learning: 20 weeks As per the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act of 2021, the upper limit for termination of pregnancy on grounds of contraceptive failure is 20 weeks.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents after a fall and is found to have bleeding from the ear on clinical examination. What is the investigation of choice in this situation?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic bleeding from the ear is a clinical hallmark of a temporal bone fracture. High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the gold standard investigation because it provides the detailed imaging required to detect fine fracture lines, ossicular chain disruption, and otic capsule involvement. A CBC (Option A) helps assess overall trauma status but cannot diagnose bone injuries. MRI (Option B) is excellent for soft-tissue or intracranial injuries but lacks the bony resolution needed to evaluate the petrous bone or ossicles. Standard X-ray (Option D) has poor sensitivity for these complex fractures and is inadequate for visualizing middle ear anatomy. Early HRCT is essential to guide management, preserve hearing function, and prevent complications like CSF otorrhea or facial nerve palsy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 21 weeks of gestation is found to have a fetus diagnosed with meningomyelocele (a type of spina bifida) and is considering medical termination of pregnancy. In this situation, what legal and medical requirements must be fulfilled to proceed with MTP?
options: Consent of Husband with opinion of one doctor
Her consent with consent of 2 doctors
questions.explanation: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 in India, for an MTP performed between 20 and 24 weeks of gestation (such as in this 21-week case with a substantial fetal anomaly), the mandatory legal requirement is the opinion and consent of two registered medical practitioners. Most importantly, only the pregnant woman's own written consent is legally required; the consent of the husband or partner (Option A) is not a requirement under Indian law. Option C is incomplete as the patient's consent is the primary legal prerequisite. For terminations up to 20 weeks, only one doctor's opinion is required. Terminations beyond 24 weeks for fetal anomalies require the permission of a State-level Medical Board. Therefore, for this specific second-trimester scenario, the woman’s autonomous consent alongside the professional agreement of two doctors constitutes the full legal and medical requirement

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which congenital abnormality or teratogenic effect is most commonly associated with the use of lithium during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Lithium is a commonly used mood stabilizer that is known to cross the placenta and exert specific teratogenic effects, particularly during the first trimester of pregnancy. The most famous and well-documented association is with cardiac defects (Option A), specifically Ebstein’s anomaly. This rare malformation involve the apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets, leading to "atrialization" of the right ventricle and potential heart failure. While the absolute risk is lower than once thought, it remains significantly higher than in the general population. Facial defects (Option B), CNS defects (Option C), and urogenital defects (Option D) are associated with other teratogens (like phenytoin or valproic acid) but are not the hallmark toxicity of lithium. Therefore, for any pregnant patient requiring lithium, detailed fetal echocardiography is recommended at 18–20 weeks to screen for these cardiac malformations

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per the national immunization schedule, which vaccines are indicated at the first visit for immunization of a 13-month-old baby who has not been previously immunized?
options: BCG, OPV 1st dose, Pentavalent 1st dose, Rota virus 1st dose
OPV 1st dose, Pentavalent 1st dose, Measles 1st dose
OPV 1st dose, DPT 1st dose, Measles 1st dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. OPV 1st dose, DPT 1st dose, Measles 1st dose

DPT-1, OPV-1 and Measles 1st dose will be given to this child.

BCG can only be given upto 1 years of age, according to the National Immunisation Schedule. BCG will not be given to this child, if the National Immunisation Schedule is followed.

Please note that BCG can be given upto 5 years of age, as part of the catch-up immunization schedule, which is put forth by the Indian Academy of Paediatrics and that is not followed in government setups.

OPV can be given till 5 years of age.

Measles can be given till 5 years of age.

DPT can be given till 7 years of age (with booster doses).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 25 year old male patient was given cisatracurium for neuromuscular blockade. Which of the following is not true regarding the class to which the drug belongs?
options: Their action is potentiated by Mg2+ and antagonized by Ca2+
Characteristic train of four fade present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metabolized by pseudo cholinesterase

Cisatracurium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (NDNMB) belonging to the benzylisoquinolinium group.

• Act as competitive antagonists at nicotinic (Nm) acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
• Prevent depolarization → flaccid paralysis
• Potentiation and antagonism:

• Mg²⁺ → potentiates blockade (↓ ACh release)
• Ca²⁺ → antagonizes blockade (↑ ACh release)

• Neuromuscular monitoring:

• Shows train-of-four (TOF) fade, a hallmark of non-depolarizing block

Unique Feature of Cisatracurium:

• Undergoes Hofmann elimination (organ-independent degradation)
• Also minor ester hydrolysis
• NOT metabolized by pseudocholinesterase

Hence, option C is incorrect

Why not other options:

A. Competitive inhibition at ACh receptors: True

B. Mg²⁺ potentiation, Ca²⁺ antagonism: True

D. TOF fade present: True (characteristic of non-depolarizing block)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · Basics Of Cell Cytoskeleton
questions.text: Tight junction is located at which part of the cell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Apicolateral

Tight junctions sit like a “sealant ring” at the apicolateral border, preventing leakage between cells and maintaining polarity. Tight junctions (zonula occludens) are located at the apicolateral border of epithelial cells, forming the most apical component of the junctional complex. Two Key Functions:

1.     Barrier function → blocks paracellular transport

2.     Fence function → maintains polarity (apical vs basolateral domains)

| -------- | -------- | -------- | ------------

| Tight junction | Apicolateral | Barrier, polarity | Claudin, Occludin

| Adherens junction | Below tight | Cell adhesion | Cadherins

| Desmosome | Lateral | Mechanical strength | Desmoglein

| Gap junction | Lateral | Communication | Connexin

Adherens junctions and desmosomes lie more basally.

Clinical correlations:

1. Leaky gut / diarrhea

• Loss of tight junction integrity → ↑ permeability

2. Cholera toxin

• Affects ion transport → overwhelms junctional barrier

3. Blood-brain barrier

• Tight junctions are extremely well-developed

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A farmer adds a chemical to a water pool that acts by inhibiting cellular respiration. The substance specifically targets Complex III of the electron transport chain, disrupting electron transfer and proton gradient formation required for ATP synthesis. Which chemical produces this effect by inhibiting Complex III?
questions.explanation: Antimycin A is a well-known antibiotic and piscicide (fish poison) that specifically inhibits Complex III (ubiquinone-cytochrome c oxidoreductase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. By binding to the Qi site, it blocks the transfer of electrons from cytochrome b to cytochrome c1, effectively halting the generation of the proton gradient necessary for ATP synthesis. Rotenone (Option A) is an insecticide that inhibits Complex I. TTFA (Option B, thenoyltrifluoroacetone) is a specific inhibitor of Complex II. Cyanide (Option D) is a lethal poison that inhibits Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) by binding to the heme iron. Understanding these specific inhibitors is fundamental for biochemistry and toxicology. Antimycin is often used in laboratory research to isolate the functions of different segments of the respiratory chain. For the farmer's use in a "water pool" as a piscicide, Antimycin's mechanism of action is the defining characteristic
questions.learning: Antimycin — A is a well-known antibiotic and piscicide (fish poison) that specifically inhibits Complex III (ubiquinone-cytochrome c oxidoreductase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about battered baby syndrome?
options: Skin lesions and bruises of various ages are seen on the body
It occurs due to the tendency of a child to fall repeatedly
The syndrome is a result of firearm injuries
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Skin lesions and bruises of various ages are seen on the body

Skin lesions and bruises of various ages are a classical feature of a child with battered baby syndrome.

A battered child is one who has received repetitive physical injuries as a result of non-accidental violence, produced by a parent or guardian, there may also be deprivation of nutrition, care, and affection.

The syndrome must be considered in any child:

• In whom the degree and type of injury varies with the history given
• When injuries are of different ages and in different stages of healing
• When there is a purposeful delay in seeking medical attention despite serious injury
• Who exhibits evidence of fracture of any bone, subdural hematoma, failure to thrive, soft tissue swelling or skin bruising
• Who dies suddenly

Skeletal survey, which includes the following, should be done in a case of suspected child abuse:

• AP views of the entire skeleton
• Dedicated views of hands and feet
• Lateral views of appendicular skeleton, skull and spine

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the population norm for an ASHA worker?
questions.explanation: Under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in India, the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) serves as a vital link between the community and the public health system. The standard population norm for an ASHA is one worker for every 1,000 people in plain areas. However, in tribal, hilly, or difficult-to-reach areas, this norm is flexible and can cover populations up to 2,500. Option A (700-1000) is incorrect as 1,000 is generally the lower threshold. Option B (1000-1500) and Option D (2000-2500) do not reflect the full standard range utilized by health planners. The ASHA is primarily a woman from the village itself, trained to promote immunization, institutional delivery, and basic nutrition. This population ratio ensures that health services are accessible and that the worker is not overburdened while maintaining close ties with her community
questions.learning: Under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in India, the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) serves as a vital link between the community and the public health system.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the logo shown in the image.
questions.explanation: The logo depicted—a red plus sign with a central circle inside a square border—is the official symbol for Suraksha Clinics in India. These clinics are part of the National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) initiative to provide specialized, stigma-free management for Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and Reproductive Tract Infections (RTIs). The International Red Cross (Option A) uses a simple red cross on a white background. The National AIDS Control Programme (Option B) often uses the "Red Ribbon" symbol. The Family Planning campaign (Option D) classically utilizes the inverted Red Triangle. Suraksha Clinics are integrated into government hospitals to offer syndromic management, counseling, and free testing to vulnerable populations. Identifying this logo is essential for clinicians to refer patients for specific STI services. Thus, the visual mark specifically identifies the Suraksha Clinic network

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Among the drugs used for the acute management of asthma, which one does not act by causing bronchodilation?
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone is a systemic corticosteroid that acts primarily by suppressing the underlying inflammatory response rather than through direct bronchodilation. It reduces airway mucosal edema and decreases the production of inflammatory mediators over several hours. Salbutamol (Option A) is a short-acting beta-2 agonist that directly relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, providing rapid widening of the airways. Ipratropium (Option B) is an anticholinergic agent that blocks muscarinic receptors, thereby preventing bronchoconstriction. Deriphyllin (Option C), a combination containing theophylline derivatives, works by inhibiting phosphodiesterase and antagonizing adenosine receptors to cause bronchodilation. While hydrocortisone is essential in managing an acute asthma exacerbation to prevent late-phase reactions and reduce the need for hospitalization, it does not provide the immediate relief of airway obstruction seen with the other listed bronchodilators. Corticosteroids are delayed-onset life-savers in asthma management, whereas beta-agonists are the immediate relievers
questions.learning: Hydrocortisone is a systemic corticosteroid that acts primarily by suppressing the underlying inflammatory response rather than through direct bronchodilation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient in the ICU undergoes an attempted subclavian vein catheterization, which is unsuccessful. Soon afterward, the patient develops hypotension with a rising pulse rate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The procedure for subclavian vein catheterization carries a significant risk of accidental pleural injury, which can lead to a pneumothorax. The entry of air into the pleural space reduces venous return to the heart, resulting in sudden hypotension (BP drop) and a reflex tachycardia (pulse rise). In the intensive care unit, this can progress rapidly to a life-threatening tension pneumothorax. Typical clinical signs include unilateral decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on percussion. While displacement or dislodgement of the endotracheal tube (Options B and D) would cause respiratory distress and hypoxia, they are not standard complications of a central line attempt. Air embolism (Option C) is a possible but less common complication that presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse and a "mill wheel" murmur. Given the specific context of a failed subclavian attempt followed by hemodynamic instability, pneumothorax is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient was brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident in an unconscious state. He has a head injury. On examination, he has bradycardia and hypertension. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 6. What is the next appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intubate and provide ventilation

The patient's clinical presentation of level of consciousness, bradycardia, and high blood pressure after a head injury, the next appropriate step is to intubate and provide ventilation to ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation while managing potential increased intracranial pressure.

Cushing reflex causes a triad of symptoms:

* Reflex bradycardia (via arterial baroreceptors)

* Hypertension (with widened pulse pressure)

* Irregular respiration (bradypnea).

When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to rostral ventrolateral neurons is compromised. This leads to local hypoxia and hypercapnia which in turn increase the discharge of the central chemoreceptors located on the ventrolateral medullary surface. This activation causes a rise in blood pressure which then restores the blood flow to the medulla.

However, the arterial baroreceptors sense this increase in the systemic blood pressure and cause a reflex decrease in the heart rate.

Other Options:

Option A: CT head is not the immediate priority in a patient with compromised consciousness and potentially raised ICP. Ensuring proper ventilation and oxygenation takes precedence.

Option C: The patient's symptoms are likely related to the head injury, and thrombolysis is not the appropriate intervention at this time.

Option D: Administering IV fluids might be important in some situations, such as maintaining blood pressure in a hypotensive patient. However, it does not directly address the patient's altered consciousness and potentially raised ICP.

Pearl PF1160: NICE Guidelines for CT in Head Injury

National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) Guidelines for Computed Tomography (CT) in Head Injury

Indications for CT imaging within 1 hour of following risk factors being identified:

* Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) <13 at any point

* GCS <15 at 2 hours after injury on assessment in emergency department

* Focal neurological deficit

* Suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture

* More than one episode of vomiting

* Post-traumatic seizure

Indications for CT imaging within 8 hours

* Age >65 years

* Coagulopathy (e.g., aspirin, warfarin, or rivaroxaban use)

* Dangerous mechanism of injury (e.g., fall from a height, road traffic accident)

* Retrograde amnesia >30 minutes

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The stroke volume depends on end-diastolic volume. This is best represented as
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Length-tension relationship

The relationship between end-diastolic volume and stroke volume is best represented by length-tension relationship.

This is explained by the ‘Frank-Starling law of heart’ which states that ‘ the volume of blood ejected by the ventricle depends on the volume present in the ventricle at the end of the diastole’. The length of the myocytes depend on the volume (and hence tension) present at the end of the diastole, which in turn, depends on the volume returned to the heart, or the venous return.

• The Frank-Starling law governs the normal ventricular function and ensures that the cardiac output equals venous return, within physiological limits.
• There is a curvilinear relationship between stroke volume or cardiac output and the ventricular end-diastolic volume.
• Agents that increase the contractility of the cardiac muscle have a positive inotropic effect and produce increased stroke volume and thereby increased cardiac output for a given end-diastolic volume. (Eg: Digoxin)
• Agents that decrease the contractility of the cardiac muscle have a negative inotropic effect and produce decreased stroke volume (and cardiac output) for a given end-diastolic volume.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 25-year-old female reported symptoms of anxiety, palpitations, sweating, breathlessness, chest pain, and a feeling of impending doom. She recalls having experienced 5-6 similar episodes in the past 6 months, each episode lasting for about 20-30 minutes. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Panic disorder

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a panic disorder.  Panic disorder refers to an acute intense attack of anxiety accompanied by feelings of impending doom. Such attacks may not only occur in response to a fearful situation, or phobic objects, or in response to obsession or separation as in other anxiety disorders.

Panic disorder is characterized by the presence of an abrupt surge of intense fear or intense discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes. During the episode, the person may experience symptoms like palpitations, sweating, trembling or shaking, shortness of breath, nausea, dizziness, chest pain or discomfort or fear of dying. The patient also might feel like losing control, having a heart attack, or going crazy.

There is a dysfunction in major neurotransmitter systems like norepinephrine, serotonin, and GABA. Panic-inducing substances or panicogens may induce such attacks and include substances like 5-35% carbon dioxide, sodium lactate, bicarbonate, yohimbine (α blocker), flumazenil (GABA antagonist), cholecystokinin and caffeine.

It is not attributable to any drug abuse, medication, medical condition or mental disorder.

Treatment of this condition can be done by cognitive behavioral therapy and drugs like benzodiazepines (alprazolam, lorazepam), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (paroxetine), tricyclic antidepressants and monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
questions.learning: Panic disorder — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a panic disorder. Panic disorder refers to an acute intense attack of anxiety accompanied by feelings of impending doom.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child presents with abdominal pain, palpable purpura, and renal involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP)

Henoch–Schönlein Purpura (HSP), now called IgA vasculitis, is the most common systemic vasculitis in children. It is an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis that classically presents with the tetrad of:

• Palpable purpura (predominantly over the lower limbs and buttocks)
• Arthritis/arthralgia
• Abdominal pain
• Renal involvement (hematuria/proteinuria due to IgA nephropathy)

Key differentiating features:

• Henoch–Schönlein Purpura (IgA vasculitis):

• Palpable, non-thrombocytopenic purpura
• Colicky abdominal pain ± GI bleeding/intussusception
• Hematuria/proteinuria
• Often follows an upper respiratory tract infection
• Chickenpox: Pruritic vesicular rash in different stages.
• Scarlet fever: Sandpaper-like erythematous rash with strawberry tongue.
• Hyaline membrane disease: Respiratory distress in preterm neonates.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby in the NICU is being evaluated for his features of microcephaly and hepatomegaly. CT scan revealed nodular periventricular calcifications. Congenital CMV infection is suspected. Which of the following samples is the best to detect the organism using PCR?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urine

Among the following options, urine is the best sample to be sent for the diagnosis of congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection.

In congenital CMV infections, the investigation of choice is PCR or viral culture. It should be done within the first three weeks of life (after this period, it is difficult to distinguish between a congenital and an acquired infection). Since not all affected infants are viremic at birth, urine is a more reliable sample than blood.

Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester. The risk of transmission is high in the third trimester. 90% of the infected babies are asymptomatic and have lesser chances of having late sequelae.

The clinical manifestations include hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. Neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss.

There is no definitive treatment for congenital CMV infection. Treatment with ganciclovir is indicated only in patients with progressive neurologic disease and deafness.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Pott’s puffy tumor is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subperiosteal abscess of frontal bone

Pott's puffy tumor is the subperiosteal abscess of frontal bone. It is a complication of frontal sinusitis.

An acute infection of the frontal sinus can cause osteomyelitis of the frontal bone. Suppurative material then breaches the frontal bone leading to subperiosteal abscess formation in the tissues of the forehead. Pus may form externally under the periosteum as a soft boggy swelling with a doughy consistency called Pott’s puffy tumor. It may spread internally causing subdural, epidural, and periorbital abscesses as well as secondary septic thrombosis of the dural sinuses. It is more often seen in adults as frontal sinus is not developed in infants and children.

CT of the brain and paranasal sinuses is the most appropriate investigation. It can show the involvement of sinuses as well as intracranial or soft tissue spread of infection.

Treatment consists of large doses of antibiotics, abscess drainage, and trephining of the frontal sinus through its floor. Sometimes, the removal of sequestra and necrotic bone may also be required.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: At what age is a child typically able to ride a tricycle, walk up stairs using alternate steps, but cannot hop?
questions.explanation: Gross motor milestones are predictable markers of a child's development. A child who can ride a tricycle and walk up stairs with alternate steps has typically reached the developmental level of a 3-year-old. Hopping on one foot is a more advanced balance skill that is usually mastered by age 4. Therefore, a child who has mastered the 3-year milestones but cannot yet hop is most likely around 3.5 years old. Option A (2.5 years) is too young, as they would still be walking up stairs "two feet per step" and likely cannot pedal a tricycle. Options C and D (4.5 and 5.5 years) are too old, as these children should already be able to hop and even skip (by age 5). Understanding these age-specific gross motor skills helps pediatricians identify developmental delays. In summary, the ability to alternate feet on stairs and pedal a trike, but failing to hop, specifically brackets the child's developmental age
questions.learning: Gross motor milestones are predictable markers of a child's development. A child who can ride a tricycle and walk up stairs with alternate steps has typically reached the developmental level of a 3-year-old.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding choledochal cyst is not correct?
options: Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of intra- and/or extrahepatic biliary system.
Majority of patients are diagnosed after 10 years of age.
It is associated with an increased risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma.
Radical excision of the cyst is the treatment of choice.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Majority of patients are diagnosed after 10 years of age.

• (a) Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of intra- and/or extrahepatic biliary system: Correct. Choledochal cysts are congenital cystic dilatations of the biliary tree, involving the extrahepatic and/or intrahepatic ducts.
• (b) Majority of patients are diagnosed after 10 years of age: Incorrect. Most patients are diagnosed in childhood, although adult presentation is increasingly recognized. Therefore, saying that the majority are diagnosed after 10 years is not correct.
• (c) It is associated with an increased risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma: Correct. Choledochal cysts are associated with an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma, particularly with longstanding cysts.
• (d) Radical excision of the cyst is the treatment of choice: Correct.Complete excision of the cyst with biliary reconstruction, usually Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy, is the treatment of choice for most extrahepatic choledochal cysts.
questions.learning: Majority of patients are diagnosed after 10 years of age. • (a) Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of intra- and/or extrahepatic biliary system: Correct.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A male patient came with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse around 20 years ago. Now, he complains of neurological symptoms and visual disturbances. Which of the following will be seen on exposure of his pupils to light?
options: Pupils react but do not accommodate.
Pupils accommodate but do not react.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pupils accommodate but do not react.

The patient most likely has acquired syphilis due to unprotected sex and has developed neurological and visual disturbances secondarily as a complication of neurosyphilis. Argyll-Robertson pupils(ARP) are seen associated with neurosyphilis where the pupils accommodate but do not react to light.

Argyll Robertson pupil is attributed to a dorsal midbrain lesion of neurosyphilis that affects the pupillary light pathway but spares the more ventrally placed pupillary near reflex pathway(Accomdation pathway), thereby causing a light-near dissociation.

Features of Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP) include:

• Bilateral small, irregular pupils in dim light
• Accommodation Reflex Present (ARP)- The eye accomdates by constricting the pupil for a near target.
• Light Reflex absent: pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light.
• Cocaine eye drops(mydriatics) induced mydriasis.

Other clinical features in neurosyphilis:

• Fleeting and repetitive lancinating pains, primarily in the legs
• acute abdominal pain with vomiting(visceral crisis)
• Tabes dorsalis with Ataxia and gait disturbances due to loss of position sense
• Loss of reflexes in the legs
• Paresthesias, bladder disturbances

Other causes of light-near dissociation are:

In unilateral eye

1. Adie pupil
2. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
3. Aberrant regeneration of the third cranial nerve

In bilateral eyes

1. Neurosyphilis
2. Type 1 diabetes mellitus
3. Myotonic dystrophy

Note: Adie's pupil more commonly manifests in young women with unilateral large regular pupil(Anisocoria) with absent light reflex and sluggish and tonic accomdation reflex.

It is caused by post-ganglionic parasympathetic pupillary supply damage and is usually associated with absent knee jerk.

Adie's pupil constricts with weak pilocarpine (0.1%) drops, while normal pupil and Argyll robertson pupil does not.
questions.learning: Pupils accommodate but do not react. The patient most likely has acquired syphilis due to unprotected sex and has developed neurological and visual disturbances secondarily as a complication of neurosyphilis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient with a history of hypertriglyceridemia was prescribed statins to help stabilize his levels. Despite taking statins, the levels remained elevated at around 600 mg/dL. Which of the following drugs can be added to help lower his triglyceride levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gemfibrozil

In this case of a 50-year-old patient with a history of hypertriglyceridemia who was prescribed statins for his elevated triglyceride levels and still had elevated triglyceride levels, gemfibrozil can be given to help lower his triglyceride levels.

Gemfibrozil belongs to the fibrate group of drugs that bind to peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARα), which stimulate fatty acid oxidation, reduce the expression of apo C-III (inhibitor of lipolysis), and thereby reduce triglyceride levels.

Gemfibrozil is a first-line drug for patients with markedly raised triglyceride levels. Episodes of acute pancreatitis are prevented in patients with chylomicronaemia and severe hypertriglyceridemia. It is most effective in type III hyperlipoproteinemia.

Other options:

Option A: Niacin - Decreases the production of VLDLs and decreases the catabolism of HDLs.

Option C: Cholestyramines are bile acid-binding resins and they increase the excretion of bile acids. This results in increased conversion of cholesterol mobile acids by the liver.

Option D: Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal sterol absorption, reduces LDL cholesterol, minimal increase in HDL level and also decreases the absorption of phytosterols.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about Trichomonas vaginalis?
options: Twitching motility is seen on wet saline mount
Cysts are seen on wet saline mount of vaginal secretions
It is not a sexually transmitted infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Twitching motility is seen on wet saline mount

Trichomonas vaginalis has a jerky or twitching type of mobility on the wet saline mount. Option B is the correct answer.

T. vaginalis is the only protozoan with one stage in its life cycle, i.e., trophozoite form (no cyst stage is seen). It is an obligate parasite and cannot live without close association with vaginal, urethral, or prostatic tissues. Sexual transmission is the main route of infection. Other modes are fomites, and babies during passage through the infected birth canal.

The incubation period ranges from 4 days to 4 weeks.

The common presentation of trichomoniasis is foul-smelling frothy vaginal discharge, itching, dysuria, and dyspareunia. Petechial hemorrhage and mucosal capillary dilation give the appearance of a strawberry cervix. Chicken-like epithelium occurs due to intracellular edema which is also a characteristic feature.

The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on cysteine-peptone-liver-maltose (CPLM) medium or plastic envelope medium (PEM). The treatment of choice is metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose.

T. vaginalis infection in women may lead to infertility, preterm birth, and low-birth-weight infants. In men, trichomoniasis has been also associated with infertility through inflammatory damage to the genitourinary tract or interference with sperm function.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of cartilage?
questions.explanation: The histological image shows hyaline cartilage, identifiable by its glassy, homogeneous extracellular matrix (ECM) rich in Type II collagen. Chondrocytes are seen residing within spaces called lacunae. Hyaline cartilage is the most common type and is found in articular surfaces, the respiratory tract, and the fetal skeleton. Elastic cartilage (Option B) contains dense networks of elastic fibers, making it more flexible, and is found in the outer ear and epiglottis. Fibrocartilage (Option C) contains thick bundles of Type I collagen, providing high tensile strength for intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis. Calcified cartilage (Option D) is hyaline cartilage that has accumulated calcium salts, often seen during bone development or aging. The lack of visible fibers in the matrix confirms this as hyaline

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with 6 weeks amenorrhea and a positive pregnancy test came with complaints of lower abdominal pain, moderate bleeding PV. She was hemodynamically stable. On USG, there was no gestational sac in the uterus. Ovaries were normal and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. What is the next line of management?
options: Declare as complete abortion and follow-up in 15 days
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Follow-up with beta-HCG

The patient presents with a history of 6 weeks of amenorrhea, a positive urine pregnancy test, abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding. However, the ultrasound examination does not reveal a gestational sac in the uterus, which could indicate either an ectopic pregnancy or an abortion. In such cases, the next line of management is to follow up with beta-HCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) levels.

Beta-HCG levels above 1500 mIU/mL are considered the discriminatory value, beyond which a gestational sac should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound.

If the gestational sac is not visible on ultrasound and the beta-HCG levels are above 1500 mIU/mL, it suggests an ectopic pregnancy. On the other hand, if the beta-HCG levels are below 1500 mIU/mL, they can be repeated after 48 hours and interpreted as follows:

• Decreasing HCG levels between day 1 and day 3 suggest a possible abortion.
• If the HCG levels rise during this period but does not double, it indicates a likely ectopic pregnancy.

Note: While some institutions set the discriminatory threshold for HCG levels at ≥ 1500 mIU/mL, others use ≥ 2000 mIU/mL.
questions.learning: Follow-up with beta-HCG — The patient presents with a history of 6 weeks of amenorrhea, a positive urine pregnancy test, abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Testosterone is converted to which of the following hormone by aromatase enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estradiol

Aromatase (CYP19) converts testosterone to estradiol.
questions.learning: Estradiol Aromatase (CYP19) converts testosterone to estradiol.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the status of the marked individual?
options: Has a disease of chronic origin
questions.explanation: In standard pedigree notation, an individual symbol (square for male, circle for female) placed within brackets indicates that the person has been adopted. Specifically, dashed brackets usually signify that the individual was "adopted in" from another family, whereas solid brackets indicate the individual was "adopted out" to a different family. Chronic or curable diseases (Options B and C) would be represented by specific shading or filling of the symbol, not by brackets. Twins (Option D) are indicated by connecting siblings to a single point on the lineage line with a diagonal bar or triangle. Therefore, the use of brackets around a pedigree symbol is strictly reserved to denote the adoption status of that family member, ensuring accurate genetic history tracking
questions.learning: In standard pedigree notation, an individual symbol (square for male, circle for female) placed within brackets indicates that the person has been adopted.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young woman experiences recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting. Which acid–base disturbance is she most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: Recurrent self-induced vomiting, as seen in bulimia nervosa, results in a characteristic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Vomiting leads to the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), which contains hydrogen ions (H⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻). Loss of H⁺ directly raises blood pH, producing metabolic alkalosis. The associated loss of chloride further impairs renal bicarbonate excretion, allowing bicarbonate to accumulate and perpetuate the alkalosis. In addition, volume depletion from vomiting activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, leading to increased potassium and hydrogen ion loss in urine, which contributes to hypokalemia and sustains the alkalotic state. Respiratory acidosis (Option A) and respiratory alkalosis (Option B) are caused by abnormalities in ventilation and are not primary consequences of vomiting. Metabolic acidosis (Option C) occurs in conditions such as diarrhea (bicarbonate loss) or diabetic ketoacidosis, which are physiologically opposite to the acid loss seen with vomiting. Therefore, the most likely acid–base disturbance in this patient is metabolic alkalosis
questions.learning: Recurrent self-induced vomiting, as seen in bulimia nervosa, results in a characteristic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Vomiting leads to the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), which contains hydrogen ions (H⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The most likely condition is traumatic cataract, which can develop months after blunt ocular trauma and commonly presents with progressive blurring of vision.
questions.explanation: Iridodialysis is the traumatic detachment of the iris from its root at the ciliary body, which typically occurs after non-penetrating blunt force trauma. The resulting structural change often creates a "D-shaped" pupil and a visible biconvex gap at the periphery, leading to symptoms like blurring of vision, photophobia, or monocular diplopia. Ankyloblepharon (Option B) refers to the abnormal fusion of the eyelid margins and is not an internal iris injury. Vossius Ring (Option C) is a pigment ring on the anterior lens capsule shaped exactly like the pupil, also caused by blunt trauma, but it does not cause a displaced pupil. Cycloiriditis (Option D) is an inflammation of the iris and ciliary body; while trauma can be a trigger, it presents with acute pain and redness rather than a structural peripheral gap. Diagnosis is made by clinical examination and slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and treatment depends on the severity of the visual symptoms
questions.learning: Iridodialysis is the traumatic detachment of the iris from its root at the ciliary body, which typically occurs after non-penetrating blunt force trauma.

questions.text: The X-ray shows an antero-posterior view of a normal elbow. What is the structure marked in the image called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Capitulum

The structure marked is called capitulum.

The lower end of the humerus forms the condyle which is expanded to form the articular part which includes:

* Capitulum ("little head"): a rounded projection that articulates with the head of the radius.

* Trochlea ("pulley"): a pulley-shaped surface that articulates with the trochlear notch of the ulna. The medial edge of the trochlea projects down 6 mm more than the lateral edge which results in the formation of carrying angle.

The image of a normal elbow joint is given below:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old shipbuilding worker with a 25- year occupational history presents with dyspnea. Which specific malignancy is most likely associated with his occupational exposure?
questions.explanation: The patient’s 25-year history of working in the shipbuilding industry is a classic occupational risk factor for asbestos exposure. While asbestos exposure increases the risk of many lung cancers, Malignant Mesothelioma (Option B) is the most specific malignancy associated with it. Mesothelioma is an aggressive cancer of the pleural or peritoneal lining and is almost exclusively linked to prior asbestos inhalation. Bronchogenic carcinoma (Option A), including small cell (Option C) and squamous cell (Option D) types, are more common overall in the general population and are primarily driven by smoking, although their risk is significantly multiplied in asbestos workers. However, the term "most specific" refers to the cancer that is pathognomonic for the exposure. Therefore, given the long-term shipyard history, Malignant Mesothelioma is the expected definitive diagnosis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by pleural biopsy and imaging showing diffuse pleural thickening

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 56-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use presents with progressive abdominal distension. On examination, there is shifting dullness and bilateral pedal edema. Diagnostic paracentesis is performed. Serum albumin is 3.2 g/dL and ascitic fluid albumin is 1.0 g/dL. What is the SAAG value, and what does it suggest about the underlying cause of ascites?
options: SAAG = 1.1 g/dL; suggests portal hypertension as the cause
SAAG = 2.2 g/dL; suggests portal hypertension as the cause
SAAG = 2.2 g/dL; suggests a non-portal hypertensive cause such as malignancy or tuberculosis
SAAG = 1.1 g/dL; suggests a non-portal hypertensive cause such as malignancy or tuberculosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SAAG = 2.2 g/dL; suggests portal hypertension as the cause

Rationale: SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin = 3.2 − 1.0 = 2.2 g/dL. A SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the underlying mechanism (due to increased hydrostatic pressure pushing albumin-poor fluid into the peritoneal cavity, while albumin itself remains largely retained intravascularly) — classically seen in cirrhosis (as in this patient with a history of alcohol use), congestive heart failure, and Budd-Chiari syndrome. A SAAG <1.1 g/dL instead points toward non-portal hypertensive causes, where the peritoneum itself is diseased and "leaky" to albumin, such as peritoneal tuberculosis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, or pancreatitis-related ascites. Since this patient's SAAG is 2.2 g/dL (≥1.1), portal hypertension — not a non-portal hypertensive cause — is the correct interpretation, making options C and D incorrect despite their correct arithmetic of "high SAAG," and option A incorrect on calculation.

Quick reference — SAAG Interpretation:

| SAAG | Interpretation | Common Causes

| ---- | -------------- | -------------

| ≥1.1 g/dL (High gradient) | Portal hypertension | Cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, CHF, Budd-Chiari syndrome, constrictive pericarditis, massive liver metastases

| <1.1 g/dL (Low gradient) | Non-portal hypertensive (peritoneal disease) | Peritoneal tuberculosis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome, serositis

Formula: SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin (both measured on the same day)

Note: SAAG is far more accurate than the older "exudate vs transudate" (total protein-based) classification of ascites.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with painful vesicles in the external auditory meatus and over the tympanic membrane. In addition to that, he also has facial nerve palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis and which is the site that is affected?
options: Ramsay Hunt syndrome and basal ganglion
Ramsay Hunt syndrome and geniculate ganglion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ramsay Hunt syndrome and geniculate ganglion

This clinical vignette is suggestive of Ramsay Hunt syndrome, and the geniculate ganglion is affected.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome, also called herpes zoster oticus, is a late complication of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection that results in inflammation of the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

The causative agent, the varicella-zoster virus, is a double-stranded DNA virus. Clinical features are facial paralysis along with vesicular rash in the external auditory canal and pinna. Intense pain around the ear in addition to the vesicles also occurs. There may also be anesthesia of the face, giddiness, and hearing impairment due to the involvement of the Vth and VIIIth nerves.

Facial nerve palsy on the affected side, vesicles in the external acoustic meatus & auricle, and pain in the ear form the classic triad.

The illustration given below shows the clinical features seen in Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

The treatment of Ramsay Hunt syndrome involves antiviral medications like acyclovir or famciclovir, as well as corticosteroids like prednisone.

Melkersson syndrome presents with a triad of facial paralysis, swelling of the face and lips, and furrows in the tongue.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A construction site worker comes in with red eyes and lacrimation. He got chuna particles in his eyes an hour ago. What is the initial step in the treatment?
options: Patch the eye after topical lubricants
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Irrigation with normal saline

The initial step in the management of a patient presenting with chemical burns is immediate and thorough irrigation with the available clean water or normal saline delivered through an IV tubing. This is done to prevent further damage.

Along with irrigation, contaminant elimination through mechanical means shall be done. In the event of residue, especially with lime (chuna), it is essential to meticulously eliminate them using a swab stick.

After the initial steps, maintenance of favorable conditions for rapid and uncomplicated healing by following measures:

• Topical antibiotic drops, for example, moxifloxacin 4-6 times a day to prevent infection.
• Steroid eye drops to decrease inflammation, neutrophil infiltration, and treat anterior uveitis. Caution is advised after 2 weeks, as steroids could disrupt collagen synthesis.
• Cycloplegics, such as atropine, might enhance comfort.

Grading of severity (Roper–Hall system) of chemical injuries is based on corneal clarity and severity of limbal ischemia:

• Grade 1  is characterized by a clear cornea (epithelial damage only) and no limbal ischemia (excellent prognosis).
• Grade 2 shows a hazy cornea but with visible iris detail and less than one-third of the limbus being ischemic (good prognosis).
• Grade 3 manifests as a total loss of the corneal epithelium, stromal haze obscuring iris detail, and between one-third and half of the limbus showing ischemia (guarded prognosis).
• Grade 4 manifests with an opaque cornea and more than 50% of the limbus showing ischemia (poor prognosis).
questions.learning: Irrigation with normal saline — The initial step in the management of a patient presenting with chemical burns is immediate and thorough irrigation with the available clean water or normal saline delivered through an IV tubing.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the splint shown below in the image:
questions.explanation: The image depicts a "Foot Abduction Orthosis" (FAO), also known as a Denis Browne bar or Steenbeek brace. It is a vital component in the management of Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV) or clubfoot. After the deformity is corrected using serial casting (the Ponseti method), the FAO is used to maintain the correction and prevent recurrence. It consists of two shoes set in 60–70 degrees of external rotation and 10–15 degrees of dorsiflexion, attached to a metal bar. Option C (Ponseti cast) refers to the serial plaster casts used before the brace. Option D (Pirani) and Option B (DiMeglio) are scoring systems used to assess the severity of clubfoot, not types of splints. Compliance with FAO use (initially 23 hours a day for three months, then at night for 3–4 years) is the single most important factor in preventing the relapse of clubfoot deformity
questions.learning: The image depicts a "Foot Abduction Orthosis" (FAO), also known as a Denis Browne bar or Steenbeek brace. It is a vital component in the management of Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV) or clubfoot.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant presents with prolonged jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. The child is exclusively breastfed and otherwise well. HIDA scan is non-excretory. What is the next best step in management?
options: Rule out galactosemia using enzyme assay.
The child has breast milk jaundice and start formula feeding after 3 weeks.
Immediate liver biopsy to confirm diagnosis.
Perform a hepatic ultrasound to look for causes like biliary atresia.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immediate liver biopsy to confirm diagnosis.

Biliary atresia should be strongly suspected in an infant with prolonged jaundice, pale (acholic) stools, dark urine, and a non-excretory HIDA scan. The next best step is liver biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate it from other causes of neonatal cholestasis.

• Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia presenting after 2 weeks of life is always pathological
• Pale stools and dark urine indicate obstructive cholestasis
• Non-excretion on HIDA scan suggests biliary obstruction but is not definitive
• Liver biopsy shows bile duct proliferation, portal fibrosis, and bile plugs, helping confirm biliary atresia

Why other options are incorrect:

• Galactosemia presents with systemic illness (vomiting, hypoglycemia, sepsis), not isolated cholestasis
• Breast milk jaundice causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal stool and urine color
• Ultrasound is useful but not the next best step after a non-excretory HIDA; biopsy provides definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Immediate liver biopsy to confirm diagnosis. Biliary atresia should be strongly suspected in an infant with prolonged jaundice, pale (acholic) stools, dark urine, and a non-excretory HIDA scan.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided should cover at least _______
options: 1/3 of the total protein requirement + ½ of total energy requirement
2/3 of the total protein requirement + ½ of total energy requirement
½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement
½ of the total protein requirement + 2/3 of total energy requirement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement

Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided must cover at least ½ of the total protein requirement and 1/3 of total energy requirement to children in schools.

The MDM scheme is also called School Lunch Programme and has been operational since 1961 in India. Currently, it functions under the broad coverage of the Minimum Needs Programme.

Some other principles of the MDM are:

• The meal provided under the MDM should only be a supplement and not a substitute to home diets.
• The cost of the meals should be reasonably low.
• The meal should be easy to cook in schools.
• Locally available foods must be used, for as far as possible.
• The menu should be regularly changed to avoid monotony.
questions.learning: ½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided must cover at least ½ of the total protein requirement and 1/3 of total energy requirement to children in schools.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital after an eye injury sustained while cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel. A foreign body was suspected to be impacted in his eye. Which of the following is the best investigation for foreign body localization?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT

CT scan is the best method for intraocular foreign body (IOFB) localization.

The foreign bodies most likely to penetrate and be retained in the eye are minute chips of iron or steel. While chipping stone with an iron chisel, the chip of the iron chisel is more likely to enter the eye than the stone. A foreign body entering the eye may cause damage by:

* mechanical effects

* introduction of infection

* reacting with the intraocular tissues

Anteroposterior and lateral view X-rays are recommended for locating an IOFB as most foreign bodies are radio-opaque. Ultrasonographic localization can tell the position of even non-radiopaque foreign bodies. CT scan is the best method of IOFB localization.

MRI is contraindicated for metallic IOFB.MRI can be detrimental for a patient with a history of an intraocular foreign body (IOFB) after cutting stone with a hammer and chisel. It can cause further damage by producing movements of the foreign body if it is magnetic. The use of MRI is contraindicated for metallic (iron) foreign bodies and is not recommended as a screening procedure.

Management: A foreign body should always be removed unless:

* it is inert and probably sterile

* little damage has been done to vision

* the process of removal will destroy sight

Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and cause atrophy.

Clinical features:

* Iris: first stained greenish and later turns reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis.

* Pupil: iron deposition in sphincter leads to mydriasis.

* Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract.

* Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium.

* Secondary open-angle Glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.
questions.learning: CT CT scan is the best method for intraocular foreign body (IOFB) localization. The foreign bodies most likely to penetrate and be retained in the eye are minute chips of iron or steel.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Patient has variable deceleration. What does that indicate?
questions.explanation: Variable decelerations are defined as abrupt decreases in the fetal heart rate (FHR) that vary in timing, duration, and shape (often appearing as a "V", "U", or "W" on the tracing). These are the most common type of deceleration and are primarily caused by transient umbilical cord compression. This compression leads to a brief state of fetal hypoxia, which triggers reflex vagal stimulation and a subsequent drop in FHR. In contrast, early decelerations (Option B) are caused by fetal head compression and mirror the uterine contractions. Late decelerations (Option C) indicate uteroplacental insufficiency and start after the peak of a contraction. Maternal hypotension (Option D) typically results in prolonged decelerations or baseline bradycardia due to reduced uterine blood flow. Therefore, the specific "variable" pattern on a cardiotocograph is the clinical signature of cord compression
questions.learning: Variable decelerations are defined as abrupt decreases in the fetal heart rate (FHR) that vary in timing, duration, and shape (often appearing as a "V", "U", or "W" on the tracing).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about corneal epithelium?
options: Regeneration is limited to the limbus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bowman's membrane regenerates

Bowman's membrane is acellular. Hence, it will not regenerate but heals by scarring when damaged.

Corneal stem cells are located at the corneoscleral limbus (Option A), so the regeneration is limited to the limbus.

The cornea comprises distinct layers:

1. Corneal epithelium is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (Option C), with microvilli on the apical layer (Option D) to enhance surface area and tear film attachment. It consists of basal, columnar, wing, and squamous cells.
2. Bowman’s membrane, a superficial stromal layer, is acellular, collagen-based, and incapable of regeneration.
3. The stroma, the thickest layer constituting 90% of corneal thickness, houses collagen fibrils with ground substances such as chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate, maintaining transparency. It cannot regenerate and heals with scarring.
4. Dua’s layer or Pre-Descemet's membrane is the toughest.
5. Descemet’s membrane extends anteriorly to Schwalbe’s line and possesses regenerative potential.
6. Endothelium, a metabolically active monolayer, lacks regenerative ability. It maintains deturgescence through active pumps, ensuring transparency with a usual cell density of approximately 3000 cells/mm² measured by specular microscopy.
questions.learning: Bowman's membrane regenerates Bowman's membrane is acellular. Hence, it will not regenerate but heals by scarring when damaged.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 24-yr-old man presents with an excessive desire for sexual intercourse. What is this called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Satyriasis

An excess desire for sexual intercourse in males is called satyriasis.

Satyriasis is also known as Don Juanism. In some men, sexual activity is a means to mask their deep feelings of inferiority. Some have unconscious homosexual impulses, which they deny by compulsive sexual contact with women. Many of them are no longer interested in the women after sex.

Other options

* Nymphomania: An excess desire for sexual intercourse in females

* Frotteurism: Sexual gratification achieved by touching or rubbing against a nonconsenting person.

* Masochism: The tendency to derive sexual gratification from one's own pain or humiliation.

Note: Don Juanism represents hypersexuality in males.

Pearl PF1284: Sexual disorders

Phase

Characteristics

Disorder

Treatment

Desire

Focuses on the patient's drives, motivation, and desires

Hypoactive sexual desire: Patients have a decrease or absence of sexual fantasies, desires, etc

Couples therapy may be indicated if due to marital conflict

Consists of a sense of sexual pleasure with accompanying physiologic changes

Female sexual arousal disorder: Persistent failure to achieve or maintain sufficient sexual interest or arousal during the sexual act

Impotence: Persistent or recurrent inability to attain or maintain an adequate erection until completion of the sexual act

Behavioral techniques, such as the use of dilators and relaxation

questions.learning: Satyriasis — An excess desire for sexual intercourse in males is called satyriasis. Satyriasis is also known as Don Juanism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with skin tightening and arthralgia. Raynaud's phenomenon was positive. Lab investigations showed ANA positive and Anti-Scl-70 antibody. The presence of which of the following conditions is associated with this antibody?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Interstitial Lung Disease

Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are characteristic of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

They are strongly associated with interstitial lung disease, which is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients.

| Antibody | Disease Type | Key Association

| -------- | ------------ | ---------------

| Anti-Scl-70 | Diffuse SSc | Interstitial lung disease (ILD)

| Anti-centromere | Limited SSc (CREST) | Pulmonary hypertension

| Anti-RNA polymerase III | Diffuse SSc | Renal crisis

A) Calcinosis cutis

• Seen in CREST syndrome (limited SSc)
• Associated with Anti-centromere antibody, NOT Scl-70

B) Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE)

• “Watermelon stomach”
• Seen in systemic sclerosis but:

• More linked with limited SSc / anti-centromere

• Not specifically tied to Scl-70

Calcinosis and GAVE are linked to limited cutaneous disease, while myositis is not a typical association.

| Feature | Diffuse SSc | Limited SSc (CREST)

| ------- | ----------- | -------------------

| Skin involvement | Widespread | Distal only

| Antibody | Anti-Scl-70 | Anti-centromere

| Lung | Interstitial fibrosis (ILD) | Pulmonary HTN

| Renal crisis | Common | Rare

| Progression | Rapid | Slow
questions.learning: Interstitial Lung Disease Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are characteristic of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. They are strongly associated with interstitial lung disease, which is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in these…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding phase Ib of a cystometrogram?
options: It is due to the elasticity of bladder
It is due to the plasticity the bladder has
The graph is flat due to the contractility of the bladder
Micturition occur at the start of Ib
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is due to the plasticity the bladder has

The true statement regarding phase Ib in the cystometrogram is that segment Ib is due to plasticity of the badder. Plasticity is the ability of an object to deform its shape without breaking.

Cystometrogram is a plot of intravesical pressure against the volume of fluid in the bladder. The curve shows three segments:

* Ia- initial slight rise in pressure when the first increments in the volume are produced

* Ib- long, nearly flat segment as further increments are produced

* II- sudden, sharp rise in pressure as the micturition reflex is triggered.

* The dotted line- pressure-volume relation if the micturition had not occurred.

The flatness of segment Ib is a demonstration of the law of Laplace. The law of Laplace states that the pressure (P) in a spherical viscus is equal to twice the wall tension (T) divided by the radius (R). This is expressed as P= 2T/R. In the bladder, the tension increases as the bladder get filled. Since the radius also increases because of the plasticity of the bladder, there is only a slight increase in pressure until the bladder is relatively full.

The first urge to void is felt at a bladder volume of about 150 mL. A marked sense of fullness is felt at a bladder volume of 400ml.

Micturition reflex is the result of sensory signals from the stretch receptors in the bladder wall, which are conducted to the sacral segments of the cord through the pelvic nerves and then efferent signals conducts back again to the bladder through the parasympathetic nerve fibers.

The micturition reflex pathway is given below.

Other options:

Option A: Elasticity refers to the ability of an object to return to its original state after being deformed by an external force. Elasticity of bladder is responsible for the recoil shrinking of the bladder after micturition.

Option C: Contractility is the ability to contract and increase the tension or decrease the length or dimensions. Contractility of the bladder is responsible for the voiding of urine. It doesn't contribute to the flat curve in Ib.

Option D: Voiding starts at the end of Ib and the start of II.
questions.learning: It is due to the plasticity the bladder has — The true statement regarding phase Ib in the cystometrogram is that segment Ib is due to plasticity of the badder.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Compared to a pregnant female, a lactating female would require a higher level of nutrient supplementation for which of the following?

Calcium intake of 1200mg/d is advised in postmenopausal women as well.

The RDA of vitamin A is increased by 50mcg in lactation as compared to pregnancy. But the increased vitamin A demand is met from the diet and it is not given as a supplement nutrient. Vitamin A supplements are given only when there is vitamin A deficiency.

The RDA of iron and folic acid is decreased during lactation compared to pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a symptom of cardiac failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-pulsatile elevation of JVP

Heart failure causes venous congestion and reduced cardiac output, producing a combination of:

• Pulmonary symptoms (left heart failure)
• Systemic venous congestion (right heart failure)

Typical symptoms include:

| System | Symptoms

| ------ | --------

| Pulmonary | Dyspnea, orthopnea, PND

| Systemic venous | Pedal edema, hepatomegaly

| General | Fatigue

Framingham Criteria for Congestive Heart Failure, a classic exam favorite used to clinically diagnose CHF. Diagnosis requires:

Either

• 2 Major criteria

OR

• 1 Major + 2 Minor criteria

Diagnostic Criteria

| Major Criteria | Explanation

| -------------- | -----------

| Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) | Sudden breathlessness during sleep

| Neck vein distension (elevated JVP) | Reflects increased right atrial pressure

| Pulmonary rales (crepitations) | Due to pulmonary edema

| Cardiomegaly | Seen on chest X-ray

| Acute pulmonary edema | Severe LV failure

| S3 gallop | Rapid ventricular filling in HF

| Increased central venous pressure (>16 cm H₂O) | Venous congestion

| Hepatojugular reflux | JVP rises with liver compression

| Weight loss >4.5 kg in 5 days with treatment | Response to diuresis

| Minor Criteria | Explanation

| -------------- | -----------

| Bilateral ankle edema | Venous congestion

| Night cough | Pulmonary congestion

| Dyspnea on exertion | Reduced cardiac output

| Hepatomegaly | Congestive hepatomegaly

| Pleural effusion | Fluid accumulation

| Vital capacity reduced by 1/3 | Lung restriction

| Tachycardia (>120/min) | Sympathetic activation

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man is unemployed because he is unable to walk after an accident. His unemployment is classified as a _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Handicap

The patient here being unemployed can be classified as handicap, according to the concept given below.

Disease → Impairment → Disability → Handicap

* Impairment is any loss or abnormality in normal structure or function.

* Disability is the inability to carry out normal actions due to impairment.

* Handicap is experiencing disadvantages due to disability and inability to discharge obligations normally.

In the given example:

* Accident: Disease (or disorder)

* Loss of foot: Impairment (extrinsic or intrinsic)

* Cannot walk: Disability (objectified)

* Unemployed: Handicap (socialized)
