questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the case of a newly occurring (morbid) disease, how does a change in incidence affect the prevalence of the disease?
options: Prevalence is not related to incidence
Incidence will increase, and prevalence will decrease
Prevalence will increase with a decrease in the incidence
questions.explanation: Incidence and prevalence are fundamental epidemiological measures linked by the formula: . Incidence represents the number of new cases of a disease occurring in a population during a specific timeframe. Prevalence represents the total number of existing cases (new and old) at a single point in time. When there is a "new onset" of a morbid disease, the number of new cases (incidence) naturally rises. As these new cases accumulate in the population, they add to the total pool of affected individuals, thereby causing the prevalence to increase as well. Option A is incorrect because the two are mathematically related. Option B is illogical, as an increase in new cases cannot lead to a decrease in total cases without a massive, simultaneous spike in deaths or cures. Option D is generally false, as a drop in incidence usually leads to a eventual drop in prevalence. Thus, for any newly emerging disease, both metrics show a rising trend
questions.learning: Incidence and prevalence are fundamental epidemiological measures linked by the formula: . Incidence represents the number of new cases of a disease occurring in a population during a specific timeframe.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During an explosion, a patient sustains a crushed injury to the lower limb due to collapse of a building. Which type of blast injury does this represent?
questions.explanation: Blast injuries are classified by their physical mechanism. Quaternary injuries are miscellaneous trauma resulting from the blast, including crush injuries from building collapses, burns, and traumatic asphyxia. Primary blast injuries (Option A) result directly from the air compression wave (overpressure) and typically damage hollow organs like the ears (tympanic membrane), lungs, and GIT. Secondary blast injuries (Option B) are caused by flying missiles or projectiles propelled by the blast hitting the body. Tertiary blast injuries (Option C) occur when the individual is physically lifted and thrown against the ground or walls, often leading to fractures or dislocations. A quinary injury category (Option E) also exists for injuries from environmental contaminants like radiation or chemicals. Since this specific patient suffered a crush injury from a structural collapse, it is definitively classified as a quaternary injury
questions.learning: Blast injuries are classified by their physical mechanism. Quaternary injuries are miscellaneous trauma resulting from the blast, including crush injuries from building collapses, burns, and traumatic asphyxia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn at birth was noticed to have a mass in the abdomen, as shown in the image below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Omphalocele

The above image depicts omphalocele.

Omphalocele is a midline abdominal defect and is covered by peritoneal or umbilical sac. Babies born with omphalocele should be thouroughly evaluated for other associated congenital anamolies like cardiac anamolies, neural tube defect and trisomies.

Management includes IV fluids, IV antibiotics, preservation of sac with a sterile saline gauze/bowel bag followed by surgical closure.

Other options:

Option A: An umbilical hernia usually arises within a week of birth but resolves spontaneously by 2 years of age. If it persists beyond 2 years, surgical repair is indicated.

Option B: Gastroschisis should be ruled out while evaluating an omphalocele. Unlike an omphalocele, it lacks a membranous sac covering. It is typically found in a paraumbilical position, most often to the right of the umbilicus.

Option D: Ectopia cordis: Failure of the lateral body wall folds to close in the midline in the thoracic region. This results in the heart remaining outside the thoracic cavity.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The addition of Vitamin A to butter is an example of which of the following public health interventions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Food fortification

Food fortification is the deliberate addition of essential micronutrients to commonly consumed foods to prevent or correct nutrient deficiencies in the population. Addition of vitamin A to butter is an example of food fortification.

Why not the other options?

• A. Food adulteration: Addition of inferior or harmful substances to food, reducing its quality or safety.
• C. Food enrichment: Restoration of nutrients lost during food processing to their original levels (e.g., adding B vitamins to refined flour).
• D. Food addition: Not a recognized public health nutrition intervention.
questions.learning: Food fortification Food fortification is the deliberate addition of essential micronutrients to commonly consumed foods to prevent or correct nutrient deficiencies in the population.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with palpitations. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard at the left third intercostal space, and a pistol-shot sound is noted over the femoral arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of an early diastolic murmur at the left third intercostal space (Erb’s point) is the classic auscultatory finding for Aortic Regurgitation (AR). Palpitations result from the high stroke volume and forceful ventricular contractions. The "pistol shot sound" (Traube's sign) refers to loud systolic sounds heard over the femoral arteries, which is a classic peripheral sign of chronic severe AR caused by the wide pulse pressure. Aortic stenosis (Option B) presents with a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur. Tricuspid regurgitation (Option C) and Mitral regurgitation (Option D) both typically produce holosystolic murmurs rather than diastolic ones . Other signs of AR include a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse and De Musset’s sign (head nodding with each heartbeat). Diagnosis is confirmed with echocardiography to visualize the regurgitant jet and assess left ventricular function. Aortic regurgitation leads to volume overload of the left ventricle and eventual failure if left untreated
questions.learning: The presence of an early diastolic murmur at the left third intercostal space (Erb’s point) is the classic auscultatory finding for Aortic Regurgitation (AR).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 20-year-old female complained of fatigue for the past 1 year along with incidences of bleeding gums. Examination revealed massive splenomegaly and her hb level was noted to be 8gm/dl. Immature cells were seen in the peripheral smear. Her blood workup showed a Total leucocyte count (TLC) of 1,50,000/microL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CML

The clinical presentation with fatigue, bleeding gums, massive splenomegaly, and peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML).

Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decade of life. The chimeric BCR-ABL gene is created by a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation(Philadelphia chromosome). This BCR-ABL gene distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative disorders and is detected by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Clinical features:

Mild to moderate anemia and hypermetabolism, fatigability, weakness, weight loss, and anorexia. Dragging sensation in the abdomen caused by splenomegaly, or the acute onset of left upper quadrant pain due to splenic infarction. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

Peripheral blood:

* Leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

* Blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells.

* Platelet count is usually increased

Bone Marrow:

* Markedly hypercellular marrow because of massively increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors. There is usually an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils.

* There is also an increase in megakaryocytes which usually include small, dysplastic forms and erythroid progenitors are present in normal or mildly decreased numbers. Typically there is an increased reticulin deposition, but overt marrow fibrosis is rare early in the course.

Sea-blue histiocytes - These are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled,green-blue cytoplasm

Other options:
Acute leukemias have a presence of immature blast cells in the bone marrow and peripheral smear usually (>20%) which is not seen in this patient.

ALL lymphoblast cells have Tdt positive which is due to DNA polymerase. These cells can be B cell or T cell subtype. They are distinguished by cell surface markers. CD 10, 19, 20 are positive on B cells while CD2-8 are positive on T cell ALL.

AML has positive staining for myeloperoxidase and auer rods are seen in the cytoplasm.
CLL is a disease seen in elderly patients(>65) and peripheral smear will show smudge cells.
questions.learning: CML — The clinical presentation with fatigue, bleeding gums, massive splenomegaly, and peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the condition given below?
options: Patient must be started on anti-gas gangrene serum therapy
It is a mixed flora aerobic and anaerobic infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is a mixed flora aerobic and anaerobic infection

The given image of extensive perineal soft tissue destruction with intact testis is suggestive of Fournier's gangrene, which is a mixed flora of aerobic and anaerobic infection.

Fournier's gangrene is a type of necrotizing fasciitis (Dartos, Scarpa, and Colle’s fascia) of the perineum, external genitalia, and perianal region. Risk factors include:

1. Immunocompromised states such as HIV, alcoholism, diabetes, etc.
2. Minor procedures in the perineal area (opening of a periurethral abscess).

Pathogenesis is due to the obliteration of arterioles supplying the scrotal skin caused by fulminating subcutaneous polybacterial infection. After a while, the blackish discolouration of the scrotum (gangrene) with crepitus can be seen (image). The testis is usually not affected.

Clinical features of Fournier's gangrene are scrotal pain, fever, prostration, and pallor. Cellulitis spreads rapidly and may be associated with eschars, necrosis, flaking skin, and crepitus.

Diagnosis of Fournier's gangrene is majorly clinical and is a surgical emergency. It should be aggressively managed by urgent surgical debridement and skin grafting in later stages. The infection is controlled by the administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Other options:

Option A: Anti-gas gangrene serum refers to refined equine antitoxin against Clostridium species. Hence, it has no role in Fournier's gangrene.

Option C: Bilateral orchidectomy is not performed as testes are not affected and need not be removed.

Option D: Urinary diversion may be necessary in a few cases, and is not compulsory.
questions.learning: It is a mixed flora aerobic and anaerobic infection — The given image of extensive perineal soft tissue destruction with intact testis is suggestive of Fournier's gangrene, which is a mixed flora of aerobic and anaerobic infection.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient develops Achilles tendonitis along with swelling of the leg after taking an antibiotic. What is the most likely mechanism of action of the drug responsible for these adverse effects?
options: Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis at 50S subunit
Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis
Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.explanation: The development of Achilles tendonitis and swelling is a well-documented adverse effect of fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin, Levofloxacin). These antibiotics work by inhibiting two essential bacterial enzymes: DNA gyrase (Topoisomerase II) and Topoisomerase IV. This inhibition interferes with negative DNA recoiling and strand separation, leading to the failure of DNA replication and transcription, which ultimately causes bacterial cell death. Option B (50S protein synthesis inhibition) describes the mechanism of macrolides. Option C (folic acid inhibition) describes sulfonamides. Option D (cell wall inhibition) is the mechanism for beta-lactams like penicillins. Fluoroquinolones are associated with a significantly increased risk of tendon rupture, particularly in the elderly or those also taking corticosteroids

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman was found dead at home. She was brought to the mortuary by the police and the following findings were noted on examination. Which of the following is the likely cause of her death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Throttling

In the given case scenario and autopsy images showing carotid intimal tear and muscle hematoma with nail marks on neck and absence of ligature mark point towards a diagnosis of throttling.

Other options

Option A- Strangulation by ligature - ligature mark with signs of a struggle would've made this diagnosis more likely.

Option B- Hanging - ligature mark with a suicide note would've made it more likely.

Option C- Drowning- Body recovered from a pond or other water body with other suggestive features like frothing etc  would've made this more likely.
questions.learning: Throttling — In the given case scenario and autopsy images showing carotid intimal tear and muscle hematoma with nail marks on neck and absence of ligature mark point towards a diagnosis of throttling.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with a history of hypertension is given the drug 'X'. Identify 'X'?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aliskiren

Drug X is the direct renin inhibitor. Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor.

Aliskiren is a nonpeptide that binds selectively to the catalytic site of renin and competitively blocks the access of angiotensinogen to this site. As a result of this, angiotensin I is not produced.

It is recommended as an alternative antihypertensive drug for those who do not respond or do not tolerate Ist-line drugs. It can also be given in combination with ACE inhibitor/ARB(angiotensin receptor blocker) to achieve a more complete renin-angiotensin system blockade and greater BP lowering.

Option A: Captopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, which prevents generation of the angiotensin II.

Option B: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that blocks mineralocorticoid receptors.

Option D: Losartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker.
questions.learning: Aliskiren Drug X is the direct renin inhibitor. Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A physician uses the STEP approach to collect essential clinical information. A patient presents with fatigue and dizziness. Which parameter would NOT be assessed using this approach?
questions.explanation: The STEP approach stands for Surveillance of risk factors of Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) as recommended by the World Health Organization. It focuses on collecting modifiable risk factor data in a stepwise manner. 1. Step : Questionnaire (behavioral factors like diet, smoking) 2. Step : Physical measurements (e.g., blood pressure) 3. Step : Biochemical measurements (e.g., blood sugar and blood lipids) Thus, blood pressure, blood sugar, and blood lipid levels are all included in the STEP approach. However, blood group is a genetic/non-modifiable characteristic and is not relevant to NCD risk assessment, so it is not included in the STEP framework. Why other options are correct (i.e., included in STEP): (B) Blood pressure: Measured in Step 2 (C) Blood sugar: Measured in Step 3 (D) Blood lipid: Measured in Step 3 Therefore, the parameter NOT assessed is (A) Blood group
questions.learning: The STEP approach stands for Surveillance of risk factors of Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) as recommended by the World Health Organization. It focuses on collecting modifiable risk factor data in a stepwise manner.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Outlet forceps are applied at which station?
questions.explanation: According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), outlet forceps application requires that the fetal scalp is visible at the introitus without separating the labia. Specifically, the fetal skull has reached the pelvic floor/perineum, and the sagittal suture is in the direct anteroposterior diameter or a slight oblique position. Station +2 (Option C) is classified as a "mid-forceps" delivery if the head is above +2 but engaged, or a "low-forceps" delivery if the leading point is at station +2 or lower but not on the perineum. Station 0 (Option B) is engagement at the level of the ischial spines. Option A (1/5th palpable) refers to the abdominal descent of the head and is not a criteria for outlet forceps. Outlet forceps are considered the safest instrumental delivery type because the fetal head is at the lowest possible point in the birth canal
questions.learning: According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), outlet forceps application requires that the fetal scalp is visible at the introitus without separating the labia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Based on the given image, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pseudoaneurysm of internal carotid artery

The given image is a digital subtraction angiogram(DSA) and it shows a pseudoaneurysm of the internal carotid artery.

The right ICA injection anteroposterior view shows the neck of the pseudoaneurysm originating from the transverse segment of the cavernous portion of the ICA.

Option A: Carotico-cavernous fistula is characterized by the premature filling of the veins as shown in the image below:

Option C: Angiofibroma is characterised by tumour blush. It is the radiological enhancement of a tumour that reveals opacification of the well-vascularized tumours.

Option D: Hemangioma can be differentiated from other vascular malformations by the presence of well-circumscribed mass demonstrating intense tissue staining, usually in a lobular pattern.
questions.learning: Pseudoaneurysm of internal carotid artery — The given image is a digital subtraction angiogram(DSA) and it shows a pseudoaneurysm of the internal carotid artery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient on immunosuppressive therapy presents with cough, fever, and pneumonitis. Biopsy shows the findings provided. Which organism is most likely responsible for this infection?
questions.explanation: The histological image provided is the pathognomonic finding for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection: large, infected cells (cytomegaly) containing prominent, basophilic, intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo, giving them an "owl's eye" appearance. CMV is a significant opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised individuals, such as transplant recipients or those on immunosuppressive therapy, often causing severe pneumonia (pneumonitis), retinitis, or colitis. EBV (Option A) is associated with atypical lymphocytes and Mononucleosis but doesn't show owl's eye inclusions in tissues. Pox virus (Option C) produces Guarnieri bodies (cytoplasmic inclusions), and Chicken pox (VZV) (Option D) produces Cowdry Type A inclusions but they lack the classic owl's eye symmetry of CMV. Recognizing these histological markers is vital for diagnosis, as CMV pneumonitis carries a high mortality rate if not treated promptly with antiviral medications like ganciclovir. This question highlights the importance of matching clinical context (immunosuppression) with classic pathological findings
questions.learning: The histological image provided is the pathognomonic finding for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection: large, infected cells (cytomegaly) containing prominent, basophilic, intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo, giving them an "owl's eye" appearance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are administering an 8-month-old infant with vitamin A supplements over the course of 2 consecutive days. What is the recommended dose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 100,000 IU

This 8-month-old infant should receive 1,00,000 IU of vitamin A orally for 2 consecutive days.

Vitamin A stores in the body last 6-9 months. So a preventive strategy involves administering it to children to prevent the development of its deficiency.

* For infants between 6-12 months - 100,000 IU orally

* For a child above 12 months - 200,000 IU orally is given every 6 months.

The same dose of Vitamin A is repeated the next day in case of deficiency.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drugs are commonly used to prevent or treat chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting?
questions.explanation: The modern management of Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting (CINV) involves a multi-modal approach targeting different neurotransmitter pathways. The combination of a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist (Granisetron), a corticosteroid (Dexamethasone), and an NK1 receptor antagonist (Aprepitant) is the standard and highly effective protocol for highly emetogenic chemotherapy. Granisetron blocks serotonin signals from the gut; Aprepitant blocks substance P in the brain; and Dexamethasone synergistically enhances the anti-emetic effect through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Other options list older, less effective agents like metoclopramide (dopamine antagonist) or doxylamine (antihistamine) which are insufficient as primary prevention for modern high-dose chemotherapy. Using this "triple therapy" has dramatically improved the quality of life for cancer patients by preventing both acute and delayed vomiting episodes. Clinicians must tailor the regimen based on the specific emetic potential of the chemotherapy being administered. This combination represents the current gold standard in supportive oncology care
questions.learning: The modern management of Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting (CINV) involves a multi-modal approach targeting different neurotransmitter pathways.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which method is used to establish the identity of an individual by matching a beheaded skull with a photograph of the person?
questions.explanation: Superimposition (specifically photo-craniofacial superimposition) is the forensic technique used to establish identity by comparing a recovered skull with a photograph of a missing person. The process involves overlaying a life-size photograph of the suspect's face onto a photograph or a digital scan of the skull to check if the anatomical landmarks, such as the eyes, nose, and teeth, align precisely. Anthropometry (Option B, Bertillonage) is an obsolete system of identification using body measurements. DNA fingerprinting (Option C) is the gold standard for definitive identification but requires a biological reference sample from relatives. Cheiloscopy (Option D) is the study of lip prints, which are absent in a beheaded skull. While superimposition is a valuable tool for exclusion or supportive identification, it is generally not considered definitive on its own in many courts. However, in cases of beheaded remains where soft tissues are lost, it provides a critical anatomical link that guides the identification process
questions.learning: Superimposition (specifically photo-craniofacial superimposition) is the forensic technique used to establish identity by comparing a recovered skull with a photograph of a missing person.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old student develops redness of the eye, a foreign body sensation, and profuse watering after using contact lenses. Corneal scraping and interference contrast microscopy suggest an infectious etiology. Which organism is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a young contact lens wearer presenting with persistent ocular pain and redness is highly suspicious for Acanthamoeba keratitis. This organism is a free-living amoeba frequently associated with poor lens hygiene or exposure to tap water. The provided microscopic image displays characteristic Acanthamoeba cysts (Option A), which have a double-walled structure, often appearing polyhedral or stellate. Naegleria fowleri (Option B) causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis and is not a common cause of keratitis. Entamoeba histolytica (Option C) causes intestinal amebiasis. Balamuthia (Option D) is an extremely rare cause of granulomatous brain infections. Acanthamoeba keratitis is notorious for being painful (out of proportion to signs) and potentially leading to a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate. Therefore, given the contact lens association and the pathognomonic microscopy, Acanthamoeba is the responsible organism
questions.learning: The clinical history of a young contact lens wearer presenting with persistent ocular pain and redness is highly suspicious for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During the pre anaesthetic evaluation of a patient, the oral cavity examined is depicted in the image given below. The image shows _________

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ASD, left ventricular hypertrophy

Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by four structural abnormalities resulting in right-to-left shunting. Right ventricular outflow obstruction leads to right-to-left shunt and cyanosis

Severity of pulmonary stenosis determines clinical presentation

Components (remember: PROV):

• Pulmonary stenosis
• Right ventricular hypertrophy
• Overriding aorta
• Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

Why option A is incorrect:

• ASD is not a component of TOF
• Left ventricular hypertrophy is not seen; instead, right ventricular hypertrophy occurs
questions.learning: ASD, left ventricular hypertrophy Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by four structural abnormalities resulting in right-to-left shunting.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 11-month-old infant previously noted to have left-sided ptosis shows abnormal eyelid movements in which the left upper eyelid elevates and depresses during feeding. The ptosis disappears when the child opens his mouth or sucks his thumb. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation: Marcus-Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon is a congenital synkinetic ptosis caused by an abnormal "miswiring" of the cranial nerves during development. Specifically, the levator palpebrae superioris muscle (supplied by CN III) is abnormally innervated by a branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) that normally supplies the muscles of mastication. Consequently, when the infant engages in jaw movements like sucking or mouth opening, the eyelid involuntarily retracts or "winks". Option A (Symblepharon) is an adhesion between the eyelid and the eyeball. Option B (Blepharophimosis syndrome) is a complex of ptosis, shortened palpebral fissures, and epicanthus inversus. Option C (Lagophthalmos) is the inability to close the eyelids completely. Marcus-Gunn phenomenon is usually unilateral. It does not typically resolve on its own, but patients often learn to mask the movement. Surgical correction is indicated if the ptosis is severe or causing amblyopia, usually involving levator excision and a frontalis suspension

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A female faked pregnancy and still presents a child later to blackmail a man. What is this child called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supposititious child

There is no real gestation or substitution of the child in the supposititious child or fictitious child.

A woman may pretend pregnancy and delivery and later produce a living child as her own, or she may substitute a male child for a female child born of her, or for an abortion. This is done for obtaining money or for the purpose of claiming property. Other legal issues involved are blackmailing a man or bringing a charge of breach of the promise of marriage against a man.

In such cases, the woman should be examined for signs of pregnancy and delivery. The medical evidence is useful only when the age of the supposititious child does not correspond to the date of the pretended delivery. DNA fingerprinting will be conclusive.

A posthumous child is a child born after the death of its father, the mother being conceived by the said father.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a patient with Diabetes Mellitus, the liver produces more TG and VLDL. What is the cause of the same?
options: Decreased action of LPL with increased action of HSL
Decreased action of LPL with Decreased action of HSL
Increased action of LPL with increased action of HSL
Increased action of LPL with decreased action of HSL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased action of LPL with increased action of HSL

In a patient with Diabetes Mellitus, the liver produces more TG and VLDL, due to decreased action of LPL with increased action of HSL.

• Lipoprotein lipase (LPL): Enzyme responsible for hydrolyzing triglycerides (TG) in VLDL and chylomicrons into free fatty acids (FFAs) for storage or energy use in tissues.
• Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL): Enzyme that breaks down stored triglycerides in adipocytes into free fatty acids and glycerol.

Insulin has an inhibitory effect on hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL). In diabetes, low insulin corresponds to an increase in HSL activity. This promotes the breakdown of lipids and a release of TG and free fatty acids from the adipose tissue.

Insulin induces the activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) which is present on the capillary walls. LPL promotes hydrolysis of TG and the degradation of the transport proteins, VLDL and chylomicrons. In diabetes, low insulin leads to decreased LPL activity which corresponds to an increase in VLDL and TG.

This results in increased production of triglycerides and VLDL in the liver.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady presents with complaints of fatigue, muscle weakness along with bilateral multiple renal calculi which were picked up on a routine ultrasound. Further workup revealed serum calcium levels of 11.4 mg%. What is the next best investigation required to arrive at a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sestamibi scan

The patient has features suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism:

• Hypercalcemia (11.4 mg/dL)
• Recurrent/multiple renal calculi (“stones”)
• Muscle weakness and fatigue

The diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism is first established biochemically by demonstrating elevated or inappropriately normal serum PTH in the presence of hypercalcemia. Once the biochemical diagnosis is made, the best imaging modality for preoperative localization of a parathyroid adenoma is a Tc-99m Sestamibi scan.

Why not the other options?

• A. MRI neck: Not routinely used as the first imaging modality; reserved for difficult or recurrent cases.
• C. CECT head and neck: Not the standard initial investigation for parathyroid adenoma localization.
• D. NCCT head and neck: Does not adequately localize parathyroid lesions.
questions.learning: Sestamibi scan — The patient has features suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism: • Hypercalcemia (11.4 mg/dL) • Recurrent/multiple renal calculi (“stones”) • Muscle weakness and fatigue The diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism is first established…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with recurrent pain and swelling in the left submandibular region, especially during meals. The swelling subsides partially after a few hours but is associated with dryness in the mouth. On examination, the floor of the mouth is tender. Imaging reveals a 1.5 cm radio-opacity with chronic inflammation. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complete excision of submandibular gland

This patient has submandibular sialolithiasis with chronic sialadenitis:

• Recurrent painful swelling during meals (meal-time syndrome)
• Dry mouth
• Tender floor of the mouth
• 1.5 cm radio-opaque stone
• Evidence of chronic inflammation

A large stone (1.5 cm) associated with chronic gland damage is best treated by complete excision of the submandibular gland.

Why not the other options?

• A. Removal of stone from duct: Suitable for small, accessible ductal stones with a functioning gland.
• B. Superficial parotidectomy: Used for parotid pathology, not submandibular gland disease.
• D. Partial excision of submandibular gland: Not the standard treatment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child with 4+ proteinuria is unresponsive to corticosteroid therapy. There is no history of hematuria and hypertension. Renal biopsy shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis, predominantly involving the juxtamedullary glomeruli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in a child with segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis on biopsy is characteristic of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).

Predominant involvement of juxtamedullary glomeruli is a classic histologic clue for FSGS.

| Clue | Interpretation

| ---- | --------------

| 5-year-old child | Suggests MCD or FSGS

| 4+ proteinuria | Nephrotic syndrome

| No hematuria, no HTN | Pure nephrotic picture

| Steroid unresponsive | NOT MCD → think FSGS

| Segmental sclerosis + hyalinosis | Histopath hallmark of FSGS

| Juxtamedullary glomeruli | Typical early involvement in FSGS

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

| Option | Verdict | Why? | Key Differentiator

| ------ | ------- | ---- | ------------------

| A) IgA nephropathy | ❌ | Nephritic picture (hematuria) | Episodic hematuria post infection

| B) FSGS | ✅ | Steroid-resistant + segmental sclerosis | Correct

| C) Membranous nephropathy | ❌ | Adults, subepithelial deposits | Spike & dome pattern

| D) Minimal change disease | ❌ | Steroid responsive | EM: foot process effacement only

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady presents with history of a painless lump in the right breast since 1 month. On examination, the lump is hard, 3 × 4 cm in size in the upper outer quadrant and is not fixed to the skin or the underlying structures. The axilla reveals firm mobile lymph nodes (level I). Rest of systemic examination is normal. The clinical stage of this disease is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cT₂N₁Mₓ

This patient has carcinoma of the breast. Clinical staging is based on the TNM classification (AJCC).

• Tumor size: 3 × 4 cm → Largest dimension is 4 cm, which is >2 cm but ≤5 cm → T₂
• Lymph nodes: Mobile ipsilateral level I axillary lymph nodes → N₁
• Metastasis: No evidence of distant metastasis has been evaluated → Mₓ

Therefore, the clinical stage is cT₂N₁Mₓ.

• T₂: Tumor >2 cm but ≤5 cm.
• N₁: Metastasis to mobile ipsilateral level I or II axillary lymph nodes.
• Mₓ: Distant metastasis cannot be assessed clinically.

Why not the other options?

• A. cT₁N₁Mₓ: Incorrect because T₁ tumors are ≤2 cm.
• C. cT₃N₁Mₓ: Incorrect because T₃ tumors are >5 cm.
• D. cT₃N₂Mₓ: Incorrect because the tumor is not >5 cm, and N₂ requires fixed/matted axillary nodes or internal mammary node involvement.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Cutaneous larva migrans is most commonly caused by which organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ancylostoma braziliense

Cutaneous larva migrans is most commonly caused by Ancylostoma braziliense.

Cutaneous larva migrans or ground itch or creeping eruption is caused by nematode larvae that infect by skin penetration.

The most common cause is non-human species of Hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense and A. caninum.

Necator americanus and Strongyloides sp also cause cutaneous larva migrans, and Toxocara canis usually causes viscreal and ocular larva migrans.

Differences between cutaneous larva migrans and visceral larva migrans:

Cutaneous larva migrans
Visceral larva migrans

Tissue involved
Skin
Various organs of the body like the liver, lungs, and eyes

Infecting Organism
Mostly by non-human nematodes
Mostly by non-human nematodes (mainly by dog and cat)

Portal of Entry
Penetration of skin
Ingestion of infected eggs

Eosinophilia
Mild

Serodiagnosis
Not developed
Well developed

Treatment
Thiabendazole

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man who recently underwent transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) presents three days later with drowsiness and altered sensorium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing "TURP Syndrome," a recognized complication of prostatic surgery. This occurs when large volumes of non-conductive irrigating fluid (like glycine) are absorbed through opened prostatic venous sinuses during the procedure. This leads to dilutional hyponatremia (low serum sodium). Clinically, hyponatremia results in cerebral edema, manifesting as drowsiness, confusion, and altered consciousness. Hypernatremia (Option A) would be inconsistent with the rapid absorption of hypotonic irrigation fluids. While a stroke (Option C) could cause altered consciousness in an elderly patient, it would typically present with focal neurological deficits rather than generalized drowsiness following a specific surgical trigger. Meningitis (Option D) would present with high fever and neck stiffness, which are not described here. Standard management for symptomatic TURP-induced hyponatremia involves fluid restriction and, in severe cases, cautious administration of hypertonic saline. Therefore, dilutional hyponatremia is the most probable diagnosis following this specific urological intervention
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing "TURP Syndrome," a recognized complication of prostatic surgery. This occurs when large volumes of non-conductive irrigating fluid (like glycine) are absorbed through opened prostatic venous sinuses during the procedure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Describe the procedure being shown in the image.
questions.explanation: The image shows removal of the head of the pancreas along with the duodenum, followed by reconstruction where the remaining pancreas, bile duct, and stomach are anastomosed to the intestine. This is characteristic of the Whipple’s procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy). This procedure is most commonly performed for carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, periampullary tumors, or duodenal malignancies. The key steps include: 1. Resection of pancreatic head, duodenum, gallbladder, and part of bile duct. 2. Reconstruction via pancreaticojejunostomy, hepaticojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy. Why other options are wrong: (A) Beger’s procedure → duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (C) Frey’s procedure → local resection + pancreatic duct drainage (for chronic pancreatitis) (D) Pancreatic redivision → not a standard named procedure
questions.learning: The image shows removal of the head of the pancreas along with the duodenum, followed by reconstruction where the remaining pancreas, bile duct, and stomach are anastomosed to the intestine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following scenarios is early cord clamping typically performed?
questions.explanation: Delayed cord clamping (DCC), usually performed 1–3 minutes after birth, is now the standard recommendation to improve infant iron stores and hemoglobin levels. However, early cord clamping is still traditionally indicated in specific scenarios, such as in an Rh-negative mother (Option D) where there is a risk of feto-maternal hemorrhage and potential sensitization. It is also indicated in cases of fetal hydrops, cord prolapse, or if the mother requires immediate resuscitation (e.g., severe hemorrhage). In diabetic mothers (Option B), DCC is generally encouraged but must be monitored as it may slightly increase the risk of neonatal polycythemia and jaundice. Preterm delivery (Option C) is actually a major indication for delayed cord clamping, as it significantly reduces the risk of intraventricular hemorrhage and necrotizing enterocolitis. Eclamptic patients (Option A) generally do not require early clamping unless maternal resuscitation is needed. Therefore, Rh-isoimmunization remains a classic indication for immediate cord management
questions.learning: Delayed cord clamping (DCC), usually performed 1–3 minutes after birth, is now the standard recommendation to improve infant iron stores and hemoglobin levels.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 4-year-old unimmunized HIV-positive child on antiretroviral therapy for the last 2 years and weighing 15 kg is brought for vaccination. His records reveal a recent CD4 count of 750/mm³, with no evidence of any opportunistic infections in the past. Which of the following statements are applicable to this child? 1. Recombinant Hepatitis B vaccine can be safely administered. 2. MMR vaccine is always contraindicated. 3. BCG may be administered if chest radiograph is normal. 4. IPV is preferred over OPV. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 4

1. Recombinant Hepatitis B vaccine: Correct

• Hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant, non-live vaccine and can be safely administered to HIV-positive children.
• HIV-positive children should receive appropriate routine inactivated/recombinant vaccines.

2. MMR vaccine is always contraindicated: Incorrect

• MMR is a live attenuated vaccine, but it is not universally contraindicated in HIV.
• It can be given when the child is not severely immunocompromised. A good CD4 count supports its use.

3. BCG may be administered if chest radiograph is normal: Incorrect for the exam

• BCG is a live vaccine and is generally avoided in known HIV infection because of the risk of disseminated BCG disease.
• A normal chest X-ray does not establish adequate immune status for BCG administration.

4. IPV is preferred over OPV: Correct

• IPV is preferred in HIV-positive children because it is an inactivated vaccine and does not carry the risk associated with live OPV in an immunocompromised host.
questions.learning: Recombinant Hepatitis B vaccine: Correct • Hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant, non-live vaccine and can be safely administered to HIV-positive children. • HIV-positive children should receive appropriate routine inactivated/recombinant vaccines.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics?
options: Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule
Inhibits the Na-CI pump in late distal convoluted tubule
Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl pump in the descending limb of loop of Henle
Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl pump in the ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule

Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits Na+-Cl- symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride.

Thiazide diuretics:

They may be used for the treatment of hypertension, heart failure, nephrolithiasis due to idiopathic hypercalciuria, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). They block the Na+/Cl- co-transporter in the DCT. This results in the loss of sodium, chloride, and water contributing to the diuretic effect. The diuretic effect of thiazide leads to decreased osmotic pressure due to the loss of Na+, Cl-, and water leading to compensatory reabsorption of uric acid thus resulting in hyperuricemia. The intracytoplasmic Na+ concentration also decreases due to the blockade of the co-transporter. To compensate, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger pumps sodium from the systemic circulation into the epithelial cells in exchange for calcium. The declining calcium levels inside the cell will draw more calcium from the lumen into the systemic circulation. This results in hypercalcemia. There is also increased loss of Mg2+, K+, and H+.

Mechanisms of antihypertensive action: Decreases plasma and ECF volume by diuresis thereby decreasing cardiac output. Even when the compensatory mechanisms restore the Na+ levels and plasma volume, a low BP is maintained by a reduction in total peripheral resistance. This reduction in total peripheral resistance is due to the persistence of a small sodium and volume deficit even after compensation. The decreased intracellular sodium is responsible for increased compliance of the vessel wall and a reduced response to constrictor stimulus.

Thiazides are the diuretic of choice for uncomplicated hypertension.

Advantages of thiazide as an antihypertensive are:

* It can be given as once a day dose and has a flat dose-response curve

* Decreased incidence of postural hypotension and relative freedom from CNS side effects

* No tolerance

* No fluid retention

* Decreased risk of osteoporotic fractures due to its hypocalciuric action

* Low cost

* Effectiveness in isolated systolic hypertension

* Thiazides are ineffective both as antihypertensive and diuretic in patients with chronic renal failure.
questions.learning: Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits Na+-Cl- symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A young patient underwent surgery under General Anaesthesia with O2, Nitrous oxide, and Desflurane. Just after extubation, the patient started to desaturate. On auscultation, there are bilateral basal crepitations. What can be the most common cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Negative pressure pulmonary edema

The complication in this patient associated with extubation is negative pressure pulmonary edema ,which is a dangerous and potentially fatal condition.

Complications associated with extubation:

* Laryngospasm and bronchospasm

* Negative pressure pulmonary edema

* Upper airway obstruction

* Hypoventilation

* Hemodynamic changes (hypertension, tachycardia)

* Coughing and straining leading to surgical wound dehiscence

* Laryngeal or airway edema

* Paradoxical vocal cord motion

* Arytenoid dislocation

* Aspiration

Factors associated with increased extubation risk:

* Airway risk factors

* known difficult airway

* airway deterioration (bleeding, edema, trauma)

* restricted airway access

* obesity and obstructive sleep apnea

* aspiration risk

* General risk factors

* cardiovascular disease

* respiratory disease

* neuromuscular disease

* metabolic derangements

* special surgical requirements
questions.learning: Negative pressure pulmonary edema — The complication in this patient associated with extubation is negative pressure pulmonary edema ,which is a dangerous and potentially fatal condition.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure arises from the left 6th pharyngeal (aortic) arch artery?
questions.explanation: The embryological development of the arterial system involves several pharyngeal arch arteries. The left 6th pharyngeal arch artery gives rise to the proximal part of the left pulmonary artery and the ductus arteriosus. The ductus arteriosus is a critical fetal structure that shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the non-functional fetal lungs. After birth, it closes to become the ligamentum arteriosum. The arch of the aorta (Option A) develops from the left 4th arch artery. The common carotid arteries (Option C) develop from the 3rd arch arteries. The right subclavian artery (Option D) develops from the right 4th arch artery and the right seventh intersegmental artery. On the right side, the 6th arch artery distal part disappears, while the proximal part forms the right pulmonary artery. Understanding these developmental origins is vital for comprehending congenital vascular anomalies, such as Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) or a right-sided aortic arch
questions.learning: The embryological development of the arterial system involves several pharyngeal arch arteries. The left 6th pharyngeal arch artery gives rise to the proximal part of the left pulmonary artery and the ductus arteriosus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young male patient with a history of a motor vehicle accident is unable to pass urine. Blood is seen at the meatus. What is the most likely site of urethral injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Membranous urethra

In the given scenario of a young patient with urinary retention, blood at the meatus, and a history of a motor vehicle accident, the most likely site of injury is the membranous urethra. The given retrograde urethrogram shows contrast leakage at the membranous urethra.

Urethral injuries in men usually occur after catheterization or during cystoscopy. Injuries following external trauma are rare, but mainly affect the bulbar or the membranous urethra.

Membranous urethral rupture usually occurs following a road traffic accident, crush injury, or a fall. It is associated with pelvic fracture and extraperitoneal bladder rupture. Clinical features include urinary retention, blood at the meatus, and a high riding prostate on digital examination. Bruising is seen over the pubic area, scrotum, and penis.

Management is by inserting a suprapubic catheter. If there is an associated bladder rupture, the bladder will not be seen on the ultrasound, and management in such a case is by exploration, repair, and placement of a suprapubic catheter.

Other options:

Option A: Bulbar urethral injury occurs following a blow to the perineum with a fall astride injury during cycling or gymnasium accidents. A typical feature is a butterfly-shaped hematoma in the perineum. Other features such as urinary retention and meatal bleeding can also be present. Analgesia, antibiotics, and suprapubic catheterization are needed. The patient should be discouraged from passing urine. Definitive management is delayed urethroplasty after 8-12 weeks.

Options B and D: Spongy and penile urethral rupture can occur following a penile fracture during coitus. Hematuria and difficulty in voiding can be present in spongy urethral injury. A pop sound followed by severe penile pain and penile deformity is characteristic of penile urethral injury. Hematoma, blood at the meatus, and voiding difficulties are also seen.

Retrograde urethrogram shows loss of smooth contour of the urethra with extravasation of the dye in case of a spongy urethral rupture. Surgical repair is needed in both.
questions.learning: Membranous urethra — In the given scenario of a young patient with urinary retention, blood at the meatus, and a history of a motor vehicle accident, the most likely site of injury is the membranous urethra.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ureteric bud develops from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mesonephric duct

Ureteric bud develops from Mesonephric duct.

• Intermediate mesoderm is a type of mesoderm that is located between the paraxial mesoderm and lateral plate.
• It develops into a part of the urogenital system as well as the reproductive system.
• Intermediate mesoderm develops into Genital ridge and Nephrogenic cord.
• Nephrogenic cord further develops into Pronephros, Mesonephros and Metanephros.
• Ureteric bud develops from mesonephros which later fuses with Mesonephric duct.
• Metanephros proliferates around the ureteric bud which forms metanephric blastema (definitive kidneys).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman has a history of urinating in public without having any remorse for it. She also has difficulty in getting motivated and has mild memory deficits. Which of the following lobes may be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Frontal

The frontal lobe is affected in this patient. The woman has difficulty in getting motivated, memory deficits, and urinary incontinence.

Frontal lobe injury is commonly due to trauma, infarcts, tumors, lobotomy, multiple sclerosis, or Pick's disease. The following features may be seen in a patient with frontal lobe injury:

• Impaired executive functions such as motivation, attention, and sequencing of actions
• Aphasia, apraxia, constructional apraxia, neglect, and memory deficits
• Urinary incontinence and fecal incontinence is commonly seen
• Changes in personality
• Apathetic indifference and impulsive behavior.

Note: Frontal lobe pathology may become apparent only under unstructured, stressful, real-life situations and are difficult to detect using Intelligence scales, as IQ mostly requires parietal lobe activation.
questions.learning: Frontal — The frontal lobe is affected in this patient. The woman has difficulty in getting motivated, memory deficits, and urinary incontinence.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following factors causes a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.explanation: A rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve indicates reduced oxygen affinity, which facilitates oxygen unloading to tissues. This occurs via the Bohr effect, where an increase in leads to increased carbonic acid formation, lowering the pH. Other factors causing a rightward shift include increased temperature, increased hydrogen ions (lower pH), and increased 2,3-BPG. An increase in (Option B) promotes oxygen binding and does not cause a rightward shift. A decrease in (Option C) leads to a higher pH and a leftward shift, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. Similarly, a decrease in temperature (Option D) stabilizes the oxygen-binding state, shifting the curve to the left. Therefore, increased is the primary physiological driver among these options for enhancing oxygen delivery to metabolically active tissues
questions.learning: A rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve indicates reduced oxygen affinity, which facilitates oxygen unloading to tissues. This occurs via the Bohr effect, where an increase in leads to increased carbonic acid formation, lowering the pH.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 56-year-old female with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presents with painless, gradual blurring of vision in the left eye. On examination, the sclera is as shown in the image. There is no ciliary congestion or significant redness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scleromalacia perforans

Scleromalacia perforans is a necrotizing anterior scleritis without inflammation, classically associated with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. It presents with painless progressive scleral thinning and minimal or no redness, with the underlying dark uveal tissue becoming visible through the thinned sclera.

• Most common association: Rheumatoid arthritis
• Symptoms: Usually painless, unlike typical scleritis
• Signs: White, avascular scleral thinning with bluish-black hue due to exposed uvea
• Complication: Risk of globe rupture/perforation despite the name “perforans” (actual perforation is uncommon)

Differentiate from Other Options:

• A. Scleritis: Severe boring eye pain, deep violaceous congestion, tenderness.
• B. Episcleritis: Mild discomfort, sectoral redness, self-limiting, no scleral thinning.
• D. Anterior uveitis: Pain, photophobia, ciliary congestion, cells and flare in the anterior chamber.
questions.learning: Scleromalacia perforans Scleromalacia perforans is a necrotizing anterior scleritis without inflammation, classically associated with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following parasitic helminths is a nematode and has zoonotic transmission?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trichinella spiralis

Trichinella spiralis is a zoonotic nematode acquired by eating raw or undercooked pork or wild game meat containing encysted larvae. After ingestion, the larvae mature in the intestine and migrate to striated muscles, producing myositis, fever, periorbital edema, eosinophilia, and muscle pain.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Taenia saginata: A cestode (tapeworm) transmitted by undercooked beef.
• C. Fasciola hepatica: A trematode (liver fluke) acquired from aquatic plants (e.g., watercress).
• D. Fasciolopsis buski: An intestinal trematode acquired by eating aquatic plants.
questions.learning: Trichinella spiralis Trichinella spiralis is a zoonotic nematode acquired by eating raw or undercooked pork or wild game meat containing encysted larvae.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 48-year-old male who has been working in a paint manufacturing factory for over 20 years presents with chronic abdominal pain, constipation, fatigue, headache, and joint pains. He also reports irritability and sleep disturbances. On examination, pallor is noted. Laboratory investigations reveal microcytic anemia. Peripheral smear shows basophilic stippling of RBCs. Which of the following enzymes is most likely inhibited in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ferrochelatase

Chronic exposure to lead (e.g., in paint factory workers) causes lead poisoning, which interferes with heme synthesis.

Lead inhibits two key enzymes in the heme pathway:

• Ferrochelatase → blocks incorporation of iron into protoporphyrin IX to form heme
• ALA dehydratase (ALAD) → inhibits conversion of ALA to porphobilinogen

Clinical features (classic):

• Abdominal pain (lead colic)
• Constipation
• Neuropathy (wrist/foot drop)
• Anemia
• Irritability, insomnia, headache

Why other options are incorrect:

• Uroporphyrinogen III synthase: Defect causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria
• Porphobilinogen deaminase: Defect causes acute intermittent porphyria
• ALA synthase: Rate-limiting enzyme; not inhibited by lead (actually regulated by heme)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following viruses can cause more severe disease and potentially serious complications upon reinfection?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the critical clinical concept of Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE) associated with the Dengue virus. As previously discussed (see Q.92), reinfection with a heterologous (different) serotype of Dengue often leads to a much more severe clinical course than the primary infection. This is due to non-neutralizing antibodies facilitating viral entry into host immune cells, potentially causing lethal hemorrhagic fever or shock. Rabies (Option B) is almost 100% fatal upon the first infection, so reinfection is not a clinical reality. Measles (Option C) and Mumps (Option D) are characterized by life-long, robust neutralizing immunity after a single natural infection or a complete vaccination series. Therefore, Dengue remains the definitive example of a virus where subsequent infections are statistically and physiologically more dangerous than the initial exposure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young male presents with a painless swelling in the right testis, which he noticed two months ago. On examination, the swelling is firm and non-tender, with no transillumination and the contralateral testis appears normal. An ultrasound reveals a hypoechoic mass in the right testis. Further imaging shows enlargement of the para-aortic and pre-aortic lymph nodes. Tumor markers, including AFP, β-hCG, and LDH, are elevated. The physician suspects testicular cancer. What is the next appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High inguinal orchidectomy

The clinical features and the raised AFP, β-hCG, and LDH levels are suggestive of testicular cancer and the next best step in management is high inguinal orchidectomy.

Clinical features of testicular carcinoma:

* Painless testicular lump is the most common presenting feature.

* Epididymo-orchitis.

* Severe pain and acute enlargement of the testis because of haemorrhage into the tumour.

* Intra-abdominal spread may cause abdominal or lumbar pain.

* Lung metastases are usually silent but they can cause chest pain, dyspnoea and haemoptysis in the later stages of the disease.

Although testicular cancers often spread to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes, including the pre-aortic nodes. A biopsy of the scrotal mass or the lymph nodes is generally not the first step.

A high inguinal approach is crucial because it allows for removal of the testicle along with the spermatic cord, minimizing the risk of further spread. This is the standard initial management for suspected testicular cancer. After removal of the affected testis, metastatic workup should be done with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.

Early-stage tumors don't require additional treatment after orchidectomy, while late-stage tumours are given combination chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide, and cis-platinum (BEP chemotherapy). They are highly sensitive to combination chemotherapy with BEP. So chemotherapy is given to high-risk cases and low-risk cases with a good prognosis are managed by surveillance protocols.

Other Options:

Option A: Lymph node biopsies, while sometimes necessary, are usually performed after a diagnosis of testicular cancer is established to assess the extent of spread.

Option B: Scrotal biopsies for testicular mass risk seeding the scrotal skin with cancer cells, potentially worsening the prognosis.

Option D: Repeating hormone markers while potentially useful for monitoring the disease after a diagnosis is made is not the priority when a suspicious scrotal mass and concerning lymphadenopathy are present.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Personal monitoring of radiation is done by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. TLD badge

Personal monitoring of radiation is done by a TLD badge.

The TLD badge (thermoluminescent dosimeter) should be positioned according to local or national practices. In India, one TLD badge has to be worn at the chest level inside the lead apron if the apron is used. An additional wrist badge has to be worn for procedures requiring hands close to the primary beam.

The thermoluminescent material used is calcium sulfate doped with dysprosium or lithium fluoride. Radiation exposure is monitored every three months. The maximum dose limit for occupational radiation workers is 30 mSv in a year, provided the cumulative dose in a block of 5 years does not exceed 100 mSv.

The given image shows a TLD badge.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text:
Match the following:

1. Facial nerve
A. Shrugging of shoulder

2. Spinal accessory nerve
B. Taste from anterior two third of the tongue

3. Glossopharyngeal nerve
C. Taste from posterior one-third of the tongue

4. Mandibular nerve
D. Chewing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1-B, 2-A, 3-C, 4-D

The correct match is as follows:

1. Facial nerve
B. Taste from anterior two third of the tongue

2. Spinal accessory nerve
A. Shrugging of shoulder

3. Glossopharyngeal nerve
C. Taste from posterior one-third of the tongue

4. Mandibular nerve
D. Chewing

Chorda tympani nerve which is a branch of facial nerve carries taste from anterior 2/3rd of the tongue.

The trapezius is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI). It causes retraction of scapula, shrugging of the shoulder and overhead abduction (along with serratus anterior). Paralysis of trapezius causes drooping of the shoulder and slight winging of the scapula (the superior angle of scapula becomes more prominent).

The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.

The mandibular nerve (V3) is responsible for chewing movements as it gives motor supply to muscles of mastication. It contains both sensory and motor fibers.

• Sensory from

• Skin of cheek, over mandible and side of head
• Teeth of lower jaw and temporomandibular joint
• Mucous membrane of mouth and anterior part of tongue

• Motor to

• Muscles of mastication (pterygoids, masster and temporalis)
• Tensor tympani
• Anterior belly of digastric
• Mylohyoid

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify this movement that takes place in the intestine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peristalsis

The given image is of peristalsis.

Peristalsis is the propulsive movement in GI tract, starting in esophagus and ends in rectum. It follows the law of gut- forward directed towards the rectum, because of intact myenteric plexus.

It begins by the local stretch produced by the food and the wave of contraction propels forward at 2-25cm/s speed. It is independent of external innervation, but autonomic activity may increase or decrease the activity.

The interstitial cells of Cajal, acts as pacemakers of GI tract,They maintain a basal electric rhythm (BER). It doesn’t cause contraction on its own but maintains a muscle tension. It’s function is to coordinate the various motility of GI tract. For example, in the absence of BER, peristalsis waves in the stomach will be irregular and chaotic.

Peristalsis:

From esophagus to rectum.

Function - Propels food forward

Stimulus - Stretch of food

Speed-2-25cm/s

Regulation- sustains by self, autonomic system and interstitial cells of cajal fine tune it.

Pearl PF0557: Mechanism of peristalsis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented with low hemoglobin, platelet count of 25,000/mL, gum bleeding, and raised PT & aPTT. The image of his peripheral smear is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. AML with t(15;17)

The peripheral blood smear shows numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes, which are characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The presentation of the patient with gum bleeding points to the diagnosis of AML with t(15;17).

Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic granules) are predominantly seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia, which is a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. It is associated with t(15;17), which results in the formation of the fusion gene called PML-RARA. The condition is associated with a high incidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Treatment includes the administration of all-trans retinoic acid.
questions.learning: AML with t(15;17) — The peripheral blood smear shows numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes, which are characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is brought after a road traffic accident and imaging reveals the fracture shown. What type of fracture is this?
questions.explanation: The X-ray depicts a fracture occurring in the region between the greater and lesser trochanters of the proximal femur. This is an intertrochanteric fracture, which is extra-capsular in nature. Because it is outside the hip joint capsule, the blood supply to the femoral head remains relatively well-preserved, leading to a much lower risk of avascular necrosis compared to neck fractures. Subtrochanteric fractures (Option A) occur below the lesser trochanter in the femoral shaft. Femoral neck fractures (Option C) occur superior to the trochanters and within the joint capsule (intracapsular). Pubic rami fractures (Option D) involve the pelvic ring and not the femur itself. Intertrochanteric fractures are often comminuted and result from high-energy trauma in young patients or simple falls in the elderly. Based on the specific bony landmarks, the diagnosis is confirmed
questions.learning: The X-ray depicts a fracture occurring in the region between the greater and lesser trochanters of the proximal femur. This is an intertrochanteric fracture, which is extra-capsular in nature.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition induced by which pair of transcription factors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. SNAIL & TWIST

Epithelial-mesenchymal transition is induced by SNAIL & TWIST.

Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a process where epithelial cells lose their cell polarity and adhesion properties, transitioning into a more motile mesenchymal cell phenotype. This is critical in embryogenesis, wound healing, and cancer metastasis.

SNAIL and TWIST encode transcription factors whose primary function is to promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). SNAIL and TWIST downregulate E-cadherin expression.

• In EMT, carcinoma cells downregulate certain epithelial markers (e.g., E-cadherin) and upregulate certain mesenchymal markers (e.g. vimentin and smooth muscle actin).
• This favors the development of a promigratory phenotype that is essential for metastasis.
• Loss of E-cadherin expression seems to be a key event in EMT.
• EMT has been documented mainly in breast carcinoma

Other Options:

Option A: TF IIA & TF IIB: These are general transcription factors involved in the assembly of the transcription initiation complex, not specific to EMT.

Option B: Cathepsin & MMP8: These are proteolytic enzymes involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, which may assist invasion during EMT but do not directly induce it.

Option D: STAT-5 & HIF-1α: While these factors are involved in cellular responses to cytokines and hypoxia, respectively, they are not directly linked to the initiation of EMT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An intern finds a patient unresponsive, and an emergency ECG reveals a cardiac arrhythmia. A DC shock is administered, but the arrhythmia persists and the patient remains unresponsive. What should be the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: The ECG waveform exhibits chaotic, irregular electrical activity without identifiable P waves or QRS complexes, which is diagnostic of Ventricular Fibrillation (VF). According to Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines, when an initial DC shock (defibrillation) fails to restore a rhythm and the patient remains unresponsive, the immediate next step is to resume high-quality Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR). CPR should be continued for two minutes before another rhythm check or shock is delivered. Synchronized cardioversion (Option A) is used for stable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse, not for pulseless VF. Delivering another immediate shock (Option C) is incorrect as it interrupts vital chest compressions. Epinephrine (Option D) is typically administered after the second unsuccessful shock. High-quality CPR is essential to maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion until a shock can successfully reset the heart
questions.learning: The ECG waveform exhibits chaotic, irregular electrical activity without identifiable P waves or QRS complexes, which is diagnostic of Ventricular Fibrillation (VF).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Photostress test is used to differentiate between:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Macula and optic nerve disease

Photostress test is used to differentiate between the disease involving the macula and optic nerve.

This test is of particular use in early macular diseases such as central serous retinopathy.

In this test, one eye is covered and the patient is asked to read the smallest line on the near chart. A bright light is then shone into the eye for 15 seconds, and the patient is asked to read the line again, and the time taken to recover is noted. The test is repeated with the other eye.

In normal people and in patients with optic nerve disease, the recovery time is not affected. Whereas, in patients with macular disease the recovery time is prolonged and is usually more than one-third of the normal recovery time. This is because, in macular disease, the photoreceptors are damaged, and there is a delay in the visual pigment regeneration process.
questions.learning: Macula and optic nerve disease Photostress test is used to differentiate between the disease involving the macula and optic nerve. This test is of particular use in early macular diseases such as central serous retinopathy.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He was driving the car when the accident occurred. On examination, it is noted that the injured leg is shortened. The image of the pelvis radiograph is shown below. Which of the following nerve is most commonly damaged in the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sciatic nerve

The above radiograph shows that the femoral head of the left hip is displaced upwards and laterally, and the affected limb is in adduction. Also, the lesser trochanter is obscured. These features indicate posterior dislocation of the left hip joint. The nerve the most commonly injured in this type of dislocation is the sciatic nerve.

Posterior hip dislocation occurs when the knee of the passenger strikes the dashboard. The affected leg is shortened, and lies in an adducted, internally rotated and slightly flexed position.

Imaging shows the following features:

* Upward dislocation of the femoral head

* The size of the femoral head appears smaller compared to the unaffected side

* Adduction of the affected limb.

* The lesser trochanter may not be visible due to the internal rotation of the affected leg

Treatment- A pure hip dislocation should be reduced as early as possible to reduce the risk of osteonecrosis and subsequent osteoarthritis. Important maneuvers to reduce posterior hip dislocation are:

* Rochester method

* East Baltimore lift

* Allis

* Bigelow

* Stimson

Complications of posterior hip dislocation are:

* Injury to the sciatic nerve

* Injury to the superior gluteal artery

* Osteonecrosis of femoral head

* Secondary osteoarthritis

* Myositis ossificans

* Recurrent instability of the reduced dislocation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32 year old female presents with grey-white vaginal discharge and on gram stain of the discharge, clue cells are seen. Clue cells are
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epithelial cells covered by bacteria

Clue cells are epithelial cells with a fuzzy border or granular cytoplasm caused by small gram-negative bacilli adhering on their surface is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis.

Bacterial vaginosis is a polymicrobial infection caused by Mobiluncus curtisii, Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma hominis, and Haemophilus vaginalis. It has a malodorous (fishy smell) vaginal discharge with minimal vulval irritation.

Amsel's Criteria is helpful in diagnosing bacterial vaginosis when 3 of the following 4 are present

• Thin, white homogenous vaginal discharge
• A pH of vaginal fluid >4.5
• Fishy odor of discharge accentuated by adding 10% KOH-Whiff test
• Presence of Clue cells on microscopy.

Treatment is oral metronidazole 500 mg BD for 7 days. Alternatively, Ampicillin 500 mg or cephalosporin 500 mg bid for 7 days is also effective.
questions.learning: Epithelial cells covered by bacteria Clue cells are epithelial cells with a fuzzy border or granular cytoplasm caused by small gram-negative bacilli adhering on their surface is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with a small nodule on the sclera as shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dermoid

A dermoid is a likely diagnosis based on the ocular finding and the given image.

An orbital dermoid is a choristoma (a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location) formed due to subcutaneous displacement of the ectoderm.

It is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and contains dermal appendages like sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. It can be located anteriorly (superficial) or posteriorly (deep) to the orbital septum.

Clinical features: Superficial dermoid presents in infancy as a painless nodule in the superotemporal part of the orbit whereas deep dermoid presents in adulthood as a gradually protruding eye or acutely as an inflamed orbit. CT imaging would show a well-circumscribed cystic lesion.

Treatment is by excision in toto.

Other options:

Option A: Pterygium is a triangular fibrovascular ingrowth of degenerative bulbar conjunctival tissue on the limbus as a result of chronic exposure to UV rays.

Option B: Pinguecula is an asymptomatic yellow-white mound of degenerated conjunctival stroma seen adjacent to the limbus. It is more common on the nasal limbus.

Option C: Dermolipoma presents in adulthood as a subconjunctival yellowish mass near the outer canthus of the eye. It contains dermal appendages and fatty tissue.
questions.learning: Dermoid — A dermoid is a likely diagnosis based on the ocular finding and the given image. An orbital dermoid is a choristoma (a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location) formed due to subcutaneous displacement of the ectoderm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A molar pregnancy is an abnormal gestation characterized by excessive proliferation of placental tissue, which may sometimes invade the uterine wall. It is often detected early due to vaginal bleeding, distinctive ultrasound findings, and markedly elevated levels of a specific pregnancy-related hormone. In the condition depicted in the image, which hormone is primarily increased?
questions.explanation: The image displays the classic "snowstorm" appearance on ultrasound, which is pathognomonic for a molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole). In this condition, the abnormal trophoblastic proliferation leads to the production of excessively high levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG). Serum HCG levels in molar pregnancies often exceed mIU/mL, which is significantly higher than levels seen in a normal pregnancy of the same gestational age. FSH (Option A), LH (Option B), and GnRH (Option C) are involved in the normal hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis and are not the primary hormones secreted by gestational trophoblastic tissue. These extreme HCG levels are responsible for clinical signs such as hyperemesis gravidarum and early-onset pre-eclampsia. Following suction and evacuation of the mole, serial monitoring of serum HCG is mandatory to ensure the levels return to zero and to detect early malignant transformation into gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (choriocarcinoma). This hormone serves as both a sensitive diagnostic marker and a vital surveillance tool
