questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with a rare homozygous recessive condition presented with ectopia lentis. In the peripheral smear, there was no megaloblastic anemia. Later, he was found to have elevated homocysteine levels in the blood. Which of the following supplementations will help the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyridoxine

The vitamin that can be used as supplementation in this patient with homocystinuria is pyridoxine (vitamin B6).

Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive disease most commonly caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of homocysteine in the blood and a clinical syndrome of intellectual disability, subluxated ocular lenses, long and slender extremities, arachnodactyly, and arterial and venous thrombi. The skeletal features of homocystinuria often mimic Marfan syndrome. Folic acid and vitamin B12 deficiency can also lead to homocystinuria with megaloblastic anemia.

Demonstration of elevated total homocysteine in the blood confirms the diagnosis. 50% of the cases of homocystinuria are termed pyridoxine-responsive because large doses of pyridoxine can enhance the activity of deficient enzymes in these patients. Administration of large doses of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) restores the activity of the deficient enzyme in half of all cases of homocystinuria.

Folate supplementation is also added to overcome any folate deficiency that might occur due to increased conversion of homocysteine to methionine. For the other 50% of the patients, the treatment consists of methionine restriction and cysteine supplementation. In addition, betaine (methyl group donor), folate and vitamin B12 may be added.
questions.learning: Pyridoxine — The vitamin that can be used as supplementation in this patient with homocystinuria is pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive disease most commonly caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase.

questions.text: Which of the following is the incorrect association?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. p53 and mucosal neuroma

Mucosal neuromas are a hallmark of MEN 2B, caused by activating RET proto-oncogene mutations, not p53.

Typical oral mucosal neuromas or neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.

PTEN is linked to thyroid malignancies (Cowden syndrome), BRCA2 to prostate cancer, and STK11 to breast cancer (Peutz-Jeghers).

questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with bitemporal hemianopia. CT is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A calcified lesion in the suprasellar region suggests craniopharyngioma. It is derived from Rathke's pouch.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a 2-week history of fever, headache, and vomiting. On examination, nuchal rigidity is noted. Lumbar puncture findings are: elevated opening pressure, predominantly polymorphonuclear leukocytes, glucose 35 mg/dL, and protein 200 mg/dL. Based on these results, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity (stiff neck) indicates meningitis. The lumbar puncture results—specifically elevated protein (200 mg/dl), low sugar (35 mg/dl), and a predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs)—are classic for acute bacterial meningitis. In viral meningitis (Option B), the sugar is usually normal, and lymphocytes are the predominant cells. Tuberculous (TB) meningitis (Option C) also shows low sugar and high protein, but it typically presents with a lymphocytic pleocytosis rather than PMNs. While the 2-week duration is slightly longer than a typical acute presentation, the PMN-rich CSF strongly favors a bacterial etiology. Meningoencephalitis (Option A) would also involve altered mental status or focal neurological deficits. Immediate treatment with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and corticosteroids is required to prevent serious neurological complications or death

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The hormone that does not play a role in the growth of the fetus is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Growth hormone

Growth hormone, despite being present at higher levels in the fetus, does not play a significant role in fetal growth.

The human fetus produces thyroxine from the 12th week of gestation. Thyroxine and insulin have an important role in regulating tissue growth and differentiation of the fetus, particularly during late gestation. Glucocorticoids play an important role towards the end of gestation in the prepartum maturation of organs such as the liver, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract.

Insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-1 and IGF-II also play an important role in fetal growth.
questions.learning: Growth hormone Growth hormone, despite being present at higher levels in the fetus, does not play a significant role in fetal growth. The human fetus produces thyroxine from the 12th week of gestation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A pap smear taken from a patient revealed hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear borders, and low maturation index involving the whole thickness but did not breach the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dysplasia

The hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear borders, and intact basement membrane are all suggestive of dysplasia.

Dysplasia is characterized by the loss in the uniformity of the individual cells and their architectural orientation. The features of dysplasia include:

• Pleomorphism
• Hyperchromatic nuclei
• High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio
• Increased mitotic figures

When the dysplastic changes involve the entire thickness of the epithelium without breaching the basement membrane it is considered preinvasive and is termed carcinoma-in-situ. If the tumor invades the basement membrane it is said to be invasive.

Dysplasia can be considered as a precursor to malignant but it does not always progress to cancer. Dysplasia usually occurs in the metaplastic epithelium but all metaplastic epithelium is not dysplastic.

Other options:

Metaplasia: It refers to the replacement of one cell type with another type. It is almost always associated with tissue damage, repair, and regeneration. The most common epithelial metaplasia is columnar to squamous.

Carcinoma: In carcinoma, there is the invasion of the basement membrane.

Hyperplasia: It refers to the increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ. It can be physiologic or pathological. Enlargement of the female breast during pregnancy is physiologic hyperplasia. Endometrial hyperplasia is an example of pathological hyperplasia.
questions.learning: Dysplasia — The hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear borders, and intact basement membrane are all suggestive of dysplasia. Dysplasia is characterized by the loss in the uniformity of the individual cells and their architectural orientation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: NADPH is used in ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fatty acid synthesis

NADPH is the source of reducing equivalent for fatty acid synthesis.

This NADPH is derived from 3 sources:

• HMP shunt pathway (main source)
• Extramitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase (minor source)
• Malic enzyme

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which organization should an official refer to for complete and regularly updated demographic data that includes records of vital events?
questions.explanation: The Sample Registration System (SRS) is the organization an official should refer to for complete and regularly updated demographic data including records of vital events. SRS provides continuous and reliable data on vital events through its dual record system combining continuous enumeration and periodic retrospective surveys. Why other options are wrong: (A) AIIMS is incorrect because AIIMS is purely a medical research and teaching institution with no mandate for maintaining national demographic databases or vital event registration systems. (B) National Sample Survey is incorrect because NSSO conducts broader socioeconomic surveys covering morbidity, family planning, health expenditure etc. It does not specifically focus on continuously updated demographic data and vital event registration. (D) Central Bureau of Health is incorrect because CBHI primarily compiles and publishes health statistics sourced from other agencies rather than independently maintaining continuous vital event registration systems at national level
questions.learning: The Sample Registration System (SRS) is the organization an official should refer to for complete and regularly updated demographic data including records of vital events.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with chronic joint pain and morning stiffness lasting about 30 minutes. Examination reveals Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes, and X-ray findings show joint space narrowing with osteophyte formation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical profile of an elderly patient with chronic pain in weight-bearing joints, short-lived morning stiffness (less than 30 minutes), and characteristic Heberden's nodes (at the DIP joints) and Bouchard's nodes (at the PIP joints) is diagnostic of Osteoarthritis (OA). The radiographic findings—narrowed joint spaces and osteophytes (bone spurs)—are the "classic" indicators of OA. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Option C) typically presents with prolonged morning stiffness (more than 1 hour), involves different hand joints (MCP and PIP), and shows periarticular osteopenia rather than osteophytes. Osteoporosis (Option A) is a systemic loss of bone density that is usually painless until a fracture occurs. Bone tumors (Option D) would present as a localized mass or focal destructive lesion rather than symmetrical joint wear. OA is a degenerative "wear and tear" disease. Therefore, based on the specific nodes and radiographic spurs, Osteoarthritis is the only viable diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following effects of puberty are not mediated by estrogen? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hair growth

• Hair growth (Pubarche): The development of axillary and pubic hair is not mediated by estrogen. It occurs due to testosterone in both sexes.
• Estrogen effects: Estrogen plays a crucial role in various aspects of puberty, including:

• Breast development (thelarche)
• Development of internal genitalia
• Menarche
• Regulation of growth spurt
• Epiphyseal closure
• Cervical mucus plug formation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are complications of acute pancreatitis? 1. Hypoxia 2. Hypercalcemia 3. Hyperglycemia 4. Reduced serum albumin Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas that can cause both local and systemic complications due to the release of pancreatic enzymes and inflammatory mediators.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Hypoxia: Correct. Hypoxia is a common systemic complication due to acute lung injury/ARDS, pleural effusion, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
• Statement 2. Hypercalcemia: Incorrect. Acute pancreatitis is associated with hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia. Hypocalcemia occurs due to fat saponification, where calcium combines with free fatty acids in areas of fat necrosis.
• Statement 3. Hyperglycemia: Correct. Hyperglycemia occurs due to injury of pancreatic β-cells, resulting in decreased insulin secretion, along with stress-induced hyperglycemia.
• Statement 4. Reduced serum albumin: Correct. Reduced serum albumin occurs because of systemic inflammation, increased capillary permeability, and protein loss into the third space. Low serum albumin is also associated with more severe disease.

Other complications of acute pancreatitis:

• Local: Pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess, infected necrosis, hemorrhage.
• Systemic: Shock, acute kidney injury, DIC, ARDS, sepsis, multiorgan failure.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas that can cause both local and systemic complications due to the release of pancreatic enzymes and inflammatory mediators.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who underwent gastrointestinal surgery has had a portion of her jejunum resected. Which of the following drugs should be added to her postoperative treatment?
questions.explanation: Large resections of the small intestine, such as the jejunum, can lead to "Short Bowel Syndrome," where the remaining gut cannot absorb enough nutrients and water to sustain the body. Teduglutide is a specialized medication that is an analog of Glucagon-Like Peptide-2 (GLP-2). GLP-2 is a natural hormone that promotes the growth and maintenance of the intestinal lining. By mimicking this hormone, Teduglutide increases the surface area of the remaining small intestine (specifically increasing the height of the villi), thereby improving nutrient and fluid absorption. This can significantly reduce the patient's dependence on intravenous parenteral nutrition. Liraglutide (Option A), Exenatide (Option C), and Semaglutide (Option D) are all GLP-1 analogs used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity; they work by increasing insulin secretion and slowing gastric emptying, which would not address the malabsorption issues in short bowel syndrome. Teduglutide represents a targeted physiological approach to managing gut failure
questions.learning: Large resections of the small intestine, such as the jejunum, can lead to "Short Bowel Syndrome," where the remaining gut cannot absorb enough nutrients and water to sustain the body.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The graph below shows oxygen dissociation curves. What does the curve marked as 'A' indicate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myoglobin

The curve 'A' shows a hyperbolic curve that is characteristic of oxygen dissociation in myoglobin.

Myoglobin is an iron-containing component of the skeletal muscle. Myoglobin can bind only to one oxygen molecule and hence lacks co-operative binding. It has a higher affinity to oxygen than hemoglobin and hence releases oxygen only at low PO2 values. This leads to a leftward shift in the myoglobin oxygen dissociation curve.

Myoglobin is present in large quantities in muscles that are commonly used for sustained contraction. During such contractions, muscle blood supply is decreased due to compression. Myoglobin facilitates oxygen supply in these conditions.

Other options:

Option B: Carbon monoxide (CO) reacts with hemoglobin to form carbon monoxyhemoglobin (carboxyhemoglobin or COHb). The affinity of hemoglobin for CO is 210 times its affinity for O2, and COHb liberates CO very slowly. An additional difficulty is that when COHb is present, the dissociation curve of the remaining HbO2 shifts to the left, decreasing the amount of O2 released.

Option C: Hemoglobin normally has ferrous ion. When it is oxidized to ferric iron, it is called methemoglobin. It causes dark-coloured blood.

Option D: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is structurally similar to hemoglobin A except for the gamma chains. It binds less avidly to 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate and hence has higher affinity for oxygen leading to left ward shift in the dissociation curve.
questions.learning: Myoglobin — The curve 'A' shows a hyperbolic curve that is characteristic of oxygen dissociation in myoglobin. Myoglobin is an iron-containing component of the skeletal muscle.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxia

Located in:

• Carotid body (most important)
• Aortic body

They respond to:

• ↓ PaO₂ (primary stimulus)
• ↑ PaCO₂
• ↓ pH (acidosis)

Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies are most sensitive to arterial hypoxemia (↓PaO₂), especially when PaO₂ falls below \~60 mmHg.

They respond rapidly to hypoxia and provide the primary ventilatory drive in low-oxygen states.

CO₂ and pH are mainly sensed by central chemoreceptors.

| Feature | Peripheral | Central

| ------- | ---------- | -------

| Location | Carotid & aortic bodies | Medulla

| Primary stimulus |  ↓ O₂ | ↑ CO₂ (via pH)

| Speed | Rapid | Slower

| Role in COPD | Important | Blunted

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A farmer presents to the emergency department with diarrhea, sweating, excessive lacrimation, and salivation. Regarding the management of this condition, which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Atropine is used as an antidote for OP poisoning
Pralidoxime has a role in reversing the enzyme in carbamate poisoning
Succinylcholine use is avoided in rapid sequence intubation
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms are characteristic of a cholinergic crisis caused by organophosphate (OP) or carbamate poisoning. A critical pharmacological difference is that carbamates bind reversibly to the acetylcholinesterase enzyme, which typically results in a shorter duration of toxicity. In contrast, organophosphates bind irreversibly through a process called "aging." Atropine is the essential antidote for both to block muscarinic symptoms (Option B). Pralidoxime (Option C) is generally considered ineffective or controversial in carbamate poisoning because the bond is already reversible, and it is primarily used for OP poisoning. Succinylcholine (Option D) is avoided because its metabolism depends on pseudocholinesterase, which is inhibited by these poisons, leading to prolonged muscle paralysis. Therefore, the statement claiming carbamates bind irreversibly is incorrect

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with a habit of biting his lips and fingers and you observe missing portions of fingers on his left hand. A detailed evaluation reveals delayed developmental milestone.On inquiry, the parents say that two male cousins on the mother's side have similar complaints and have been diagnosed with a genetic disorder. Lab reports reveal hyperuricemia. Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase

The given clinical scenario of self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones, positive family history and hyperuricemia is highly suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. It occurs due to the complete deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT).

Purines can be converted to nucleoside triphosphates to be reused by the body. This pathway is called the salvage pathway for purines.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the HGPRT enzyme. This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine resulting in increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) and decreased levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and guanosine monophosphate (GMP). This causes increased de novo purine synthesis and excessive amounts of uric acid.

The clinical features include compulsive self-mutilation, intellectual disability, delayed milestones, dystonic movements, and hyperuricemia.

Diagnosis is made by deficient HGPRT enzyme activity in the erythrocyte.

The treatment of this condition includes:

* Allopurinol for hyperuricemia

* Behavioral management using restraints for self-mutilation

Partial deficiency of HGPRT leads to Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome.

Other options:

Option A:  Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency results in decreased function of T cells but B cells are normal. This leads to multiple infections, neurologic abnormalities, and autoimmune diseases.

Option C: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency results in the accumulation of adenine. This is oxidized to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine which is insoluble. This leads to urinary calculus formation with crystalluria, urinary tract infections, hematuria, and renal failure.

Option D: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is one of the major causes of severe combined immunodeficiency.

Pearl PF1567: Purine salvage deficiencies: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and Adenosine deaminase deficiency(SCID)

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency(SCID):

Adenosine deaminase enzyme deficiency is one of the major cause of SCID. It is also called as Glanzmann–Riniker syndrome.

SCID patients are usually affected by severe bacterial, viral, or fungal infections early in life and often present with interstitial lung disease, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome:

It is due to deficiency of the enzyme Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase(HGPRT). It is an X-linked recessive disease.

Clinical features:

* Intellectual disability

* Self-mutilation

* Aggression

* Hyperuricemia

* Gout

Treatment:

* Allopurinol

* Febuxostat
questions.learning: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase — The given clinical scenario of self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones, positive family history and hyperuricemia is highly suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: New A patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. An X ray was taken which showed dilated bowel loops as given in the image below. Identify the segment involved.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Jejenum

The given clinical scenario and X-ray suggest intestinal obstruction with involvement of the jejunum. The obstructed bowel loops are central in location and show valvulae connivente (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel). The presence of valvulae connivente with gas bubbles trapped between them gives a string of beads/ ladder effect. Radiological features of bowel obstruction

* Small bowel - The involved dilated segments are straight and mostly centrally located.

* Jejunum - It is characterized by the presence of valvulae conniventes with gas bubbles trapped between them. This gives a string of beads/ ladder effect.

* Ileum - The distal ileal obstruction is usually featureless.

* Caecum - A rounded gas shadow in the right iliac fossa is suggestive of caecal obstruction.

* Large bowel - The presence of haustrations is a feature of large bowel obstruction. Haustral folds are not regular. They are not present in the caecum and do not traverse the whole diameter of the bowel.
questions.learning: Jejenum — The given clinical scenario and X-ray suggest intestinal obstruction with involvement of the jejunum. The obstructed bowel loops are central in location and show valvulae connivente (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The following pelvic X-ray was seen in a patient. All the following signs will be present except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gaenslen sign

The X-ray shows:

• DDH of hip with shallow acetabulum and displaced femoral head.
• DDH presents with:

o   Ortolani sign: palpable “clunk” on reduction of dislocated hip

o   Barlow sign: hip can be dislocated with adduction and posterior pressure

o   Narath sign: increased distance between greater trochanter and pubic symphysis (proximal migration of femur)

Gaenslen sign is not associated with DDH; it is used to detect sacroiliac joint pathology (eg, sacroiliitis).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How does the World Health Organization (WHO) define blindness?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides a standardized definition for blindness to facilitate global health comparisons and resource allocation. According to these criteria, blindness is defined as a visual acuity (VA) of less than (Snellen) or its equivalent in the better eye with the best possible correction. This means the individual cannot count fingers from a distance of 3 meters. Additionally, a visual field of less than 10 degrees from the point of fixation in the better eye is also classified as blindness. A visual acuity of less than but better than or equal to (Option B) is categorized as "severe visual impairment" rather than blindness. Standardizing this definition is critical for programs like "VISION 2020: The Right to Sight" to monitor the prevalence of avoidable blindness. Properly identifying these thresholds ensures that public health interventions are targeted toward those with the greatest need for rehabilitative or surgical services

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child is evaluated for recurrent infections. Physical examination shows that the child’s height-for-age is markedly reduced, with a Z-score below −2 standard deviations. The parents report a history of inappropriate feeding practices. What is the correct term used to describe this nutritional condition?
questions.explanation: In pediatric nutritional assessment, stunting is specifically defined as low height-for-age. A height Z-score of less than -2 standard deviations below the WHO growth standard median confirms the diagnosis. Stunting results from chronic, long-term malnutrition and recurrent infections, often due to improper feeding practices over a prolonged period. Wasting (Option D) is defined as low weight-for-height and reflects acute, recent malnutrition. Kwashiorkor (Option B) is a severe form of protein-energy malnutrition characterized by edema and skin changes. While malnutrition (Option C) is the broad umbrella term, "stunting" is the specific anthropometric term used to describe a permanent deficit in height resulting from early childhood neglect. Stunting is associated with irreversible long-term consequences, including impaired cognitive development and reduced physical work capacity in adulthood
questions.learning: In pediatric nutritional assessment, stunting is specifically defined as low height-for-age. A height Z-score of less than -2 standard deviations below the WHO growth standard median confirms the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman presents to the gynecology OPD with foul-smelling frothy vaginal discharge, severe itching, and a strawberry cervix on examination. Which statement regarding the causative organism is incorrect?
options: It exists in cyst and trophozoite form
The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM or PEM
The treatment of choice is metronidazole
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of frothy vaginal discharge and a "strawberry cervix" is pathognomonic for trichomoniasis, caused by the flagellated protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. A key biological characteristic of T. vaginalis is that it exists ONLY in the trophozoite form and does not have a cyst stage. It is an obligate parasite (Option B) that cannot survive long outside the human body. The gold standard for definitive diagnosis remains culture on specialized media such as Diamond's, CPLM, or PEM (Option C). The treatment of choice is indeed Metronidazole (Option D), and it is essential to treat sexual partners simultaneously. Therefore, the statement regarding a cyst form is incorrect as it applies to other protozoa like Entamoeba or Giardia, but not to Trichomonas
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of frothy vaginal discharge and a "strawberry cervix" is pathognomonic for trichomoniasis, caused by the flagellated protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In which type of cataract surgery is suturing with 10-0 nylon commonly performed?
questions.explanation: In Extracapsular Cataract Extraction (ECCE), a relatively large limbal incision (approximately 8–10 mm) is made to remove the lens nucleus in one piece. Because of the size of this incision, multiple interrupted or continuous sutures—typically using fine 10-0 nylon—are mandatory to ensure a watertight closure and prevent complications like iris prolapse or endophthalmitis. Phacoemulsification (Option A) utilizes a very small incision (2.2–3.0 mm) that is typically "self-sealing" and requires no sutures. Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (MSICS) (Option D) also uses a self-sealing tunnel incision (usually 6 mm) that generally does not require suturing. ICCE (Option C) is an older technique where the entire lens and capsule are removed through a large incision, also requiring sutures, but it is rarely performed today compared to ECCE. While Phaco is the global gold standard, ECCE remains an important technique for extremely hard (black or brown) cataracts where ultrasound energy may be insufficient or unsafe
questions.learning: In Extracapsular Cataract Extraction (ECCE), a relatively large limbal incision (approximately 8–10 mm) is made to remove the lens nucleus in one piece.
